In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, Unit
items.text:
Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
- Published
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.
In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.
United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.
The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.
The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.
Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.
Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.
The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".
The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

items.summary:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Ant
items.text:
In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
- Published
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 lines long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.
A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

items.text:
Fossil fuel talks deadlock pushes COP31 climate summit into overtime
EU warns COP31 risks turning into a ‘fossil summit’ as critical climate commitments are omitted from the draft deal.
The COP31 climate summit has gone into overtime as nearly 200 countries remain deadlocked over a draft deal that no longer mentions fossil fuels.
The two-week talks in Antalya, Turkiye, were due to end on Friday, when a late closing session approved some technical matters, but not the wider political deal.
“We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet,” COP31 President and Turkiye’s Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates.
Environmental groups tracking the two-week conference said the meeting lacked ambition to address the worsening climate crisis and was on track to be the “worst COP ever”.
A third draft is expected on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.
The fossil fuel fight
An opening draft from cohost and lead negotiator Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Oil producers have also resisted similar language at past talks, including at COP28 in 2023. The revised text also dropped a $120bn target for money to help poorer countries adapt to climate change.
The European Union said the draft “risks turning this climate COP into a fossil summit”. Panama, which signed a letter with a dozen other countries demanding “a clear transition away from fossil fuels”, threatened to walk away from the talks.
“It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover document that does not even mention fossil fuels, and we simply will not put up with it,” Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, told a news conference.
Other contested points
The draft proposes raising the share of the world’s final energy consumption that comes from electricity to 35 percent by 2035. It does not say the power must come from renewables, and some countries want the target to say “clean”.
Some countries also reject a push to expand carbon capture, a technology that traps emissions from power plants and factories. They say it is costly and unproven, and could let polluters keep burning oil and gas.
“We want to see the references to false solutions removed,” said Vanuatu’s climate minister, Ralph Regenvanu.
Developing countries are angry that rich nations are falling short on climate finance. “We didn’t come here to beg,” said Ghana’s environment minister, Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings.
Tough backdrop
A UN report last month found the world is set to pass the 1.5-degree-Celsius (2.7F) warming limit set under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
The United States, the largest historical emitter, is absent for a second year after President Donald Trump ended climate cooperation.
The US-Israel war on Iran and higher living costs have also drawn attention away from the talks.
Environmental groups say the summit lacks ambition.
“This has been the worst COP ever,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the think tank Power Shift Africa.

items.title: Bayern Munich confirm Harry Kane ‘out for next few months’ with ankle injury
items.summary:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.
Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied
items.text:
Bayern Munich have confirmed Harry Kane will be “out for the next few months” with ankle ligament damage sustained in their 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday.
Kane was substituted after 20 minutes of the Bundesliga game, having been left limping after a challenge from the Cologne defender Joël Schmied. The Ballon d’Or winner was substituted with the returning Bayern coach, Vincent Kompany, saying afterwards that the injury would take “months” rather than weeks to heal.
A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”
The Tottenham loanee Mikey Moore fired the visitors ahead before Kane’s injury, but Bayern levelled things up when Nathaniel Brown scored before the break. Bayern also lost Michael Olise to injury for the second half, and Said El Mala missed an excellent late chance to earn Cologne’s first win at Bayern since 2009.
The 33-year-old may face a race to be fit for the Nations League quarter-finals, with the first leg in Norway taking place on 27 March – just over four months away. The Bayern sporting director, Max Eberl, said on Friday that club doctors were “currently discussing whether or not to recommend surgery” for Kane’s injury.
Part of Kane’s recovery period will come during the Bundesliga’s winter break from 20 December to 8 January. He will, however, miss Champions League games away to Lille next week and at home to Slavia Prague next month, as well as the January trip to Manchester United and the league phase finale at home to Real Betis.
Kane’s setback adds to an extensive Bayern injury list, with Michael Olise also going off during Friday’s game with a foot contusion. Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry, Alphonso Davies, Ismael Saibari and Manuel Neuer were already unavailable, leaving Kompany short of options for a busy month of fixtures.
Kompany returned from his own month-long absence for Friday’s game with his arm in a sling, having dislocated his shoulder when he collapsed on a training pitch in October. The Belgian was taken to hospital for meningeal irritation treatment after his collapse, and has been recovering at home.
Cologne took a surprise lead with 12 minutes gone as Moore started and finished an excellent break. The teenage winger pounced on a mislaid Olise pass and drove forward, finding Linton Maina who laid off for El Mala, whose no-look backheel pass allowed Moore to round keeper Jonas Urbig before sliding the ball home.
Kane was then brought down in the Cologne box from behind by defender Schmied, who got the ball first but clattered into Kane’s left leg in his follow-through. Kane’s penalty appeals were waved away, but he was left visibly limping and received treatment on his ankle before being replaced by Tom Bischof on the 20-minute mark.
The hosts levelled 17 minutes later as full-back Brown sliced a low shot into the bottom-right corner, but suffered another blow just before the break when Olise went down. The France star did not return to the field for the second half, and was seen leaving the stadium shortly after on crutches – but it appears unlikely he will miss a significant amount of time.
Just before the hour mark, El Mala and Maina forced a spectacular double save from Urbig just before the hour mark. Recent Germany call-up El Mala then had a golden chance to put Cologne in front with eight minutes to go when one-on-one with Urbig – but he cut his close-range shot inches wide of the post.
Now a point behind Bayern, chasers Borussia Dortmund can move into outright first in the table if they win at bottom club Mönchengladbach on Saturday. Freiburg can also move level on points with Bayern if they can defeat promoted Elversberg.
Kane earlier this month signed a new deal with the Bundesliga giants until June 2029 which is reportedly worth in excess of £400,000 a week, making him the highest-paid player in Europe before bonuses.
Since arriving from Tottenham three years ago, Kane has bagged an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances, helping Bayern win a league and cup double last season.

items.summary:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of
items.text:
French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
- Published
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".
  - Published27 November 2020

items.text:
NFL great Brady could buy Chelsea stake
- Published
American football great Tom Brady is looking to invest in Chelsea through ownership group Clearlake Capital.
The seven-time Super Bowl winner has recently divested his stake in Championship club Birmingham City, which he bought into following Tom Wagner's Knighthead Capital takeover in 2023.
It now appears he could move into Chelsea, where he has a positive relationship with influential co-owner Behdad Eghbali, having been a star guest at the after-party following the club's Club World Cup triumph in 2025.
Brady would have no voting rights or control at Chelsea, although the ownership group could look to appoint him to the board if it suited all parties.
The move is not said to be linked to Todd Boehly and Mark Walter's £950m sale of their stakes to Clearlake Capital, which must be completed by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss remains a significant minority stakeholder at Stamford Bridge.
The investment is also not part of a funding round, according to senior sources, and is not intended to dilute Clearlake Capital's control.
However, other interested parties are said to have approached them about investing since Boehly and Walter agreed a deal to leave.
Former quarterback Brady, a three-time NFL most valuable player, retired in February 2023 after 23 seasons in the NFL, having won six Super Bowl rings with the New England Patriots and one with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.
Following the end of his playing career he acquired a stake in the Las Vegas Raiders, while also becoming part of the ownership group of the WNBA's Las Vegas Aces.
On top of that, Brady's commitments include him being a lead NFL analyst for Fox Sports.

items.summary:
Lauren Price makes boxing history for Wales with first undisputed championship win as she shuts out Michaela Kotaskova
Lauren Price beat Michaela Kotaskova at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff to become the undisputed welterweight world champion; winning a unanimous decision saw Price add the WBO title t
items.text:
Lauren Price makes boxing history for Wales with first undisputed championship win as she shuts out Michaela Kotaskova
Lauren Price beat Michaela Kotaskova at the Utilita Arena in Cardiff to become the undisputed welterweight world champion; winning a unanimous decision saw Price add the WBO title to the WBA, WBC and IBF belts she already had; Price is Wales' first undisputed champion in the four-belt era
Friday 20 November 2026 23:28, UK
Lauren Price made history for Welsh boxing when she beat Michaela Kotaskova to become the undisputed welterweight world champion.
With a unanimous decision victory over Kotaskova at the Utilita Arena, a shutout 100-90 for all three judges, Price added the vacant WBO 147lbs title to the IBF, WBC and WBA belts.
An Olympic gold medallist in 2021, Price is the first Welsh boxer to become an undisputed world champion in the four-belt era.
The first female British champion too, the skilful southpaw started busily and with intent. She planted stiff left crosses through the middle, that back hand arrowing between Kotaskova's gloves and catching her chin.
Price stamped her authority on the fight, teeing off with flurries. Firm right hooks shook Kotaskova.
Price moved backwards and off to the sides, leaving the tall Kotaskova striding after her. When the Czech planted her feet to swing wildly, Price beat her to the punch with rapid, accurate salvoes.
Kotaskova absorbed hits and marched forward. But her grim efforts yielded scant result and in the fifth round Kotaskova was badly cut by her left eye after an accidental head clash.
She didn't let that dissuade her but Price continued to dictate the action. In the sixth round the Welsh star dug her feet into the canvas to uncork a hard three-punch combination.
In the next round Price hammered the body once more and brought a right hook back up to the head. She moved away well, as Kotaskova ran out of ideas.
A swiping left hook from Price knocked Kotaskova away. Price ground in draining body shots.
Kotaskova desperately sought to apply pressure in the 10th and final round, but she could not pin the Welsh star down, who picked her off and raised her arms to celebrate in the final seconds before the bell to end it.
Kotaskova had made her work but the decision was still a formality, and a reflection of Price's dominance.
"I just feel so lucky to be Welsh," Price told the BBC. "This goes out to you lot, thank you, it means the world.
"Nothing really tops that. Winning the Olympic gold medal, that's a dream from the age of eight.
"As a professional everyone's dream is to become undisputed and I can honestly say I've ticked every accolade there is in boxing. I'm not finished. I've got many years left in me.
"It's all about the big fights now and it's all about that legacy," she continued. "I'm undisputed at welterweight but I can move up.
"I just want to stay on this journey with these fans."

items.text:
Harry Kane: England and Bayern Munich striker set to miss three months with ankle injury
Harry Kane was withdrawn after 20 minutes of Bayern's Bundesliga game against Cologne; the injury comes days after the England captain became his country's most-capped player; Kane won the Ballon d'Or earlier this month; Michael Olise also taken off injured in 1-1 draw
Friday 20 November 2026 22:32, UK
Harry Kane is expected to be sidelined for three months after suffering an ankle injury during Bayern Munich's Bundesliga game with Cologne on Friday.
Sky Germany report Bayern sporting director Max Eberl confirmed shortly after the 1-1 draw that Kane had suffered a "syndesmosis ligament tear" - also known as a high ankle sprain.
The Ballon d'Or winner - who became England's most-capped player last week - was seeking a first goal in five matches for the Bundesliga leaders.
- How Bayern Munich fell in love with Harry Kane
- Kane becomes first Englishman to win Ballon d'Or for 25 years

However, as he looked to latch on to Michael Olise's deflected low cross at the back post, Cologne full-back Joel Schmied got to the ball first and clattered into Kane's left leg in his follow through.
Kane immediately clutched his lower leg and writhed in pain for a few moments before gingerly getting back to his feet, but he was a virtual bystander for the next couple of minutes.
The 33-year-old gestured to the dugout, sunk to the turf and then received treatment on his ankle before making way for Tom Bischof, limping off the field alongside two physios.
Kane had a quick exchange with Vincent Kompany, who was back in the Bayern hot-seat for the first time in six matches after being diagnosed with meningeal irritation last month, before heading down the tunnel.
To make matters worse for Bayern, Olise was also taken off injured at half-time.
How many games will Kane miss?
A three-month period on the sidelines would rule Kane out for 11 Bundesliga games, the DFB-Pokal round of 16 tie against Hertha Berlin, as well as all four of Bayern's remaining Champions League league phase matches.
Providing his recovery goes to plan, that would give the striker just over a month to prepare for England's Nations League quarter-final.
The Three Lions face Norway in Oslo in the first leg on March 27, before the return leg at Wembley on March 30.

United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they
items.text:
US lawmakers push for tougher AI chip rules amid China export crackdown
Washington has new rules restricting remote access to advanced US AI chips, but lawmakers want more.
United States lawmakers say more regulations are needed to protect advanced AI chips once they leave the country, even as they support the recently imposed chip export controls.
This week, the US Department of Commerce announced a new rule to restrict how advanced US AI chips can be accessed remotely in the wake of the previous Nvidia CEO’s affair with a suspected spy for Beijing. The move would close what officials described as a loophole that allows Chinese companies to tap into computing power through data centres in third countries, bypassing US restrictions.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), which sits under the Commerce Department, said the rule would require data centre customers in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Brazil to apply for a special licence to buy advanced chips from US companies, including Nvidia, because they “present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion”.
“The export controls should have been in place, certainly,” Democratic Representative Pramila Jayapal told Al Jazeera. “I also think it’s a bigger conversation about who dominates the AI market. We should not have this consolidation of all the AI knowledge in a couple of companies because that poses an enormous threat on multiple levels, including national security.”
In October, Jayapal introduced a policy framework that would require every AI company operating in the US to obtain a federal charter in an effort to protect the public interest.
The AI charter, the framework says, is modelled after existing regulatory frameworks, combining the round-the-clock federal oversight, strict safety mandates, and structural separation built into national bank charters with the rigorous pre-release federal testing required for nuclear materials and dangerous weapons.
The framework also bans AI companies from building empires, releasing risky models, stealing through surveillance, exploiting workers, or causing harm.
Lutnick probe
Jayapal is a member of the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee, whose ranking members announced a probe to determine whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had blocked efforts to stop the suspected smuggling of advanced Nvidia chips to China.
Lutnick is facing criticism, including from members of US President Donald Trump’s cabinet, for allegedly refusing to impose restrictions on companies accused of diverting advanced chips to China, including Megaspeed, which is at the centre of the Nvidia probe.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee also announced that the Trump administration had approved exports of 879,000 chips manufactured by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026.
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress in January, expressed a desire to better limit chip exports amid growing scrutiny over the extent to which US computing power may have reached China.
“I’m excited to get these gavels and go through the investigatory work that’s necessary, but also to rein in and regulate artificial intelligence. The very industry is asking to be regulated by Congress,” Democratic Representative Everton Blair told Al Jazeera.
‘Tremendous penalties’
The US accounts for nearly 75 percent of the world’s AI spending and computing power, followed by China.
US tech giants, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, operate nearly 90 major AI computing hubs globally, according to an Oxford University study. The same research found that US companies were building 63 AI computing hubs outside the country as of 2025.
Stephen Ezell, vice president for global innovation policy at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation (ITIF), said Washington would find it difficult to enforce the BIS rule.
China has rejected the restriction, calling it “economic coercion” by the US.
On Friday, after his return to the White House from his historic trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian presidents in Shenzhen, China, Trump promised to prohibit US companies from developing data centres in other countries.
“We’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it,” Trump said.
It was unclear what Trump had envisioned, or how he would enforce it.
At the same time, he urged Americans to embrace data centres in their neighbourhoods, despite communities’ increasing concern about the centres’ impact on quality of life, environment and energy demands.
Analysts say the recent export regulation has likely not had much effect on China’s efforts to become the global leader in AI semiconductor chips.
“China does not want to depend upon American or other foreign semiconductors. They want to develop them themselves, and one can argue that we’ve slowed them down a little bit with our export controls, but in no way has it changed China’s aspirations to become the global AI semiconductor chip leader,” Ezell said on Al Jazeera’s This Is America.

items.title: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
items.summary:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the y
items.text:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

items.title: Paris police officers sentenced to prison over 2020 beating of Black man
items.summary:
Paris police officers sentenced to prison over 2020 beating of Black man
A Paris court on Friday sentenced three policemen to serve time over the 2020 beating of Black music producer Michel Zecler, a rare such ruling. The assault, which was captured on camera, sparked nationwide outrage and renewed
items.text:
Paris police officers sentenced to prison over 2020 beating of Black man
A Paris court on Friday sentenced three policemen to serve time over the 2020 beating of Black music producer Michel Zecler, a rare such ruling. The assault, which was captured on camera, sparked nationwide outrage and renewed scrutiny of police violence and racism in France.
A French court on Friday sentenced three policemen to serve time over the brutal beating of a Black music producer in 2020, in a rare such ruling in a police brutality case.
The first two were sentenced to five years in jail, including three and three-and-a-half years suspended, for the assault on Michel Zecler, whom the officers had accused of not wearing a face mask during the Covid-19 pandemic.
The third was sentenced to five years, four of which were suspended, and was to serve the one year with an ankle tag instead of behind bars.
The assault on Zecler, now 47, triggered renewed outrage in France over police violence, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions claim is limited to isolated cases.
Campaigners and rights groups saw the case as further evidence of what they see as the French police's systemic racism, in a country where they say ethnic minorities receive far harsher treatment than white people.
Read moreParis police officers suspended over brutal beating of Black man
Police brutality has also been thrust back into the spotlight by the student-led protests in recent weeks, including after a 14-year-old lost most of his teeth when a police officer appeared to fire a grenade at him at very close range.
Police stopped Zecler outside his Paris studio on November 21, 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask and suspecting him of cannabis use.
They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio's security cameras.
The medical report noted craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to perform his job for 45 days.
In their arrest report, the officers claimed the producer had hit them and tried to seize a truncheon, a version of events refuted by the camera footage that French media website Loopsider released several days later.
Few cases of alleged police brutality make it to criminal court in France, as most are dealt with internally.
In another case to go before a judge, a French policeman is to be tried over shooting dead 17-year-old Nahel Merzouk at point-blank range in June 2023 outside Paris. Video footage also contradicted the police's version of events in that incident, sparking nationwide protests.
Read moreFrench policeman to be tried over 2023 killing of teen Nahel
Guilty verdicts in alleged police brutality cases are rare.
In 2024, a judge gave suspended jail sentences to three officers who inflicted irreversible rectal injuries on a black man, Theo Luhaka, during a stop-and-search in 2017.
Young men "perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa" are four times more likely to be stopped than the rest of the population, according to a report last year by France's rights chief.
They are 12 times more likely to be subjected to more severe measures, including being frisked during checks, it said after a survey of more than 5,000 people.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.title: Lampard calls for fairness after Coventry penalty row
items.summary:
Lampard calls for fairness after Coventry penalty row
- Published
Frustrated Frank Lampard has called for fairness from officials after Coventry were denied a clear penalty - with the boss claiming it got less coverage because they are a smaller club.
The Sky Blues were furious they were not awarded
items.text:
Lampard calls for fairness after Coventry penalty row
- Published
Frustrated Frank Lampard has called for fairness from officials after Coventry were denied a clear penalty - with the boss claiming it got less coverage because they are a smaller club.
The Sky Blues were furious they were not awarded a first-half spot kick in the 3-1 defeat at Everton before the international break.
James Tarkowski pulled Caleb Yirenkyi's hair in the area but was not penalised by referee Stuart Attwell or video assistant referee (VAR) Timothy Wood.
The Key Match Incidents Panel, which assesses the contentious incidents and whether the officials got them correct, this week voted unanimously that the Sky Blues should have been awarded a penalty.
It would have given Coventry a chance to go 1-0 up, before Yann Gboho fired them ahead early in the second half - only for Everton to recover.
Thierno Barry scored twice, and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall added the third for the hosts but Lampard also argued because the decisions went against Coventry they were not given the same scrutiny as others.
"I'm not sure how much coverage it got in the days after, maybe because we're Coventry, move on everybody," said Lampard, with defeat leaving them 17th in the Premier League.
"We lost a game and we move on but we need fairness.
"If the decision is rightly for us give it to us, I'm not asking for anything beyond that.
"We're not asking for anything beyond fairness to get the right decision, to spend enough time on the decision. We're fighting on so many levels here as a promoted club.
"We've been out of the league for 25 years, we've got a lack of experience in the squad because the boys that have come up haven't played in the Premier League.
"Financially what we do in the league, in terms of where we are and the wages, we know we're right at the bottom and all these things, so we're fighting for every moment and we're grafting a lot and you just really do want that fairness."
Coventry also felt they could have had a penalty when Taiwo Awoniyi was tripped by Vitalii Mykolenko early in the second half and that Everton striker Thierno Barry handled the ball before scoring his crucial second goal.
Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb has spoken with Lampard and Coventry sporting director Dean Austin over the decisions, with Webb acknowledging the wrong decision over the hair pull.
The hair pulling guidance was relaxed in the summer with referees advised it would not necessarily mean a straight red card, although sources accept the softening of guidance could lead to more grey areas at times - something Lampard disputed in this instance.
"There was no grey area with this, they missed it. They watched the video and they missed it," said Lampard, before Saturday's visit of Crystal Palace.
"They watched it for a good minute and a half. I've seen it and I've heard the footage. They missed it completely.
"I got fined once for talking about a referee as manager of Everton and I hate talking about it but when you work for the club you feel the pain yourself.
"You fight all week for a result and there's something with real clarity that can't really be missed. The Tarkowski one, it can't be missed at this level.
"So that's quite hard to take as well because we all saw it on the Sky broadcast pretty much straight away. So I respect and appreciate Howard Webb saying that to myself and Dean in a meeting afterwards.
"I like that side of things. Howard Webb was, when I was playing, one of the best referees in the world and I think he's very good at his job. He was upfront about the fact they missed it."

Australia captain Pat Cummins has been scrutinised after Cameron Bancroft's damning account of the 2018 sandpaper scandal; Josh Hazlewood defended Cummins in a new interview and que
items.text:
Josh Hazlewood defends Pat Cummins over 'Sandpapergate' and backs Australia's Test captain to continue after "pile-on"
Australia captain Pat Cummins has been scrutinised after Cameron Bancroft's damning account of the 2018 sandpaper scandal; Josh Hazlewood defended Cummins in a new interview and questioned how the Test team would react if he was forced to step away as captain
Friday 20 November 2026 22:10, UK
Josh Hazlewood has defended Pat Cummins over a “pile-on” around Sandpapergate and refused to rule out boycotting the Test team if he is made to step down as captain.
Hazlewood became the latest player to break their silence over his involvement in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, which has dominated headlines again since comments from Australian team-mate Usman Khawaja in his new autobiography 'Sabr' claimed the whole team were aware of using sandpaper.
Cameron Bancroft plunged Australian cricket into further turmoil with a 4,000-word statement, backing claims "the whole team" knew about the plot and contradicting strong denials Cummins offered in his press conference a few days earlier.
- Pat Cummins faces fresh scrutiny over Sandpapergate claims
- Sandpapergate LIVE! Latest reaction to ball-tampering scandal
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Cummins had branded Khawaja's testimony "complete and utter nonsense" and "100 per cent wrong", leading Bancroft to go public with his story, while Australia's Test captain has had his future speculated after how he has handled the incident.
"It feels like it's been a bit of a pile on the last few days [at Cummins] from different people," Hazlewood told CodeSports. "I want to back Pat [Cummins] and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he's done for the last five or six years in particular as captain.
"To get the group where it is now and in a position where something like that [sandpaper] is never going to happen again - I think is just a remarkable job. He's a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you'd hear the same response.
"If we turned up for the first Test and he wasn't the captain and it was someone else, honestly, I don't know how that would go."
Australia are next in Test action when they face New Zealand in a four-match series, beginning on December 9 in Perth, where Hazlewood would consider whether to feature if Cummins was no longer captain.
"I'd have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you'd have to think about it, yeah," Hazlewood added.

items.title: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
items.summary:
Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
- Published
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency said
items.text:
Denmark accuses Russia of plotting to assassinate US-Ukrainian rapper
- Published
Denmark has accused Russian intelligence services of plotting to assassinate a Ukrainian-American near Copenhagen, saying they had "planned" and "initiated" the attempt.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency said it had stopped individuals who were intending to kill the person, named by Danish media as rapper Kyivstoner, at a concert in September. Two people were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service, and pleaded not guilty.
Denmark's foreign minister said Russia's defence attaché will now be expelled.
Russia's Embassy in Denmark called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and said Copenhagen failed to provide evidence of Moscow's involvement.
In a statement posted on social media, the embassy claimed a "Danish model" had emerged, which it described as a "Russian trace" allegedly being discovered and "exploited for a propaganda spectacle". It accused Denmark of "provocations" intending to "frighten the Danish population in order to justify... a prolonged confrontation with Russia".
Russian state media cites the foreign ministry in Moscow as saying it will respond to the expulsion of its official "accordingly".
Danish media named the target of the assassination attempt as the rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasiliev.
Denmark's security and intelligence agency (PET) said the individuals who allegedly tried to assassinate him were associated with a banned Danish gang named Loyal to Familia. The group is "known for extensive, serious and violent criminal activity", according to the agency.
PET, which worked with police on the case, said three individuals were stopped while travelling by car near the music venue where Kyivstoner was set to perform on 25 September.
Firearms and knives were found in the vehicle, PET said.
Since then, two people linked to the case have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service.
Both individuals pleaded not guilty to the charges, local media reported.
In July, Russia's FSB security service accused Vasiliev and the Ukrainian authorities of organising a "terrorist attack" on military facilities and personnel in Russia. The rapper denied this allegation on social media.
In a statement on Friday, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the alleged assassination attempt was Russian "intimidation" and an attempt to make Denmark "waver" in its support for Ukraine.
Russia's defence attaché must leave the country within seven days, Rasmussen said.
He also said Denmark wants the EU to restrict the ability of Russians to travel throughout Europe, saying even though Denmark is already very reluctant to issue visas, Russians can still get a Schenegen visa in another country and travel to Denmark. Denmark wants these visas to apply only in the country that has issued them, he added.

Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, w
items.text:
Shevchenko lying about drugs test claims - Mudryk
- Published
Mykhailo Mudryk has accused Ukraine legend Andriy Shevchenko of lying about the circumstances surrounding the winger's positive drugs test as his dispute with the country's football federation continues.
Tottenham Hotspur winger Mudryk, who is on a season-long loan from Chelsea, was suspended from November 2024 to July 2026 after testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.
In an interview on Wednesday, Mudryk said he blames the Ukrainian Association of Football (UAF) for his failed drugs test and subsequent ban, believing it entered his system while on international duty.
In response, Shevchenko, the UAF president, accused Mudryk's representatives of repeatedly asking for a UAF employee to "falsely" take the blame for his failed test.
Former Chelsea and AC Milan striker Shevchenko also said Mudryk's comments amounted to a "baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally", and called on the player to retract his words.
In a statement on Friday, Mudryk refuted Shevchenko's accusation, saying it was a "lie" and that "neither I nor my representatives made any such request".
Mudryk has also accused the UAF of attempting to mislead his team's investigation into the reasons behind his failed test, and claims to have evidence proving it.
"My team and I repeatedly asked the UAF to help establish how I might have been exposed to meldonium and who, if anyone, might have been responsible," said Mudryk.
"In several letters to the UAF at the time, my lawyers made clear that we were seeking truthful information that could be independently verified. One of those letters was leaked to the media by the UAF earlier today and clearly shows that my lawyers wanted 'true, verifiable and reliable information'.
"Further, the UAF were repeatedly unhelpful and even attempted to mislead my team in order to distance themselves from the case. For example, UAF staff testified at my hearing that I was not using the UAF's supplements and Mr Shevchenko has repeated that assertion in his statement - but I have WhatsApp messages that prove that I was using their products during their training camps. That is, I have evidence to prove that their repeated assertions are wrong."
Mudryk also said the UAF was "repeatedly slow" to respond to requests from his team and "withheld important information and documents" from his lawyers.
BBC Sport has contacted the UAF for comment.

items.title: 'Licence to kill': French parliament adopts police shootings law slammed by activists
items.summary:
'Licence to kill': French parliament adopts police shootings law slammed by activists
French senators gave final approval on Friday to controversial legislation granting police officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when using firearms, fulfilling a long-standing demand of the far right e
items.text:
'Licence to kill': French parliament adopts police shootings law slammed by activists
French senators gave final approval on Friday to controversial legislation granting police officers a presumption of legitimate self-defence when using firearms, fulfilling a long-standing demand of the far right even as weeks of student-led protests have thrust the issue of police brutality back into the spotlight. Left-wing lawmakers have vowed to challenge the bill before France's Constitutional Council.
France's parliament on Friday granted further protection to law enforcement officers using their weapons, after alleged police brutality was thrust back into the spotlight in student-led protests in recent weeks.
Backers of the new bill – including the government and the party of far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen – say the law is needed to avoid officers being automatically suspected of using disproportionate force.
Activists, however, argue it would amount to a "licence to kill", as it would hamper the opening of investigations and make holding security forces accountable even harder in a country where alleged police brutality cases rarely reach a criminal court.
Read moreWounded French protesters to sue interior minister over police brutality
The right-leaning Senate approved the text 205 votes to 110, after the lower house did so in July.
The text stipulates that "when they use their weapons", police officers "are presumed to have acted" within the framework of the law.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Thursday said it would "put an end to the automatic practice of taking into custody a police officer or gendarme who has used their weapon".
He said it would "correct this reflex of systematically calling into question the daily, highly demanding work of our security forces".
But France's Human Rights League has argued it will "block the opening of an investigation in the event of a police shooting following a failure to comply" with a traffic stop "or in the context of crowd control" during protests.
The left has pledged to appeal to the Constitutional Council, the country's highest constitutional authority, to try to halt the bill from coming into law.
Young men "perceived as Arab, Black or from North Africa" are four times more likely to be stopped than the rest of the population, according to a report last year by France's rights chief.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

items.text:
Cristiano Ronaldo edged closer to his 1,000th career goal and missed a first-half penalty as Al Nassr slipped to a 3-1 defeat at Saudi Pro League rivals Al Ahli.
Ronaldo fired Al Nassr in front in the 15th minute, volleying into the far corner from João Félix's assist to register his 986th goal in total and his 10th of the season in all competitions for his club.
- CF7: Portugal move on from Ronaldo with 'special' goal from new No. 7 Forbs
The 41-year-old missed the chance to add to his tally four minutes later when his penalty struck a post after Nawaf Al-Boushail had been brought down in the box.
Ronaldo has now missed both of his penalty attempts for Al Nassr this season, the first time he has failed to score with consecutive penalties in the competition.
Brazilian midfielder Galeno equalized for Al Ahli on the stroke of halftime with a superb effort from outside the penalty area.
Al Ahli went ahead in the second period through Ivan Toney's penalty -- the England striker's 14th goal of the season -- and Brazil defender Roger Ibañez extended the home side's lead four minutes later.
Al Nassr remain third in the table after their second league defeat of the season, while Al Ahli's win lifts them up to fourth, four points behind Ronaldo's side.
Ronaldo's total of 986 includes a disputed goal scored on Oct. 23 against Al Faisaly, which was awarded to the Portuguese forward by the Saudi Pro League but was declared an own goal by stats provider Opta.
The record-holder for men's international appearances and goals, Ronaldo retired from playing for Portugal earlier this month.
Information from PA contributed to this report.

items.title: Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
items.summary:
Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.
United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his
items.text:
Trump defends Putin relationship, warns AI data centres must stay in US
The US president also spoke about the war in Iran and praised trip to China during a wide-ranging news conference.
United States President Donald Trump has praised his recent trip to China and defended the relationship with his “friend” Vladimir Putin, but questioned whether the Russian president was a friend to the US.
On Friday, during a White House news briefing, Trump was asked about the “friend” remark — made during his historic summit with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping earlier this week — and whether the Russian leader was a friend to the US.
“I can’t speak to America,” Trump told reporters before saying Putin had been “very nice” during what he described as the “Russia hoax” investigation after his 2016 presidential campaign.
“I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship. And it’s actually very good,” Trump added as he talked about Russia’s nuclear weapons capabilities.
“I think it gives us a lot of additional strength,” he said.
Trump also spoke about the historic nature of his meeting with Xi and Putin, praising the “first of its kind trilateral peace agreement”.
“We had one of the most momentous international summits in many years. That was the first ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the United States, Russia and China,” Trump said.
No major deals were announced from the summit. But Trump, on Friday, played up his agreement with the two leaders to hold future discussions on nuclear proliferation.
The US president’s remarks came during a wide-ranging news conference, where topics from Iran to artificial intelligence were also discussed.
Trump accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end the war, which is about to mark its 10-month anniversary.
“They want to make a deal, but they don’t want to make a deal that’s acceptable to me,” he said. “We wanna make a real deal, not a fake deal.”
Trump added: “They’ve been b*********** people for 51 years.”
During the news conference, US Vice President JD Vance and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, both possible 2028 presidential contenders, flanked Trump in the White House press briefing room.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Defence Secretary Hegseth, as well as newly minted White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, were also present.
Trump denied he was upset at Vance for blaming US Republicans’ historic midterm losses on the Iran war, saying, “People that work for me, they have a right to their opinion.”
“I thought his statement was fine, except I would have had one other thing that, if we were asked, I would have said that, would you do it again, and absolutely the answer is yes,” Trump said. “I saw that, but no problem there at all.”
No data centres abroad
Vance was asked by reporters about his thoughts on his party’s midterm drubbing.
“I think the president is the one who makes the decision. And the president has said he would do it again,” Vance said. “My goal, in my job, is to support the President of the United States.”
Trump also warned US tech companies against building new artificial intelligence data centres overseas. Otherwise, he said, they will face a “tremendous tax”.
“We’re not allowing data centres to go into other countries because China will take all of them”, Trump said. “And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”
Trump did not provide details on how he would enforce such a policy and said he had not yet told his own officials about his plan.
Al Jazeera has reached out to the White House for comment but has not yet heard back.

Two Salvadoran soldiers have been killed in Haiti while handling explosive material, El Salvador’s army said, markin
items.text:
Two Salvadoran soldiers killed in Haiti while handling explosives
Two others were injured in the explosion, marking the first deaths among troops deployed to Haiti since late October.
Two Salvadoran soldiers have been killed in Haiti while handling explosive material, El Salvador’s army said, marking the first deaths among the roughly 2,500 troops who have been deployed to the country since late October.
Two others were injured in the explosion at one of the camps and are receiving medical care, the army said in a post on X on Friday. It did not reveal the identities of the soldiers.
The deaths come just over a month after El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele sent troops into Haiti, announcing a rescue mission to find four aviation technicians who went missing on October 18 after an attack on their vehicle near the capital, Port-au-Prince.
They were working with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) at the time.
The rescue mission has since broadened into an offensive against Haiti’s gangs, with Salvadoran soldiers working alongside Haitian and international forces.
Salvadoran officials have said they plan to leave once the four missing technicians are found.
Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told The Associated Press news agency earlier this month that the men were dead, although he provided no evidence. El Salvador’s government maintains they are alive.
The Haitian government has suggested it wants the deployment to be extended, and some Haitians took to the streets in Haiti and elsewhere earlier this week in large rallies to express support for the troops and Bukele.
The terms of the bilateral agreement between Haiti and El Salvador have not been revealed publicly, but according to the UN, most Salvadoran soldiers are operating outside the GSF and do not fall under the UN’s reporting mechanism for that mission.
Bukele has been promoting the intervention on social media, posting videos of strikes on homes belonging to gang leaders, and Haitian officials announced earlier this week that they retook control of the national football stadium.
Analysts, however, have questioned how much the Salvadoran deployment has contributed to recent gains and whether those gains would last.
They have also raised concerns about the risk to civilians, citing a lack of transparency around the rules of engagement and how Salvadoran troops are monitored.
On Thursday, Bukele officially launched his bid for a third presidential term. The elections are scheduled for February.

items.text:
Sudan’s war leaves disabled children missing out on education
War forces schools, rehabilitation centres to close, forcing children with disabilities to lose access to education.
Khartoum, Sudan – Four-year-old Muzan Abdelrahman should be preparing to start her educational journey. But she has a hearing impairment, and in Sudan, a country devastated by war, the specialised support she needs to attend school is not available.
When conflict broke out in April 2023, Muzan was only a few months old. Many hoped that the war between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces would be over by now, and Muzan could grow up in an environment where she could get the assistance she needs.
Instead, the war has dragged on, with no end in sight and a humanitarian crisis consuming the country. For Muzan, that means the specialised education and rehabilitation centres she relies on have closed.
“My daughter needs training and continuous follow-up at this age. I try to help her at home, but I am not a specialist and cannot provide the rehabilitation sessions or educational tools she needs,” Muzan’s mother, Abeer Osman, told Al Jazeera. “What frightens me most is that these important years will pass without her getting the opportunity to learn how to communicate and express herself.”
The family’s experience is not isolated. Across Sudan, children with disabilities face obstacles to education and support as institutions are destroyed and families are displaced.
For 14-year-old Mohammed Ahmed, who has a physical disability, getting to school is a challenge, but so is moving around once he arrives. Inaccessible entrances and staircases leave him dependent on others.
“I want to continue my education like the rest of my classmates, but I struggle to reach classrooms and move between them,” Ahmed told Al Jazeera. “What frustrates me most is that I want to learn, but the school environment does not always make that possible.”
“I do not want my disability to deprive me of education or limit my future opportunities,” he added. “I want a school where I can access classrooms and facilities independently and with dignity.”
Generation locked out of education
The war is restricting access to schooling for children across Sudan.
According to UNICEF, at least 8 million school-age children lack access to formal education. As of August, about 30 percent of the country’s schools were not operational, with around 1 percent being used as shelters for displaced people.
But the issue is particularly acute for children with disabilities.
Before the war, Sudan had more than 230 schools for disabled children, according to figures from the UN children’s agency. Many have since closed, although the exact number is uncertain, with no up-to-date information available. Al Jazeera reached out to the Sudanese government for comment, but had not received a response at the time of publishing.
Aisha Abbo remembers the services her son, eight-year-old Ali Hassan, had access to before the war.
Ali, who has Down’s syndrome, used to attend a school for children with disabilities before the war, and received support to develop academic, communication, and social skills.
Those services were provided by the government, but now the same facilities are shut, and private centres are simply too expensive.
“When the war broke out in Khartoum, we could no longer afford to continue his education,” Aisha told Al Jazeera. “We are calling on the government to pay attention to children with disabilities, reopen specialised centres and provide the teachers, specialists, and programmes they need. These children cannot wait until the war ends and life returns to normal. Every day without education or training affects their development and abilities.”
In Khartoum, the impact is clear at the Usratuna Sudanese Association for Children with Disabilities, whose facilities were partly hit by shelling at the start of the war more than three-and-a-half years ago. A projectile struck its classrooms, while damage to buildings and the loss of equipment have made it harder to resume activities.
Badr al-Din Tawfiq, the association’s project manager and representative of its director, said most rehabilitation and support services had stopped because of the war, funding shortages and damage to its facilities.
“At present, we are unable to provide most of our services. We receive children’s registrations and collect their information, but we cannot respond to families’ requests because funding is unavailable. The premises need rehabilitation, the classrooms are unsafe, and we do not have the equipment needed to run rehabilitation programmes,” he told Al Jazeera.
Tawfiq said the association had registered more than 100 children for physiotherapy, speech therapy, behavioural support and vocational rehabilitation. Families had also requested hearing aids and batteries.
“So far, we have been unable to provide the services families are requesting. There are no tools or equipment, and we have not been able to resume our work as it was before the war,” he said.
Rebuilding services
Some activities that do not require funding, including psychosocial support and advocacy, remain possible. The association’s inclusive kindergarten in Dar al-Salam, Omdurman, also continues to operate. But most of its other activities in Khartoum have stopped, while its branches in Zalingei, in central Darfur, and Blue Nile state are no longer operating.
Nagi Mansour, director-general of the Sudanese Coalition for Education for All, said the education of children with disabilities had faced significant challenges even before the war.
“The main problems included poor infrastructure, a shortage of specialised schools and qualified teachers, and a lack of adapted curricula, Braille materials and sign-language teaching resources,” he told Al Jazeera.

Russian ornithologist jailed over donation to Navalny foundation

Helives in Israel, while So
items.text:
Russian ornithologist jailed over donation to Navalny foundation
November 20, 2026
Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.
Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.
On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.
A biologist who dedicated her life to Arctic birds
Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.
Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.
She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.
"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.
Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.
"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."
Protecting birds in Russia and beyond
Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.
Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.
"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."
More than 225 cases over donations to FBK across Russia
In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.
Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.
"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".
For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.
There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.
A year of court hearings and travel restrictions
Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.
Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."
Leaving Russia was never an option
"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.
Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.
Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.
Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.
The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."
This article was originally published in Russian.

items.text:
Seven-time Super Bowl champion quarterback Tom Brady has bought shares in Chelsea soccer club, sources confirmed to ESPN and NFL Network.
The NFL legend left the ownership group of second-tier English club Birmingham City earlier this month after becoming a minority owner with a 3.3% stake.
Defense attorney Alex Spiro is part of Brady's ownership group and helped negotiate the deal.
Brady had also held a position on the club's advisory board via a partnership with Birmingham's owner, Knighthead Capital Management, headed by his friend and business partner Tom Wagner.
Todd Boehly and fellow co-owner Mark Walter sold their stakes in Chelsea this past September in a deal that gives Clearlake Capital full control of the English Premier League club.
Private equity firm Clearlake, led by Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano, previously owned a 61.5% stake in Chelsea, while U.S. businessmen Walter and Boehly each owned 12.83%. Swiss philanthropist Hansjörg Wyss, who also owned a 12.83% stake, remains a partner in the ownership group.
The consortium bought Chelsea for £2.5 billion ($3.3 billion) in 2022 with a further £1.75 billion ($2.3 billion) committed to investment in the club after former owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned because of alleged ties to Russia President Vladimir Putin following the country's invasion of Ukraine.
The Financial Times reported that Walter and Boehly will receive £950 million ($1.3 billion) for their combined stake in a deal that values the club at £5 billion ($6.7 billion) including debt.
Neither Chelsea nor Clearlake Capital has replied to ESPN's request for comment about Brady's purchase of shares.
Brady purchased a 5% minority stake in the Las Vegas Raiders in 2024 after NFL owners unanimously approved the deal.
ESPN's Adam Schefter and James Olley as well as NFL Network's Ian Rapoport contributed to this report.

Pressure? What pressure?
Mauricio Pochettino said the experience of coaching the United States at the World Cup stands him in good stead for taking over Manchester United and trying to resurrect one of soccer's fallen giants.
Pochettino left his role with the U.S. this week to take over a United tha
items.text:
Pressure? What pressure?
Mauricio Pochettino said the experience of coaching the United States at the World Cup stands him in good stead for taking over Manchester United and trying to resurrect one of soccer's fallen giants.
Pochettino left his role with the U.S. this week to take over a United that has not won the Premier League in 13 years and sits in the relegation zone after its worst start in 40 years.
- Pochettino wants input on Man United transfer decisions
- Ex-U.S. coach Arena: Federation doesn't 'have a clue' how to replace Poch
- Pochettino's Man United squad audit: Big calls to make on stars like Fernandes, Rashford
On Friday, he said his time in America means he arrives at Old Trafford at the height of his powers.
"We are much better coaches now after work in the national team like USA because the expectation and the pressure was massive," the Argentine said. "I remember in SoFi [Stadium in California], our first [World Cup] game against Paraguay, the pressure was massive. There was more than 200 celebrity people expecting us to win and to play well and all the country was behind us.
"When you are in the Premier League or in LaLiga or in France, OK, you feel the pressure when you manage these types of clubs, but being there, I promise, was massive pressure."
Pochettino teared up when he farewelled the U.S. program but on Friday he looked in his element at his first news conference in Manchester after two days working with the team.
The former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea manager said he'd missed the day-to-day rhythm of club soccer.
"We were missing a lot," he said.
"I think we are animals of the grass. We like to feel the grass. We need to smell the grass and try to help the players to improve every day. It's true that it's a different job when you are in the national team, but in the same time you learn a lot and I think we are much better coaches now."
Pochettino takes over a club in crisis, on a run of one win in 10 games. United was 18th in the standings and things could get worse with a daunting trip to Liverpool on Sunday.
"It's a race to arrive in condition to be competitive against Liverpool," Pochettino said. "We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, from our own ideas and philosophy in the way that we love to work.
"What we need to do is to be very open-minded ... the players need to buy the idea of what we need to improve. After a few days working the job is to try to find a way from Sunday to perform and to start to get the results that the club historically needs.
"Manchester United need to be in a different place than we are now."
Pochettino led the U.S. men's national team to an 8-0 aggregate win over Haiti in the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals earlier this week in the final act of his two-year stint as coach.
While U.S. Soccer looks for a permanent replacement for Pochettino, U.S. U23 coach Steve Cherundolo will lead the senior team for its December camp, which will entail a friendly with Jamaica on Dec. 13.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

items.title: Kane forced off early with injury in Bayern Munich game
