The England striker was hurt while attempting to get on the end of a deflected Michael Olise cross in front of goal, when Cologn
items.text:
Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane was forced off with an apparent injury to his left leg in the first half of Bayern Munich's Bundesliga clash at home to FC Cologne on Friday.
The England striker was hurt while attempting to get on the end of a deflected Michael Olise cross in front of goal, when Cologne defender Joel Schmied got to the ball first and clattered into Kane's left leg in his follow through.
Kane immediately clutched his lower leg and writhed in pain for a few moments before gingerly getting back to his feet, but he was a virtual bystander for the next couple of minutes.
The 33-year-old gestured to the dugout, sunk to the turf and then received treatment on his ankle before making way for Tom Bischof in the 20th minute, limping off the field alongside two physios.
Cologne were leading 1-0 at the time through a 12th-minute goal from Mikey Moore before Nathaniel Brown equalized in the 37th minute.
The game was Bayern's first since the November international break, in which Kane scored in England's Nations League wins over Spain and Croatia.
Bayern, who had Vincent Kompany back on the sidelines after illness, began the game level on points with Borussia Dortmund at the top of the Bundesliga.
PA contributed to this report.

Müller, 37, who joined the Whitecaps in August 2025 and renewed his deal through next year, is the most
items.text:
Vancouver Whitecaps star Thomas Müller has said that because MLS does not have a promotion/relegation system, the players feel less pressure and the playing style is more "careless, defensively."
Müller, 37, who joined the Whitecaps in August 2025 and renewed his deal through next year, is the most decorated German player of all time. In his 17-year career with Bayern Munich, he won a record 13 Bundesliga titles, six DFB-Pokals, eight Supercups, two Champions Leagues, two UEFA Super Cups, and two FIFA Club World Cups.
When asked to compare MLS to the Premier League or other European Leagues, the 2014 World Cup winner said MLS playing style suffers without promotion and relegation.
"It's difficult to compare because of the system," he told Canadian media outlet Global News. "There is no relegation. There is no big pressure."
He said the lack of pressure means that players lack the attention "to be focused over 90 minutes."
"[In Europe with relegation] The players have maybe no contracts for next year when you go down, so the playing style changes," he said. "When you play a bottom of the league team in Europe they fight for their lives. And sometimes I have the feeling, because of the [MLS] system, the playing style is a little bit more, let's say, optimistic, or careless, defensively.
"So a little bit, just a little bit more, the French would say, laissez faire," he said. "That's maybe good for seeing some nice offensive plays when the games are opening up. When I compare it I see sometimes really, really good individual actions in players.
"What I miss sometimes is maybe the consistency, the good and the bad, the gap is bigger.
"But the good is, we can compare it with golf, you know, even a 10-handicapper has sometimes shots a professional couldn't do better. So it's maybe the free kick, top corner free kick. But the bad shots of a professional would be never that bad. And that's a little bit, sometimes it's more like the attention of the players to be focused over 90 minutes, that's what I see sometimes, they're lacking."
Müller, who helped the Whitecaps into the MLS Cup for the first time in the club's history in 2025, only to be beaten by Inter Miami CF and Lionel Messi, said the fear of relegation helps keep teams sharp.
"[In MLS] There is, oh yeah, we do a rebuild," he said. "Nobody is happy to lose but it's totally different when you fight for getting relegated. Maybe yeah, you lose budget for the next year, the whole club. You lose people working at the club when the budget changes. It's totally different for fans."

items.title: KC Current 'peaking' at right time for NWSL Championship after past failure
items.summary:
WASHINGTON -- One year after the Kansas City Current's historic regular season was cut short in the playoffs, the team finds itself in Saturday's NWSL Championship at Audi Field against the Washington Spirit.
This year's Current was not nearly as dominant as last year's squad, but Kansas City defend
items.text:
WASHINGTON -- One year after the Kansas City Current's historic regular season was cut short in the playoffs, the team finds itself in Saturday's NWSL Championship at Audi Field against the Washington Spirit.
This year's Current was not nearly as dominant as last year's squad, but Kansas City defender Kayla Sharples said the team is better positioned to win a postseason title for the first time.
"Speaking about peaking, I do think it's different but in a better way for this season, because last year we didn't have a lot of adversity," Sharples told reporters on Friday in the press room at Audi Field.
"Winning also helps. Winning consistently masks a lot of things, so this year, we went through those ups and downs and I think that it taught us a lot about resiliency and grit, and how important that is and vital it is in order to be successful at the end of the season.
"So, because of going through that journey this season, I do believe we are peaking at the right time and that almost carries more weight than last season."
Kansas City has won seven straight games entering Saturday's final, including their quarterfinal and semifinal.
Last year's Kansas City Current team was arguably the best in NWSL history, setting several records including most points and most wins in a season while clinching the NWSL Shield earlier than any other team. But that Kansas City team, with two-time league MVP Temwa Chawinga sidelined by an injury, lost in the quarterfinals of the playoffs.
On Saturday, the Current return to Audi Field, where they lost to the Portland Thorns in the 2022 NWSL Championship, their only other appearance in the final. This time, they will face a partisan crowd in Washington's favor.
Kansas City's 2026 campaign started in turmoil for a team with explicit ambitions of being the world's best.
Chris Armas was hired as head coach in the offseason, replacing fan favorite and highly successful Vlatko Andonovski, who shifted exclusively to the sporting director role before leaving the club in September.
Multiple Kansas City starters were recovering from injuries at the beginning of the season, including Chawinga and forward Michelle Cooper.
The Current lost three straight matches in March followed by a 4-0 loss to the Spirit at Audi Field in April that left Kansas City in 14th place after Week 5 of the season.
Armas said after that third straight loss in March that the team was "building a house in a hurricane."
On Friday, ahead of the NWSL Championship match in his first year in charge, Armas said that there was "a lot of adversity and a lot of joy" through that storm.
"It was a stretch of months long of just trying to get the motor going, and it would stall a little bit and get it going, but we were building all along," Armas told reporters. "And teams do go through the phases. You either perform, and then the storm, and then you normalize. You would like to be at your best when it matters most and we think that we are probably at that moment, which means we have a chance."
Included in the Current's seven-game winning streak was a 2-1 win over the Spirit in Kansas City in October.
Armas said he remembers a 3-0 win over the Denver Summit on July 3 in Colorado, and how loud and celebratory the team bus was afterward. That stood out to him as a potential turning point, although he rejected the notion that there was a single inflection point in the season.
"I think if you asked everyone, I'm not sure we'd all have the same answer," Armas said. "I don't think it was one actual moment. The whole season has just been this process. And it oftentimes is, but it has been a story that we've been talking about, that we are the authors of. We have so much in our control."

items.text:
Iran: Lawyers increasingly under pressure
November 20, 2026
UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.
"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts said in a statement in mid-November.
They said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.
Defending the politically persecuted is becoming dangerous
A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.
"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.
In October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.
"The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," said Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers."
Even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.
Yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.
Criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.
Restrictions on the right to choose a lawyer
Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.
According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense."
"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this."
Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.
"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired."
Fear and self-censorship among lawyers
In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.
"This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior."
Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.
Referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect."

items.text:
COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'
- Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20, 2026:
COP32 hosts Ethiopia call the conferences a relay, not a single race
The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.
Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.
Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos said the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.
His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.
Late-night plenary session convenes after delay
Shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.
The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.
"We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and said the world "waits for good news from this room."
But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.
Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.
The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical issues, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.
IN DEPTH — Climate science disputes and disinformation hinder action at COP
Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.
Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar issues complicating COP31 here.
IN DEPTH — US is strong at climate talks despite Trump no-show
The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.
Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.
IN DEPTH — Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar said about climate financing in this report.
Activist Menotti: Europe has 'learned a few of the Trump tactics'
Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.
"We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti said. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more."
He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.
"Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.
"We need the North to act first," Menotti said. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to."
Talks formally enter overtime as scheduled close elapses
You can cross off another box on your COP31 bingo cards, dear readers.
As of the top of this hour, the session has officially gone past its scheduled end time of 1500 GMT/UTC on Friday, or 6 p.m. local time on site in Turkey.
This is something of an annual tradition at COP summits, which are always scheduled to finish at the end of a working week but also almost invariably run into the closing weekend. Delegates and members of the media tend to book their travel plans with this in mind.

items.text:
Russia complains of ‘new Iron Curtain’ as Estonia shuts its borders
Tallinn’s decision to shut road border crossings comes after an attack on a drone manufacturer.
Moscow has accused Estonia of planning to build a “new Iron Curtain”, and promised to respond, after the small Baltic nation formally decided to close all border crossings with Russia to the east and south.
Estonia’s government on Friday approved a preliminary six-month closure of its road border crossings from December 1, and will decide next year whether to extend it.
Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova told a news briefing in Moscow that “should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and diplomatic measures in response to safeguard its national interests.”
“Such moves are tantamount to attempts to erect a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East,” Zakharova added.
In Tallinn on Friday, Estonia’s Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna described the border closure as “an important measure”.
“It will reduce opportunities to exploit cross-border movement to recruit people, conduct influence operations, organise acts of sabotage or circumvent sanctions,” he said.
Estonia, a NATO and EU member and a staunch supporter of Ukraine, first announced the border closure earlier this month, accusing Russia of being behind an attempted arson attack on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Kremlin denied the accusation at the time, saying it was part of what it called a pattern of false allegations levelled against Moscow by European countries.
Estonia’s northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Of the 760,000 people who crossed the Estonia-Russia border this year, 307,000 were Russian nationals, 175,000 were Estonian citizens and 54,000 held Finnish passports, Estonian police data showed.
Rail freight is not affected by the road closure, but remains subject to strict customs checks, Estonia said.

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk believes he can keeping playing for "many more years" - but says he does not yet know whether that will be at Anfield next season.
The 35-year-old centre-back, who has won two Premier League titles and the Champions League during his time at Liverpool, is out of contract in the summer.
He told Sky Sports that, currently, he is uncertain on what will happen beyond this campaign.
"The main thing for me is that I feel good and I'm looking after myself and I still have many more years in my opinion," he said.
"Whatever's going to happen after this season, we'll see.

"At this moment of time, if anyone says that or put out that they know what I'm going to do next season, it's untrue because at this moment of time, speaking to you, I've got no idea either.
"But I'm relaxed with it because if you know me, I only focus on what I can control and that's at the moment the Manchester United game. Then we'll focus to the Champions League and whatever happens in the new year coming, we'll see then.
"But it's been an incredible journey, almost 10 years this summer and it's been a big part of my life and I'll forever be grateful for anything that happened over those years.
"If it's getting extended, we'll see then.
"If not, then I'm going to say goodbyes in the summer."
Asked about how emotional that exit would be, he said: "Well, yeah, probably for me the most and the family because it's been an incredible time.
"But I don't look too far in the future and that's been, in my opinion, also a little bit of a success. I won't change it now either.
"Whatever happens, happens. Let's see."
Van Dijk on his partnership with 'outstanding' Jacquet
Van Dijk has made a positive start to this season, partly thanks to his encouraging connection with new centre-back partner Jeremy Jacquet.
The Dutchman has been impressed by his young team-mate and says they have been working together on and off the pitch to build up their relationship and help each other perform to the highest level.
"He's been outstanding so far I must say," said Van Dijk when asked about Jacquet. "Very young but he plays like a very mature player. He's still 21, he's still going to get so much better and that's a good thing.
"Obviously, I speak to him a lot during the game but after the game and training and certain moments as well where I feel like I can help him.
"As a centre-back partnership, you have to be able to understand what your qualities and what your flaws are at times and then complement each other on those things. You only get there by playing games.
"It's been good because he's helping me, I help him and that's how it should be. I must say I'm impressed with how we started and now it's down to him to keep that level, keep that consistency, stay calm because you can easily get carried away because there's a lot of plaudits coming his way and rightly so. But I know how it can work when you have maybe one lesser game or not up to the standard that you have.
"He just has to keep going, keep staying important and be fit and then things will be working out pretty well."

items.text:
Israeli drone attacks kill seven Palestinians in central Gaza
Buzzing of drones causes ‘fear and panic’ among Palestinians as Israel continues attacks on the Strip despite ‘ceasefire’.
Israeli attacks have killed at least seven Palestinians and wounded others in the central part of the Gaza Strip, as attacks continue despite a “ceasefire” agreement.
Four Palestinians were killed on Friday when an Israeli drone struck the Bureij refugee camp in Deir el-Balah, medical sources told Al Jazeera.
Witnesses said the drone targeted a group of civilians within the camp.
Separately, a medical source at al-Awda Hospital reported the arrival of the body of a Palestinian killed by an Israeli drone strike in the Nuseirat refugee camp.
Two Palestinians were also killed when an Israeli drone struck civilians near the entrance to the city of Deir el-Balah.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Deir el-Balah, said the injured were brought to hospitals in central Gaza that operate at reduced capacity due to a lack of medical supplies and staff.
Mahmoud added that drones were “causing fear and panic” among Palestinians in Gaza.
“People cannot run simple errands because of the ongoing fear of being attacked and killed on the road,” he said.
The buzzing of drones adds to the sound of explosions from home demolitions and to that of fighter jets, our correspondent added.
The Israeli army on Friday carried out demolition operations near areas under its control in the al-Shuja’iya neighbourhood in the eastern part of Gaza City using explosive-laden drones.
It also carried out three large-scale demolitions near the “Yellow Line”, east of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
By June 16, 2026, an estimated 201,290 structures in Gaza had been damaged or destroyed, about 82 percent of all structures in the Strip, according to the United Nations Satellite Centre (UNOSAT).
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and homes in the Gaza Strip amid ongoing military operations and disputes over the “ceasefire” line.
Israel has repeatedly violated the so-called “ceasefire” agreement that entered into force on October 10, 2025.
Since then, Israeli attacks have killed more than 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza. Since the genocidal war began in October 2023, Israel has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured 176,000 others.
Separately on Friday, which marks World Children’s Day, Palestinian prisoner groups said that around 350 Palestinian children were being held in Israeli prisons, where they face torture, starvation and deprivation of medical care, education, and family visits.
The Palestinian Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs and the Palestinian Prisoner Society said dozens of children from Gaza were detained during the war, but enforced disappearance and restrictions on visits have made it impossible to determine their numbers.

V8 engines returning to Formula 1 in 2030 as FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem describes move to 'reconnect with DNA' of the sport
Multiple Formula 1 drivers had backed for V8 engines to return to the sport; FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has confirmed V8 engines will return from 2030 after a 17-year absence; watch the Las Vegas GP on Sky Sports F1, with qualifying at 4am on Saturday and the race at 4am on Sunday
Friday 20 November 2026 20:24, UK
Formula 1 will return to V8 engines from 2030 in a move FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has described as "an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA" of the sport.
Earlier this week, Ben Sulayem teased the possibility of V8 engines ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix, live on Sky Sports F1, with the sound of a screaming F1 car with a caption: "You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon."
On Friday, the FIA announced a technical framework had been unanimously agreed between the FIA, Formula One Management (FOM), the teams and Formula 1 power unit manufacturers to move to a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 power unit.

The agreement means the more popular V8s will make a comeback in 2030, 17 years after the sport abandoned them in favour of "road relevant" engines, a decision already backed by several drivers.
The current power unit, which is around 53 per cent electrically powered, has been criticised by some drivers this year as it has led to an unusual style of driving and racing at some tracks, with the drivers sometimes unable to push flat out in a traditional manner.
"This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1," said Ben Sulayem.
"From the outset I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.
"The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition."
Verstappen: F1 going in the right direction
Max Verstappen has been one of the most vocal critics of the new 2026 power units and warned the long straights in Las Vegas this weekend will be "painful" to drive on as the cars will effectively slow down before the braking zone.
Verstappen feels the FIA have listened to the drivers and realised the 2026 regulations are "not what you want" and, if he was in charge, would get rid of the turbo aspect completely and effectively have a fully normally aspirated engine.
"In some tracks then you're not allowed to race because it will be too loud because if it's up to me I would take the turbo off," he explained.
"I would get rid, maybe you can use it as a push to pass, but not too much of the battery side. But then on some tracks, you're not allowed to race, so fuel consumption goes up a lot without a turbo, so you need a bigger tank if you don't want to do refuelling in the races, so I understand that you want to have a turbo.
"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that not something realistic. This [news] is good. This is for sure in the right direction."
Lewis Hamilton, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas are the only drivers who drove in the previous V8 era which ended in 2013.
Most of the grid have driven V8-powered F1 cars in demonstration of show runs at fan events and Mercedes driver George Russell says it's important for a hybrid element to remain so the cars can have over 1,000 brake horsepower.
"When I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps," said Russell.
"It's about just that high-pitched squeal that I'm missing from this era. The purists will say take away all electrical power, but I think when you look at how a lot of these cars have evolved in recent years, and the power output from some of these electrical motors these days, Formula 1 is going to continue to be the fastest race cars on the planet, you need to have it, that's just the reality.
"You need to have some sort of hybrid, because the power you get, you can't really produce that just solely on internal combustion."

items.text:
Nepali cricket fans in Qatar want to see their team competing with the best
As thousands from Qatar’s Nepali community watch their team play, they hope for the team to rise in global rankings.
Nepal cricket fans celebrate their team’s global rise
Doha, Qatar – On a warm Friday afternoon in Qatar, the country’s only international cricket stadium was a sea of Nepal’s uniquely triangular crimson and deep blue flags.
Nepal’s supporters arrived with flags draped across their shoulders, held them aloft to flutter in the breeze, cheering every delivery and waving them wildly in celebration of every wicket.
The events on the field seemed nearly inconsequential against the loud cheers of the thousands of fans who had filled the West End International Cricket Stadium on the outskirts of the Qatari capital, as the nation with the world’s highest mountain faced the most powerful force in cricket.
Nepal were bowling first against India A – India’s second XI – in their first group match of the Asian Cricket Council’s (ACC) Rising Star Asia Cup 2026 in Qatar.
Indian captain Tilak Varma and his batting partner Kumar Kushagra kept finding boundaries. Nepal’s bowlers faced the wrath and their fielders could barely keep up.
But the noise in the stands barely subsided.
The supporters followed every ball closely, their attention firmly focused on the team they rarely get to watch up close, especially living thousands of kilometres from home.
A cricket nation on the rise
Qatar is home to at least 367,000 Nepalis, according to the Non-Resident Nepali Association of Qatar, making them the Gulf country’s third-biggest diaspora community.
Pradeep Kumar Yadav was one of the few thousand Nepali fans who were on a mission to provide vociferous support to their cricket team this weekend.
Yadav arrived at the stadium with seven Nepali friends, who had been planning to come as soon as the tournament’s fixtures were announced.
“This is our first time watching Nepal play outside our country,” Yadav told Al Jazeera.
For Nepal’s sizeable diaspora in Qatar, the cricket team provides a reason to gather around a national passion and often draws large crowds.
The supporters are happy to travel to stadiums to back a team that has risen through the international ranks over the past decade.
Nepal’s modern cricketing journey can be traced back to 1996, when the country became a member of the International Cricket Council (ICC) and the men’s team first competed in an international tournament.
The turning point came when the South Asian nation qualified for its first ICC event at the T20 World Cup 2014.
Soon, Nepal’s players were being noticed on the international stage and leg-spinner Sandeep Lamichhane’s selection in major T20 leagues around the world raised the country’s cricketing profile.
Back home, cricket has spread far beyond the capital Kathmandu into towns and villages, backed by efforts to build the sport’s structure at grassroots level.
‘A passionate people’
For Qatar-based fan Himmat Joshi, the Nepali cricket team’s success has resulted in a sharp rise in the popularity of the sport.
“I feel a lot of happiness,” Joshi said while watching the team play against India. “In the past, fewer people followed it but it has grown over the years,” he said.
Mohammad Zahoor, who was among the thousands in the stands, sees the national team’s progress as a source of pride. He describes the Nepalis as a hardworking nation and says the country is building a domestic cricket system capable of competing with higher-ranked international teams.
“There is a lot of pride in seeing Nepali cricketers represent the country. We are a passionate people,” Zahoor said.
The ambitions extend beyond the T20 format.
Nepal’s supporters want to see the country compete against established cricketing nations and eventually earn a place among the teams playing Test cricket.
For Zahoor, defeating a Test-playing country would be an important step towards that ambition.
He also hopes cricket will become part of Nepal’s international identity, alongside its reputation for mountaineering, the Himalayas and being home to Mount Everest.
“Nepalis play the game like a festival,” Zahoor explained.
“Our expectations and hopes are that one day Nepali people are known for their cricket as they are known for their culture of mountaineering and Mount Everest.”
At the stadium in Qatar, the flags, chants and sheer number of supporters reflected that ambition.
In the end, India broke their hearts with a crushing 306-run win.
But it mattered little to the thousands cheering on their team, despite the loss.
For some, including Yadav and his friends, it offered a unique opportunity to watch Nepal play abroad.
Others were simply happy to get a chance to follow a team that has given the country, and its passionate supporters, a growing presence in international cricket.

items.text:
Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved?
November 20, 2026
The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.
Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.
The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.
'Very confident we've solved the mystery'
The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.
For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.
But now there has been a breakthrough.
After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.
The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."
Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.
Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.
And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.
In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.
Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"
Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.
Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."
A handy tool: the iPhone
The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.
Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.
The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.
Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.
Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.
The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures
There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.
Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.
In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.
In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.
Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.
Greece, however, considers them stolen.
For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.
The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.
This article was originally written in German.

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino has spoken out on his training session being leaked by drone footage, Bruno Fernandes and his side's running data; watch Liverpool vs Man Utd live on Sky Sports Premier League from 4pm on Sunday; kick-off 4.30pm
Friday 20 November 2026 20:15, UK
Mauricio Pochettino has questioned what could have been gained from the drone footage of a Manchester United training session ahead of his first game in charge against Liverpool.
A 12-minute video taken over United's Carrington training ground showed the Argentine overseeing various tactical drills with his new team as they prepared for a trip to Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.
The operator has since apologised and taken down the video, but footage has been viewed over eight million times on reposts from other X accounts and has since been reuploaded by several other YouTube channels, collectively attracting hundreds of thousands of views.
Sky Sports News understands the club do not plan on taking legal action, but will not rule out doing so in the future if further incidents occur, and Pochettino questioned the motivation behind the filming.
"What are you going to find?" Pochettino said in an exclusive interview with Sky Sports. "We have young guys training with us. It’s not nice. It’s not good.
"What do they want to show? Yes, we were working on shape. We were very organised. What is the point of doing something that can be very dangerous?
"I don't want to be upset, but I think it's a process the club is caring a lot about. For sure, something will happen."
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola admitted that he was sent the footage after it was released, but said that the act should've been illegal.
"They sent me it yesterday, the footage. But the important part of this is it shouldn't be legal," Iraola said in his pre-match press conference.
"Yesterday you had access to our training, the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes of our training. You know who trained with us, you know who didn't train but it's not a matter of the advantage. It's the fact someone can do this.
"There is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Away from the training footage, Pochettino was quizzed on how much influence he wants to have over the club as he looks to become the man to finally restore glory at Old Trafford.
The Argentine has officially been appointed as head coach, the same as predecessors Ruben Amorim and Michael Carrick. That was a point of contention from the former during the final press conference before his sacking, as he defiantly labelled himself the manager.
However, the term doesn't bother Pochettino as he still hopes to be involved in all the key decisions as time progresses.
"I know that I'm the head coach. I am the guy who is going to decide the squad for Sunday, and I'm going to pick the starting XI," he said.
"I'm going to make the changes, and of course, in the future I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen in the squad.
"Sometimes I worked much better when I was head coach or when I was coach than manager.
"It's not necessarily the case that if you are manager, you make all the decisions. Maybe you are a coach and you have more power in the decisions. It depends on the structure, depends on the communication, the relationship, with all the areas there."
Captain Bruno remains very important to Poch
Another point of contention at United remains the future of club captain Bruno Fernandes.
The PFA Player of the Year has struggled with his form this season and his contract at Old Trafford is due to run out at the end of the season.
The club do hold an optional one-year extension, and CEO Omar Berrada has confirmed that the club remain in discussions over a new deal for the Portuguese international.
Pochettino confirmed his intentions to keep Fernandes as captain and stressed his importance.
"Bruno is our captain, and I think he's a very important player, but all the players need to feel that they are important, from the top to the bottom or from the bottom to the top," he said.
"But Bruno is our captain and he is a very important player. I think we will have time afterwards to talk about the things that you ask me."
Poch keen to improve data as running stats called into question
In terms of what is on his immediate agenda, Pochettino is focusing on improving the data metrics across the club.
"When we arrived, I think we found a group of players and we proposed the football that we feel [is the best]. That's being brave, being Man Utd. I think it is about proposing that idea, and they revise it; it is to be brave and try to bring that to the field.
"I need to be honest, sometimes data shows something that you can then see on the field. We are going to be very focused and try to improve our data, our numbers, in every single area of the field.
"We are here not to denounce things. We are here to build something with our players and with the club, and try to perform and win games."
United's running and intensity off the ball has been a major criticism of them throughout the season, with former boss Carrick flippantly saying of his players after their 4-1 defeat to Como in October "whatever tactics you play, if you don't run back, you ain't going to win."

items.summary:
Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s future security arrangements.
Nuseirat refugee camp, Gaza Strip – It was late on Tuesday evening when a group of arme
items.text:
Palestinian anti-Hamas groups accused of role in Israel Gaza operation
Israeli-backed Palestinian militias accused of expanding operations, raising concerns over their role in Gaza’s future security arrangements.
Nuseirat refugee camp, Gaza Strip – It was late on Tuesday evening when a group of armed men stopped outside a house sheltering displaced Palestinian women on ad-Dawa Street, on the northern edge of the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza.
The streets were gradually emptying, and drones could be heard overhead. The men wore no military uniforms or insignia. They were Palestinians in civilian clothes carrying light weapons, believed to be members of Israeli-backed local militias, locals said.
The gunmen surrounded the house and forced the women into the street and questioned them by torchlight about a man they were looking for. They threatened those who refused to answer and fired into the air before withdrawing minutes later without detaining anyone.
Hours later, on Wednesday, the Israeli military launched a ground operation near the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps, west of the so-called “Yellow Line” that demarcates areas under Israeli military control following the October 2025 ceasefire.
The military closed Salah al-Din Street, Gaza’s main north-south thoroughfare. About 6,000 Palestinians fled, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
Israel said the operation targeted a tunnel that posed a threat to its troops. On Thursday, the military said that the operation had been completed. At least one Palestinian was killed in Israeli attacks near where the incursion took place.
The sequence of events raises questions about the extent of coordination between Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups, whose activities have expanded across Gaza in recent weeks.
‘Engineering chaos’
A Palestinian security source in Gaza told Al Jazeera that security authorities had documented the local armed groups’ participation in this week’s Israeli military operation in central Gaza.
Their activities included “terrorising civilians and pressuring families to evacuate homes and shelters”, the source said.
Speaking on condition of anonymity, the source said the groups benefitted from Israeli military fire cover and the closure of Salah al-Din Street, which also impeded humanitarian operations.
The source described them as “gangs”, financed and armed by Israel to undermine Palestinian internal cohesion by “engineering chaos”.
Israel has publicly acknowledged supporting armed groups opposed to Hamas in Gaza, as it fought its genocidal war on the Palestinian enclave, killing more than 74,000 people. “What’s wrong with that?” asked Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last year, claiming that the policy had saved the lives of Israeli soldiers.
Expanding military and intelligence roles
Palestinian political analyst Iyad al-Qarra told Al Jazeera that Israel had expanded the armed groups’ reach from Rafah and Khan Younis in the south to central Gaza and Gaza City.
He accused the groups of carrying out kidnappings and attempted assassinations targeting Palestinians, including members of Palestinian factions, in which they benefitted from Israeli aerial protection and fire cover.
Al-Qarra linked their expanding activities to Israel’s demolition of buildings and forced displacement of Palestinians, which have enabled the groups to operate in areas that Israeli forces would otherwise struggle to access.
He said the Israeli military uses the fighters in front-line operations before committing its own troops.
The groups also gather intelligence through local social and family networks while receiving information from the Israeli military, al-Qarra said.
Who are the Israeli-backed anti-Hamas groups?
The groups emerged during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, with some accused of looting aid supplies before taking on broader roles through Israeli funding, weapons and coordination with the military and intelligence services.
Published estimates point to about five main groups with several hundred members in total. In April, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) monitor reported that Israel had increased its support for them, including deploying attack drones during their clashes with Hamas.
The groups include the Popular Forces in Rafah, led by Ghassan al-Duhaini, since founder Yasser Abu Shabab was killed in December 2025; Hussam al-Astal’s group east of Khan Younis; and Shawqi Abu Nuseira’s group in central Gaza.
Two others, led by Rami Helles and Ashraf al-Mansi, operate in eastern Gaza City and northern Gaza, respectively.
A permanent security presence?
Palestinian political analyst Wesam Afifa told Al Jazeera that Israel seeks to establish local security influence that it could retain even after a partial military withdrawal.
He cited Israel’s historical support for the South Lebanon Army before its withdrawal from Lebanon in 2000, and more limited forms of collaboration during the first and second Palestinian Intifadas.
What distinguishes the situation in Gaza, Afifa said, is the groups’ transition from limited support roles to conducting armed operations outside areas under direct Israeli military control.
He pointed to their involvement in searching and obstructing travellers returning through the Rafah border crossing, which he said contradicted existing agreements and the role of the European Union monitoring mission.
In February, the United Nations Human Rights Office documented accounts from Palestinian returnees alleging intimidation, searches and theft by armed Palestinians purportedly backed by Israel.
Afifa warned that the groups’ continued presence could extend Israeli security influence beyond a military withdrawal, raising the possibility that Israel could push for their inclusion in Gaza’s future security arrangements.

items.title: Washington Spirit provide hope and joy in a city that badly needs it
items.summary: In the moments after the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 semi-final victory over the Utah Royals last weekend, all of Audi Field was in rapture. In the stands, around 20,000 Spirit supporters had filled the stadium to capacity, the sixth time they’ve done so in 2026. They filled the place with the type of w
items.text:
In the moments after the Washington Spirit’s 2-1 semi-final victory over the Utah Royals last weekend, all of Audi Field was in rapture. In the stands, around 20,000 Spirit supporters had filled the stadium to capacity, the sixth time they’ve done so in 2026. They filled the place with the type of wondrous noise that’s become alien in DC sports in recent years, the type of gleeful adoration reserved for the city’s rare winners. The Spirit will return to their home stadium to face the Kansas City Current in the NWSL championship this Saturday.
In short order, the Spirit’s players made their way to the north end of the stadium, taking their celebrations into the crowd with their supporters. Perhaps no player has done more to push the Spirit into not only local but national relevance than US women’s national team forward Trinity Rodman, and Rodman herself grabbed a flag from a fan, jubilantly waving it above the crowd. Moments later, she bolted back onto the field and track down the club’s owner, Michele Kang, cajoling the businesswoman into a celebratory dance.
In the echo of all of this, many media members covering the match in the press box received an email from DC United, the local Major League Soccer club that operates and rents out Audi Field to the Spirit. It was a press release announcing the dismissal of their head coach, René Weiler. As the Spirit celebrated a third consecutive championship appearance on the pitch below, some unfortunate soul in a nearby office was tasked with sending that notice, the final nail in yet another dreadful season. While the women have thrived, the local men’s team has not made the playoffs in nearly a decade.
The Spirit, who share not only United’s stadium but also their training facility, are not asking to be compared to them. In reality no NWSL team is, as the audiences for men’s and women’s teams in the same city frequently prove to be quite different. Yet the differing fortunes of the two clubs and the stark difference in atmosphere at their games makes it nearly impossible not to do so. Once-mighty United, four-time MLS Cup champions, have become a laughingstock. That has not stopped the club’s ownership from seeking hundreds of millions of dollars from the DC government to renovate their eight-year-old stadium. While they lobby for that assistance, their matches have become borderline funerary affairs.
The Spirit? The club has become a beacon of hope and joy in a city that badly needs it. The District is a wildly diverse, deeply progressive place and its residents have struggled at times to come to terms with the political realities of hosting the current presidential administration. Thousands of National Guard troops roam the streets, more than a year into an anti-crime deployment that many believe hasn’t helped the city at all. In the shadow of all of this, Spirit matches have become a refuge. And while much of that relief comes from soccer the club plays – technical, entertaining – much of it comes from a deeper place.
“I think it’s the way that we bring the fans into everything that we do,” Rodman told the Guardian. “I think the way we interact with them after games, it’s not just a meet and greet. We truly do have conversations, and it feels like they’re our friends in a way. I think that’s amazing. The way that we celebrate, we’re always celebrating and interacting with them in the stadium - I feel like it’s a very safe, inclusive environment.
“There is always new people coming to each and every game and what I’ve heard is that everybody feels comfortable when they come to a game, there’s so many friends made. The comfort in it, the safety, the inclusivity of it at all.”
The Spirit have been mentioned as potential benefactors of United’s push for renovations at Audi Field, but Spirit ownership has long harbored bigger ambitions. The club have strong ties to the NFL’s Washington Commanders, who are moving into a new 65,000-seat home as part of a $4bn deal in the coming years, and “opportunities for women’s soccer” made up part of the pitch for that stadium’s public funding. Kang has spoken about aspirations of constructing a standalone training facility and moving the club out of the one it shares with United, a glorified collection of shipping containers in exurban Loudoun county, Virginia.
“I’m hoping in the future we do have that,” said Rodman. “Especially with how great we’ve done and how this organization is as a whole, that would be the cherry on top. Sharing facilities isn’t the greatest for anybody; to be able to have our own facilities with our own logos on it, our own space, not worried about timing would be great and I’m hoping it happens soon.”
All of it feels plausible. Should the Spirit remain competitive, and continue to endear to the District’s residents, it almost feels probable.

Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.
The UK-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.
Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion, the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.
Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size, Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.
Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.
Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.
Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviating concerns about AI’s energy consumption.
Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.
“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website. “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while pro
items.text:
Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
- Published
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out.
In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of t
items.text:
Gérard Depardieu and French author investigated over sexual allegations
- Published
Warning: this story contains graphic content
French authorities are investigating disgraced actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.
The source told the BBC that a judicial investigation was launched after a complaint was filed in May 2025.
Depardieu has already separately been convicted of unrelated sexual assaults. The BBC has contacted Depardieu's lawyers and Houellebecq, an acclaimed French author and occasional actor, for comment.
The actress, who has not been named publicly, accused Depardieu of penetration without consent and Houellebecq of forcing her to perform oral sex, in an interview with Mediapart, a French investigative site which first reported the allegations.
She told the outlet that none of this had been written into the script, and that she experienced "profound humiliation" and "unspeakable shame".
French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.
The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.
Nicloux told Mediapart that the scene had been improvised and he had not intervened as he had not observed "any constraints, verbal or physical opposition, or even discomfort".
The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.
The actress told the outlet that she had told friends, her agent and others involved in the film's production in Normandy about the incident at the time, but only filed the complaint after other women accused Depardieu of sexual misconduct.
The Asterix and Obelix star will next week find out whether he will stand trial for allegedly raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould.
On Monday, Depardieu dropped his appeal against a separate conviction for two counts of sexual assault during another film shoot, for which he was handed an 18-month suspended sentence.
Several other women have made allegations against the 77-year-old in the media.

items.title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
items.summary:
Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
An Indian national has been sentenced to more than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder
items.text:
Indian man sentenced to 19 years in US Sikh separatist assassination plot
Nikhil Gupta jailed for conspiring to hire a hitman to kill New York-based Sikh leader, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun.
An Indian national has been sentenced to more than 19-and-a-half years in prison in the United States in a murder-for-hire plot targeting a prominent Sikh separatist leader living in New York City.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to three conspiracy charges for plotting to hire a hitman to assassinate Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen, lawyer and vocal advocate for a sovereign Sikh state.
US District Judge Victor Marrero handed down the 235-month sentence at a federal court in Manhattan on Friday. Gupta faces deportation to India after completing his prison term.
Addressing the court on Friday, Gupta said he regretted straying from the nonviolent example set by Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. “I’m sorry to Mr Pannun, I’m sorry to the communities I hurt, I’m sorry to my own family,” he said.
Prosecutors accused Gupta of conspiring with an Indian government official to kill Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer for the US-based separatist group Sikhs for Justice, in New York. Pannun is also a proponent of independence for Punjab, the northern Indian state where Sikhism was founded.
Court documents showed that Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to someone who could kill Pannun. But the person turned out to be an undercover law enforcement officer posing as a hitman.
Gupta was arrested in Prague and has been held without bail since his extradition to the US in June 2023. A plea agreement called for him to serve at least two decades in prison.
Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear whether he has hired a defence lawyer.
India’s government has denied any involvement in the plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.
However, multiple alleged assassination plots against Sikh separatists have been uncovered in the US and Canada, testing relations with India. New Delhi denies involvement in the plots.
‘A foot soldier’
Prosecutors with the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison for Gupta.
“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices in this country, ever.”
Pannun was in court on Friday to see the sentence handed down. He described Gupta as “just a foot soldier acting at the behest” of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist who has opposed the independence movement.
Pannun said the Modi government wanted him dead “because I lead the campaign openly, defy threats and intimidation”.
Pannun also told the court he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.
“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eu
items.text:
Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

items.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167 year-old Riemann Hypothesis — and a human did, too
items.summary:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and des
items.text:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
The Hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.
Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …
The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.
For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.
But that comment was followed by twenty readers reacting 🤯.
It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source language that essentially helps verify mathematical proofs.
Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.
Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.
Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.
Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann Hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”
In a brief introduction his proof, which he said is the result of twelve years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”

The mayor of Serbia’s capital city, Belgrade, has been charged with injuring a female opposition politician du
items.text:
Belgrade mayor charged with assaulting opposition politician in Serbia
Prosecutors say Aleksandar Sapic caused serious facial injuries to a female councillor and seek a three-year sentence.
The mayor of Serbia’s capital city, Belgrade, has been charged with injuring a female opposition politician during an argument they had in September.
Serbian prosecutors charged Aleksandar Sapic, a senior figure in the right-wing nationalist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), on Friday. He is accused of grabbing Belgrade city councillor Tatjana Micic by the arm and punching her in the face.
Prosecutors said Micic suffered fractures to her nose and part of her upper jaw, and injuries to her right arm and neck, which the prosecutors said constituted grievous bodily harm.
“Within less than two months of the incident, the Prosecutor’s Office examined witnesses, reviewed video surveillance footage, obtained medical records as well as the findings and opinion of a forensic expert, and filed an indictment proposal,” prosecutors said in a statement.
“In protecting the physical integrity and safety of citizens, the Prosecutor’s Office applies the same criteria to every defendant, regardless of the position they hold,” it added.
They are seeking a three-year sentence for Belgrade mayor Sapic, and are seeking to block him from approaching and communicating with councillor Micic.
Sapic denied attacking Micic, but acknowledged an argument and a scuffle with her husband. Opposition parties have demanded Sapic resign from his role, but he has resisted their calls. Sapic’s SNS party, which had headed up the government since 2012, lost an election to a student-led opposition movement in October.
The party, however, retains control of the capital, Belgrade.
