items.title: Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet
items.summary:
Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.
He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach
items.text:
Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.
He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.
“We’ll do maybe two days on, one day off, and then three days on, one day off,” says Peters. “We’ve been doing that for just over a year now. It’s full-on. It’s pretty much as if you were at a club.”
Dele rose as a teenager to a level of stardom few experience and, used to media attention, doesn’t mind that his absence from football draws scrutiny. But he disagrees with the suggestion that choosing to stream on Twitch is a sign he has lost interest in the game that made him wealthy enough to never need to work again.
To a modest Twitch audience, he sometimes plays video games, sometimes just talks. He has a knack for creating viral content, sharing a phone call with Harry Kane and playing a game of EA Sports FC with IShowSpeed, one of the most famous online influencers. When he lost that game – and a bet – he wore an Arsenal shirt, apologising to Spurs fans before burning it. When TalkSport pundits claimed Dele was wasting his potential by becoming a streamer, Dele responded in a live stream, pointing out he was recording himself in his spare time and if he was out at nightclubs, it would be worse. Even then he was polite.
“When people see him online streaming or whatever he does in his private time, the initial thought is: ‘He’s done with football, then,’” Peters says. “He’s been training for a year and a half by himself. If he was done with football he wouldn’t be doing that. His actions show that the hunger is still there. A lot of people would come out of the game and then stop and lose the hunger for it, but he’s still chipping away every day, trying to get back and get to somewhere that he’s happy with.”
Dele broke through at MK Dons as a slight but devilish defensive midfielder, dominating League One midfields full of hardened professionals, before being scouted by Tottenham. Mauricio Pochettino attended MK Dons’ 4-0 League Cup win against Manchester United in 2014 and saw enough to leave early and convince Daniel Levy to pay £5m.
By the time Dele turned 21, his statistics were superior to Cristiano Ronaldo’s at the same age: 26 goals and 14 assists to Ronaldo’s 14 and 13. His 40 goal involvements equalled Frank Lampard, Steven Gerrard and David Beckham combined at the same age.
“He’s scored more in his first 50 league games than Steven Gerrard, Wayne Rooney and Frank Lampard,” Pochettino wrote in his book Brave New World. “He may go on to be better than all of them because he has the quality; now he just needs consistency.”
But there were, perhaps, warning signs of what would happen at Spurs. One source who worked closely with Dele describes him as a “cheeky chappy”; charming and universally popular.
He wasn’t one to miss training, but there were concerns he wasn’t leading the pristine lifestyle of many elite players, and tabloid stories about his private life trailed him. Pochettino was concerned when he saw Dele’s WhatsApp photo, a cartoon of a boy surrounded by people wanting a piece of him, believing he needed support from the right people. John McDermott, the head of coaching and development, said: “When the trough is full, the pigs come from all over to feed.”
When Dele voluntarily liquidated one of his companies this month, documents showed an estimated surplus after costs of £7.6m, suggesting the 30-year-old has not squandered the millions he earned at his peak in wages and sponsorship agreements, including a five-year deal with Adidas. He also owns a property portfolio worth more than £1.5m.
In the early days Pochettino warned Dele about the danger of not giving maximum effort in matches and training, a sentiment later shared by José Mourinho when he became Spurs manager. “I think one day you will regret, if you don’t reach what you can reach,” Mourinho told Dele in his office as Amazon Prime’s cameras rolled.
Although Dele formed a formidable relationship with Kane on the pitch, and was twice named the Professional Footballers’ Association’s men’s young player of the year while playing behind the striker, he was closer to Eric Dier off it. And perhaps it was those anchors – Pochettino and Dier – that Dele lost later in his career.
His time with Pochettino was fondly remembered. For the Argentinian’s 50th birthday celebrations, Dele recorded a heartfelt video for his former manager. “The message was beautiful,” says one party-goer.
In almost five years since leaving Spurs, he has made one league start at Everton and 10 at Besiktas, before a loan at Como, where Cesc Fàbregas tried to rediscover the player he once was. He came off the bench once and was sent off nine minutes later.

items.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
items.summary: Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does. Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.
For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.
Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.
This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.
Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”
This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”
It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.
Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.
Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.
The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal. It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.
Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook. He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.
Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.
“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”
Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.
Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.
Why are United turning now to a manager they have previously overlooked? Pochettino is not about to dwell on that because he is in dream-come-true territory. He will love how the United support stand behind their manager, esp

items.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
items.summary:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While
items.text:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”
Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”
Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.
We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.
So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

items.title: Sarr focused on Palace return after Liverpool interest
items.summary:
Sarr focused on Palace return after Liverpool interest
- Published
Crystal Palace forward Ismaila Sarr says he has moved on from Liverpool's interest in signing him and is keen for a "fresh start" under new manager Thomas Frank.
The Senegal international, 28, is keen to put that episode behind him a
items.text:
Sarr focused on Palace return after Liverpool interest
- Published
Crystal Palace forward Ismaila Sarr says he has moved on from Liverpool's interest in signing him and is keen for a "fresh start" under new manager Thomas Frank.
The Senegal international, 28, is keen to put that episode behind him after Liverpool explored a move at the end of the summer transfer window.
Ultimately, Palace rejected advances for Sarr, who scored 21 goals in 45 games in all competitions last season as his side won the Conference League, while Liverpool opted to keep Cody Gakpo despite interest from Manchester City.
In his first interview since Liverpool's pursuit of him, Sarr - who has been nominated for the African footballer of the year award - told BBC Sport: "Liverpool is one of the biggest clubs in world football and, when a club like that shows an interest in you, of course it's something you take seriously.
"I don't think any player would be indifferent to that kind of opportunity. It was an interesting possibility, and naturally, I considered what it could mean for my career.
"Today, that chapter is behind me. I've always believed that you can't move forward if you're constantly looking in the rear-view mirror.
"I'm a Crystal Palace player, I'm proud of what we've achieved together, and my focus is on getting back on the pitch and helping the team."
Sarr is still sidelined with a groin injury, but talks are ongoing with Palace over an improved contract - despite his current deal running until 2029.
He added: "Yes, there have been discussions with the club. For now, I prefer to let those conversations happen privately and concentrate on football."
Sarr missed most of Pierre Sage's spell in charge, making just two brief substitute appearances in the Premier League this season.
Sage was replaced by former Tottenham Hotspur and Brentford manager Frank this week.
"Of course, it's a difficult moment for everyone at the club," Sarr said. "After everything we achieved last season, nobody expected us to be in this position.
"But I know the quality of this squad. We have very good players, a strong group and the ability to turn things around.
"The arrival of Thomas Frank is an opportunity for a fresh start, new energy and a different approach. We all have to take responsibility, work together and fight for every point.
"I'm confident we can overcome this difficult period and achieve our objectives this season."
Sarr hopes award goes to Senegalese player
Sarr is on 10-man shortlist for the African Player of the Year award, which will be presented on 7 December in Lagos, Nigeria.
It follows Sarr being named Conference League Player of the Season, scoring nine goals as Palace won their first European title. He also collected both the club's player of the year and players' player of the year awards.
Sarr went on to score four goals for Senegal at the 2026 World Cup, after featuring in a controversial Africa Cup of Nations final in January.
In March, Senegal's final victory over Morocco was overturned after players left the pitch without the authorisation of the referee.
As Senegal appeal to be reawarded with their title at the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), Sarr remains proud that his side "became the African champions on the pitch".
Asked about his chances of winning the African Player of the Year award, he said: "I'm proud of the season I've had, both with Crystal Palace and Senegal. It's been a special year, with important trophies and individual achievements.
"But African football has so many outstanding players, and several of them have also had fantastic seasons.
"I'm thinking particularly of my Senegalese brothers Sadio Mane and Pape Gueye, who also deserve recognition for what they've achieved.
"Of course, winning the award would be an incredible honour. Every African player dreams of that.
"But honestly, what matters most to me is seeing the trophy go to Senegal. I'm incredibly proud of what we accomplished together."

items.title: Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
items.summary:
Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled i
items.text:
Ukraine strikes Kerch Bridge as Putin ally declares ‘no one needs Europe’
Russia-Europe tensions rise as Ukraine uses its own weapons and communications tech to hit the Kerch Bridge.
Ukraine’s fourth and most complex operation on the Kerch Bridge brought down its road section and may have crippled its rail section over three days of strikes, taking a crucial Russian supply route into Crimea off the map.
“The short supply route from Russian territory has been destroyed,” declared Ukraine’s General Staff.
“Once again, the myth of Russia’s greatness has been shaken,” said Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), which took part in the operation.
It was part of a wider set of strikes against oil facilities and supply routes in the Rostov and Krasnodar Krai regions abutting Ukraine – an apparent strategy to asphyxiate Russian forces in southern Ukraine.
“The alternative route is overland, along the front line, where our drones are waiting for the cargo,” said the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence.
For a month, Ukraine’s military said it “systematically destroyed enemy air defence systems, radars, and electronic warfare equipment along the way to the target.”
On November 16, Ukrainian drones damaged the bridge’s road surface and compromised its steel arched span that allows shipping between the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea.
On November 17, the SBU said it used “Palyanytsia kamikaze drones to target the roadway section of the Crimean Bridge, causing it to collapse.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Neptune and Flamingo missiles and Ruta drones struck the separate railway span.
During this 48-hour period, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it intercepted 4,305 Ukrainian drones compared with a daily average of 882 during the previous week.
On November 18-19, Ukraine again used Neptune missiles to strike the railway span, saying rail service had been suspended. It was unclear whether those strikes had permanently disabled the rail bridge.
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the operation as a strike against “a purely civilian facility … We haven’t even transported oil or petroleum products across the bridge.”
Ukraine’s General Staff disagreed, saying it had targeted the Kerch Bridge because it “was a vital artery, supplying fuel, ammunition, equipment, and personnel”.
The Ukrainian Defence Ministry called the bridge “a war machine”.
On the same day as the main strike on the Kerch Bridge, Ukraine also struck Russia’s main overland route to its southern forces, the M-14 Rostov-Crimea highway.
In addition, Kyiv also struck a series of refineries and oil depots in southwestern Russia that are nearest to the front, including in Azov, Ilsky and Afipsky.
“Fuel from such depots has a short route to the front,” it said.
Ukraine has already put Russia’s Black Sea and Azov Sea fleet of oil and fuel carriers out of action, striking at least 300 ships between July and September, leaving fuel supply dependent on road and rail transport.
Southern Ukraine is where Russian offensive efforts are now most active.
Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces, has said Russian casualties are heaviest near Dobropillya and Huliaipole in Zaporizhia. Ukraine’s General Staff has also confirmed this is where the highest number of assaults takes place.
Defying two superpowers
Ukraine made a point of saying its Kerch operation was entirely autonomous.
“The strike was carried out exclusively with Ukrainian weapons – our technology, our solutions,” said Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhen Khmara.
This also meant that Ukraine did not rely on the US-controlled Starlink and Starshield satellite systems, on which it depends for short-range drone navigation. On November 6, those services began to cut out when drones exceed 160km/h (100mph). They were later restored, but Zelenskyy said they were again compromised beginning on November 13.
For the Kerch Bridge operation, Ukraine instead designed a system of drones that acted as signal repeaters. Video released by Ukraine showed an FP-5 missile relaying video up to the moment of impact, indicating that operators had control of it.
During the past week, Ukraine also targeted Russian refineries as far-flung as Volgograd and Samara, Salavat and Tatarstan, in an ongoing strategy to deprive Russia’s war machine of export revenue and diesel.
Almost half of the output of the Volgograd refinery is diesel, Ukraine said – a blow not only to Russia’s military, which consumes the fuel, but also to its promise to export 1.7 million tonnes of diesel this year as part of a deal struck with US President Donald Trump to lower fuel prices.
US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have reportedly threatened Ukraine with an intelligence cutoff if it continues to strike Russian refineries.
As Ukraine defied them, Putin and Trump took to the global stage as the guests of Chinese leader Xi Jinping in the city of Shenzhen on November 19.
It was the first time Putin and Trump had met since their summit in Alaska in August 2025, and the first time all three men had met.
Kremlin-aligned media made much of the event, picking up Putin’s comparison with the Big Three conference in Yalta at the end of the second world war.
“The world’s three most consequential powers – have met. As the Big Three, they have emerged as the principal force in shaping a new architecture for international and European security,” wrote Putin’s deputy on the National Security Council, Dmitry Medvedev. “Today … no-one needs Europe.”
Asked whether peace in Ukraine was any closer as a result of the summit, Putin said he and Trump were still aligned on the proposals they discussed in Alaska. Those involved Ukraine handing over to Russia the one-fifth of the eastern Donbas region it cannot take by force, and to agree not to join NATO.
In the recent negotiations at Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, Ukraine was reportedly offered a green light to join NATO in return for the Donbas.

items.title: Pochettino's Man United squad audit: Big calls to make on stars like Fernandes, Rashford
items.summary:
Mauricio Pochettino has arrived at Manchester United and the former United States men's national team coach has no time to waste as the new manager of the Premier League's fallen giants.
Pochettino's immediate task is to halt the team's slump and drag United out of the relegation zone, starting with
items.text:
Mauricio Pochettino has arrived at Manchester United and the former United States men's national team coach has no time to waste as the new manager of the Premier League's fallen giants.
Pochettino's immediate task is to halt the team's slump and drag United out of the relegation zone, starting with Sunday's trip to Liverpool as his first game in charge. Securing a first league win since August is also a priority for the former Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea boss.
However, the 54-year-old must look beyond the short term at Old Trafford. He must begin to shape a team in his own image, with players capable of playing the Pochettino way.
- Man United, Pochettino's to-do list based on what's gone wrong
- Pochettino can't fix United on his own. The owners have to do their jobs
- Where are they now? Every Utd player, coach, exec since Glazers' takeover
Former United captain Gary Neville said last week that, while interviewing him at Spurs in 2014, Pochettino was sat in front of a whiteboard with two lists of players: those he could trust and build around, and those he decided he could not work with.
Having inherited a squad built by United's six previous managers dating back to Louis van Gaal's signing of Luke Shaw in 2014, Pochettino must quickly assess his players and draw up a similar list of who will stay and who will go.
So with the Pochettino era about to start at United, what will his whiteboard look like at the end of the season? Who stays, and who has to go?
Jump to: Goalkeepers | Defenders | Midfielders | Forwards
Goalkeepers
Senne Lammens (24 years old)
The Belgium international had an impressive first season at United last term, but his form has dipped at Old Trafford since a costly error at the FIFA World Cup led to Belgium's elimination against Spain. But while United could find an upgrade, Lammens is not one of the team's problems and he deserves to stay.
Verdict: Stay
Karl Darlow (36)
Signed as a free agent this summer after his exit from Leeds United, the Wales international is United's No. 2, but he is not a top-class keeper and nowhere near the level of his counterparts at the Premier League's top clubs.
Verdict: Go
Defenders
Diogo Dalot (27)
Ordinarily, Dalot would have no future at United and been offloaded years ago. But his versatility and fitness record -- the Portugal defender has missed just 18 games due to injury since January 2020 -- have made him a regular starter. Dalot lacks defensive qualities, but he is durable and committed. With both of those qualities in short supply at Old Trafford, Pochettino might need him to hang around.
Verdict: Stay
Noussair Mazraoui (29)
A £15 million signing from Bayern Munich in 2024, the Morocco international was recruited as a squad player. He has played in a variety of positions in defense and midfield and even once, unsuccessfully, as a No. 10. But he's not good enough for any role and has an unreliable fitness record.
Verdict: Go
Matthijs de Ligt (27)
United's football department opposed De Ligt's €45 million signing from Bayern Munich due to concerns over his injury record, but ultimately sanctioned the deal as a means of backign manager Erik ten Hag. According to Transfermarkt, De Ligt has been unavailable for 343 days due to injury since arriving at Old Trafford in August 2024.
Verdict: Go
Harry Maguire (33)
Once the world's most expensive defender following his £80 million transfer from Leicester City in 2019, Maguire has had an up and down United career, but he earned a new one-year contract last summer. In a mediocre defensive unit, Maguire brings leadership and experience, albeit with a lack of pace. With with a huge defensive clear-out likely, Maguire's positives outweigh his negatives in the short-term.
Verdict: Stay
Lisandro Martínez (28)
The Argentina defender is out of contract next summer and even though the former Ajax player may develop a connection with fellow countryman Pochettino, he remains too reckless and injury-prone to have a long-term future. His form has been poor all season, so there are no reasons to offer him a new contract.
Verdict: Go
Leny Yoro (21)
The France defender has struggled with form and fitness since arriving from Lille two years ago. However, his age, potential and pace are all positives Pochettino can exploit. Yoro needs to develop defensively, but he is a player who can become a top player at his position with the right coaching.
Verdict: Stay
Luke Shaw (31)
The former England left back has made 241 Premier League appearances for United in more than 12 years since arriving from Southampton -- just over half of the 466 league games played by the club in that time. Shaw knows Pochettino from their time together at Saints, but even that connection is unlikely to save him when his contract expires at the end of the season.
Verdict: Go
Ayden Heaven (20)
The former Arsenal youngster has made over 30 senior appearances for United and has shown potential, but has also struggled for form in an inconsistent team. It is too soon to assess whether he can be a United player and he may need a loan move to gain more experience.
Verdict: Stay
Harry Amass (19)
The naturally left-sided full back hasn't made a Premier League appearance since May 2025 having been loaned to Sheffield Wednesday and Norwich last season. He was overlooked by former manager Michael Carrick in the league this season, but expect Pochettino to give him a chance in the weeks ahead.
Verdict: Stay
Midfielders
Mason Mount (27)
The former Chelsea midfielder has completed 90 minutes in a Premier League game on just four occasions since arriving at Old Trafford in 2023, and has missed 71 games due to injury in that time. Mount is under contract until 2028, but Pochettino can't rely on him in any way.
Verdict: Go
Bruno Fernandes (32)
United's best player and captain, but his future is a big dilemma for Pochettino. United can trigger a one-year contract extension on Fernandes' deal to keep him until 2028, when he will be approaching his 34

items.title: Liverpool are terrible at Anfield this season, but will it matter vs. Man United?
items.summary: When Manchester United traveled to Anfield to face Jürgen Klopp's beleaguered Liverpool side in March 2023, former United captain Gary Neville was sure his old club would emerge triumphant. "I'm not nervous," he told Sky Sports. "I've never been more relaxed coming here in the last nine years as a M
items.text:
When Manchester United traveled to Anfield to face Jürgen Klopp's beleaguered Liverpool side in March 2023, former United captain Gary Neville was sure his old club would emerge triumphant. "I'm not nervous," he told Sky Sports. "I've never been more relaxed coming here in the last nine years as a Manchester United fan."
His conviction stemmed from the fact that United had only lost once in their last 13 Premier League games and had climbed up to third in the table under Erik ten Hag. Liverpool, meanwhile, were languishing in sixth and losing ground in the race for UEFA Champions League qualification.
The outcome of the game? Liverpool defied expectations by subjecting United to a 7-0 thrashing, the biggest win in the fixture's history. It was a powerful reminder that, regardless of form, Anfield at its best has an enduring power to propel Liverpool to the greatest heights.
However, in the three years since that memorable victory, Liverpool have failed in all three attempts to beat United when playing at home.
In December 2023, Klopp's side spurned the chance to go top of the table after their faltering archrivals held them to a 0-0 draw. The spoils were shared again the following season, when Amad Diallo netted late on in a 2-2 draw to end United's run of three straight defeats. And last term, Ruben Amorim's men went one better, beating Arne Slot's Premier League champions 2-1 to claim United's first win at Anfield in almost a decade.
On Sunday, Liverpool will host their old foe again in what will be a first taste of the fixture for both Andoni Iraola and new United manager Mauricio Pochettino. Struggling United are in the relegation zone (18th) and recently sacked Michael Carrick, so it is Liverpool, who are in the race for Europe (fourth), who should be confident. But their form at the iconic home stadium needs to change, and fast, if they are to spark their season into life.
Liverpool's dismal record at Anfield predates this season
United are not the only team to have enjoyed success at Anfield in recent times. This season, only bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace and 16th-place Nottingham Forest have picked up fewer points at home than Liverpool.
Iraola's side have won just one of their five Premier League games at Anfield, drawing and losing twice respectively -- the same home record as United.
That Liverpool have the best away record in the top flight this term -- winning four and drawing one of their five games on the road -- makes their struggles at Anfield all the more bewildering. Despite the stadium's reputation as one of the most feared venues in Europe for visiting teams, it is Liverpool's home form which is preventing them from establishing themselves as genuine title contenders this season.
There is some mitigation for the Reds' troubles at Anfield. Against both Manchester City and Arsenal, Iraola's side were on the receiving end of controversial refereeing decisions.
They collapsed against City after Ryan Gravenberch was contentiously sent off for two yellow-card offences, while the Premier League's Key Match Incidents (KMI) Panel ruled Liverpool should have been awarded a penalty for a shirt pull on Alexander Isak in the 1-0 defeat to Arsenal. The KMI Panel also ruled in September that Forest should not have been awarded a penalty in the previous month's 2-2 draw at Anfield.
But while Liverpool can feel aggrieved about some of the decisions that have gone against them at home, it must also be acknowledged that their own performance levels have not been good enough. Against Arsenal, Iraola's side failed to have a single shot on target for the first time in 442 league matches at Anfield. In the 0-0 draw with Fulham in September, Liverpool were blunt and lethargic against a team that had yet to claim a single Premier League point.
That kind of insipid display was commonplace last season, when Liverpool failed to win 47% of their home games (winning just 10 out of 19). The underperformance of big-ticket signings such as Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak did not help matters, with fans often left wanting to see more from their new stars.
The increasing competitiveness of the Premier League -- where even teams towards the bottom of the table have the financial power to sign elite players -- means almost every game demands a certain level of performance. Too often over the past year, Liverpool have failed to reach that bar.
While it is impossible to pin down one definitive theory for the Reds' struggles, the events of the summer of 2025 -- when striker Diogo Jota and his brother André Silva lost their lives in a car accident -- cast a shadow over the whole campaign.
On an emotional level, there was debate about the supporters' decision to sing Jota's song at the 20-minute mark of every home match, and how much of an impact that had on his former teammates. More practically, the knock-on effect the tragedy had on Liverpool's pre-season preparations left several players struggling for fitness, particularly late on in games when the team needed a goal.
"It's difficult to pinpoint one overriding reason for why Liverpool's Anfield form in 2026 has been as indifferent as it has for at least a decade, but the origins perhaps trace back to the start of last season," Paul Gorst, Liverpool correspondent for the Liverpool Echo, told ESPN.
"Arne Slot took an undercooked, grieving squad of Premier League champions into the 2025-26 campaign after considerably rejigging the first team's makeup with several new players signed. As performances and results started to suffer from late September onwards, the noise on the Kop began to quieten down. Slot's brand of football quickly became one-paced and ordinary.
"A confidence-shot group of players, who by [former Liverpool defender] Andy Robertson's own admission, had no interest in football at that time, ran out of ideas and were unable to give the crowd the sort of jolt that launches them into action on the terraces."
Across the whole of 2026, Live

items.summary:
A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court

District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the
items.text:
A second judge blocks Trump's arch, saying it's unlikely to succeed in court
A federal judge in Virginia plans to issue a preliminary injunction blocking President Trump's triumphal arch indefinitely.
District Judge Leonie Brinkema said during a Friday hearing that she would grant the request of the county board of Arlington, Va., which sued over the arch in October. Democracy Forward, the nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, confirmed the ruling in a statement shared with NPR.
"We are pleased that the court has recognized the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court," said senior counsel Kate Talmor.
Justice Department spokesperson Matthew Nies told NPR it will appeal the decision immediately.
The 250-foot arch would be built in Memorial Circle, which is part of D.C. but sits on the Virginia side of the Potomac River, a short distance from both Arlington National Cemetery and Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, both in Arlington.
Arlington County has argued that the arch would "cause significant harm" to its residents in multiple ways, including increasing noise and air pollution and "clogging thoroughfares needed for emergency transport services." And it said an arch that doubles as a military complex — as Trump has suggested — would pose public safety risks and require additional county resources to manage.
Arlington also argues the arch would disrupt historic sightlines between Arlington National Cemetery and D.C.'s National Mall, and pose logistical challenges for the roughly 24 to 27 funerals the cemetery holds every weekday. The county also has concerns about air and road traffic, saying construction-related delays could cause more accidents and disrupt emergency vehicles far beyond the traffic circle.
"In the last 60 days, Arlington police, fire, and emergency units have responded to approximately 200 incidents in the area surrounding the Circle, including traffic stops and assisting with unconscious persons within Arlington National Cemetery," they wrote. "And the visitors the Arch is intended to attract will increase demand for those same emergency services."
The plaintiffs, like many critics of the arch, accused the Trump administration of rushing through federally mandated environmental reviews and failing to consider alternatives. The National Park Service has defended the federal review process — which ended in approval earlier this month — and said building the arch somewhere else would defeat its purpose.
"The County brings this lawsuit to halt the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the Arch and to ensure that the 'hard look' mandated by [the National Environmental Preservation Act] is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities," the plaintiffs wrote last month.
NPR has reached out to the White House for comment. Spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR earlier this week that the administration will "continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."
Brinkema, an appointee of President Clinton, is the second judge to rule against the arch this week.
On Wednesday, D.C. District Judge Tanya Chutkan extended a restraining order that prevents the Trump administration from breaking ground through Dec. 3 while she considers the underlying legal arguments.
That case was brought earlier this year by a group that includes Vietnam War veterans and was joined by the governments of D.C. and Virginia last month. Nine Kennedy family members moved to get involved last week.
Friday's ruling goes even further, preventing construction while Arlington's legal challenge plays out.
And Brinkema suggested that Arlington is likely to prevail. The judge said in court that she didn't see "any way" the government could win the case on the merits.
She reiterated that the project lacks congressional approval, which the Trump administration has not sought. It argues that the arch is covered by a 1925 law authorizing a pair of much shorter columns at that same location, which were never built. Both judges have frowned upon that argument.
"It hurts your credibility with the court by focusing on that," Brinkema told lawyers Friday, according to Reuters.
Brinkema also called it a "rushed job," and seemed to find the government's analysis of the structure's environmental and economic impact inadequate, particularly concerning the impact of construction cranes — which the government has said would be taller than the arch itself — on airspace.
The Federal Aviation Administration has said the arch would not pose a hazard to aircraft as long as it is lit a certain way, including with a controversial eternal flame on top. But aviation safety experts are concerned that the structure would add an additional layer of risk to an already notoriously complicated airspace. They say that's especially true if it has any military capabilities, which were not included in the FAA's analysis.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, se
items.text:
Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032
The plan would replace the jail complex with four smaller jails and reduce the number of people behind bars.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has unveiled a plan to close the notorious Rikers Island jail complex by 2032, setting out how his administration hopes to shut down a facility long criticised for violence, overcrowding and poor sanitation.
The plan, released on Friday, proposes closing the jail five years after a deadline of August 2027 that was set under then-Mayor Bill de Blasio.
With less than a year to go, the four smaller jails in four New York boroughs that are meant to replace Rikers are still under construction.
The jail complex mostly holds people awaiting trial rather than serving sentences after conviction.
“For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane,” said Mamdani in a statement.
“We have a legal and moral obligation to close Rikers,” he said.
How does Mamdani plan to close Rikers Island?
The mayor’s strategy involves reducing the number of people held at Rikers from 6,700 to no more than 4,100 by expanding alternatives to detention, restoring online bail payments, investing in programmes that aim to reduce repeat offending, and shortening court delays.
Court delays can leave people “detained for years in what is essentially legal purgatory”, said Mamdani at a news conference on Friday. The city plans to set up a task force to deal with bottlenecks and improve how agencies share evidence.
Under the new timeline, the first replacement jail will open in Brooklyn in 2029, with the rest completed by 2032. The city plans to also make hospital beds available for people in custody who have serious mental health or medical needs.
“Any family member of someone held at Rikers will tell you how isolating that jail is, how it can take hours to visit a loved one,” Mamdani said, adding that the new jails would be closer to courts and public transport, and would help integrate imprisoned New Yorkers back into the city.
Why is Rikers Island notorious?
Rikers Island, near LaGuardia airport in New York’s East River, opened in 1932 and has long faced criticism over violence, abuse, and unsanitary conditions, with campaigners pushing for its closure for over a decade.
The facility has been tied to cases like that of Kalief Browder, who spent three years there awaiting trial before the charges against him were dismissed. He died by suicide in 2015 aged 22, two years after his release.
City lawmakers voted to close Rikers in 2019, and Mamdani has blamed the city’s inability to meet the 2027 deadline to build the replacement jails on the previous administration.
Once the jail closes, Mamdani said he wants the island to be used for renewable energy and projects to help the city withstand the effects of climate change.
“Our hope is that the new Rikers Island will be unrecognisable,” he said.

items.title: Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
items.summary:
Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
- Published
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty
items.text:
Indian man sentenced to 19-plus years in plot to assassinate US-based Sikh separatist leader
- Published
A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.
US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019. He previously told the BBC, "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".
India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.
At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.
"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."
- Indian man admits plot to kill US-based Sikh separatist leader 
  - Published14 February
- Who was Canadian Sikh leader Hardeep Singh Nijjar? 
  - Published2 October 2023
- Why are some Sikhs calling for a separate state? 
  - Published1 December 2023
- Canada accuses India of role in Sikh leader's murder 
  - Published19 September 2023
India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.
In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."
Nadine Yousif contributed to this report.

The club have also been warned about their fut
items.text:
Chelsea fined £150,000 for discriminatory chanting
- Published
Chelsea have been fined £150,000 by the Football Association as part of a punishment for anti-Catholic and anti-Irish chants during an FA Cup third-round win at Charlton Athletic in January.
The club have also been warned about their future conduct and had an action plan imposed on them in relation to the offence.
"Chelsea FC failed to ensure its spectators and/or supporters (and anyone purporting to be supporters or followers) did not behave in an improper, offensive, abusive or insulting way with either an express or implied reference to religion or belief," said an FA statement., external
Chelsea admitted the charge but had an appeal against the fine issued by an independent regulatory commission rejected.
The FA's written reasons stated that although the discriminatory chanting "lasted approximately one minute and was not repeated, the scale of participation was a significant aggravating feature".
"We unequivocally condemn this behaviour," said a Chelsea statement., external "Sectarian abuse - chanting that creates division targeted towards a particular religious or political group - and discriminatory language of any kind has no place in our football club.
"Chelsea takes a zero-tolerance approach towards discriminatory behaviour in whatever form it takes. We will always take steps to identify those responsible and take appropriate action where necessary."
The FA itself was fined by Uefa for a similar incident of chanting, from England's away support during their Nations League victory in Spain on Sunday.

items.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
items.summary:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said
items.text:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published2 hours ago
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published2 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published2 hours ago
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
'Brainstorming process'
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
'Endless betrayal'
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

items.title: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
items.summary:
At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
November 20, 2026
The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms
items.text:
At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
November 20, 2026
The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.
But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.
"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.
The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.
Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.
"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."
2028 climate report card risks delay
At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.
That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.
The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.
"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.
But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.
The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.
Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.
"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking off the record.
It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.
Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable. "We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."
But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.
EU stresses need to 'protect the integrity of climate science'
In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."
The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: at past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.
Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."
Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.
Disinformation hindering climate action
The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.
DW was able to obtain a copy of a presentation which included misleading statements on the COP's electrification targets, one of the key goals at this year's talks. Turkey has proposed boosting global electrification to 35% by 2035, to reduce the world's reliance on planet-warming fossil fuels.
The contents of the presentation, said to have been leaked to some states in advance, was confirmed to DW by two countries. Its origin, however, could not be verified.
The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.
The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.
This article was originally written in Ger

Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unrav
items.text:
US tech sell-off continues as Anthropic tumbles after mega IPO
Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing but that was not the case on Friday.
Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street has fizzled out a day later, as a dramatic unravelling of the artificial intelligence trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector.
On Friday, the stock, the biggest public stock offering ever and which surpassed $2 trillion in value at one point, was trading at $87.95, about 9.5 percent down from Thursday’s close, at about 11:30am in New York (16:30 GMT).
Widely seen as a proxy for the AI trade, Anthropic’s listing had been viewed as a potential boost for an industry struggling to regain its footing after a turbulent stretch. But the slump in price within a day of listing – though still higher than its offer price of $83.30 – while losses across other technology heavyweights suggested the IPO had done little to reverse the broader selloff.
“Investors still believe in AI but are becoming more selective about what they will pay for that growth,” said David Miller, chief investment officer at Catalyst Funds.
Among the Magnificent Seven stocks, Nvidia was down nearly 7 percent, Meta Platforms fell almost 4 percent, while Amazon and Microsoft dropped 2.1 percent and 1.7 percent, respectively.
Chip stocks also slid, with AMD down 11.2 percent, Sandisk down nearly 15 percent and Intel losing 4.3 percent.
More stocks were gaining ground within the S&P 500, but AI stocks with hefty market values have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
AI stocks have been losing ground partly over worries that their big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also run up against the recent midterm elections, where there has been a shift in power after the Republican Party, seen as more friendly to the industry, suffered an electoral sweep.
Anthropic’s stock could find support later in the year; London-based index rebalance analytics firm Intropic estimates index-tracking funds could account for purchases of up to 30 percent of Anthropic’s shares by year-end.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for the biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 percent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. On Friday, the stock was down about 7.4 percent.

Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Large rallies took place across Germany with young people protesting in Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and elsewhere
- Young people feel politicians are not taking their concerns seriously
- Chancellor Merz announces Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech
- Lufthansa to reportedly slash 1,000 positions at Frankfurt and Munich hubs
Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany on Friday, November 20:
Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in new German defense and technology investments.
During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz said, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation."
The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry."
That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences.
The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels.
The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace."
Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations."
Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.
He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.
Germany's Sky TV won't send staff to F1 race in Qatar
The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East.
Sky TV announced the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.
Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.
F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights.
The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since.
Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.
Sky TV said it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.
But it said it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis."
Gen Z protesters rally around Germany
Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.
Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.
"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.
"Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.
"So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he said. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters."
Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are currently non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.
Merz urges Ukraine to push reforms in return for investment
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Ukraine must continue to push ahead swiftly with reforms, particularly on the rule of law and tackling corruption, if it hopes to receive a prerequisite for further financial aid and investment.
Merz made the comment at a business summit in Berlin that was organized by the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.
"It is now essential to press ahead with these reforms swiftly and resolutely —particularly, and I say this openly, with regard to the rule of law and corruption," Merz told attendees.
The German chancellor said that sustained reform efforts by Kyiv were necessary to justify long-term Western support for Ukraine, adding that Germany would step up its backing in defense and humanitarian aid as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure ahead of winter.
"What we invest in Ukraine now, we will receive back many times over as dividends in the form of stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and growth," the German chancellor said.
In 2025, the two countries traded goods worth around €12 billion ($13 billion).
"Freedom and security are now unleashing forces of progress and resilience on a scale never seen before. This is precisely the stance we are now taking against the autocratic and imperialist actors of this world. We are the world of freedom," Merz added.

items.title: Chips can survive the space environment. Can their financing?
items.summary:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data cente
items.text:
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?
The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and re-sell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Research Index, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.
But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above the Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.
That may not matter to the company in the near-term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that buildout by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.
However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center buildout. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.
Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, how when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Company, Sophia Space, Orbital and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terrafab, in the US, but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.
