items.summary:
Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high l
items.text:
Protests held across Europe over wages, services, high living costs
Workers and students take to the streets as protests inspired by demonstrations in France show no sign of abating.
Protesters have rallied across 25 European countries amid a wave of public discontent over issues ranging from high living costs to military spending and the climate crisis, ramping up pressure on political leaders they accuse of ignoring the concerns of young people.
Inspired by demonstrations that have shaken France in recent months, thousands took to the streets in countries including the United Kingdom, Austria, Germany, Spain, Italy, Sweden and Croatia on Friday.
Tens of thousands of workers and students protested in more than 100 Italian cities to demand higher wages and greater investment in public services.
The rallies coincided with a general strike by Italy’s largest trade union, CGIL, that involved workers in both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare.
“Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change is growing,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said at a rally in Rome.
Demonstrators in Rome threw objects at the Ministry of Education, while in Bologna some protesters clashed with police, news agency ANSA reported. In Milan, demonstrators set fire to a cardboard tanker as well as cardboard figures depicting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and United States President Donald Trump.
The Italian rallies followed a nationwide mobilisation on October 17 that descended into rioting and looting and prompted the right-wing government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni to approve sweeping security measures and deploy the army alongside police in subsequent demonstrations.
Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry.
Opposition leaders joining demonstrations on Friday criticised Meloni’s government and its budget policies amid rising living costs. Elly Schlein, leader of the centre-left Democratic Party, said the 2027 Budget Law “does not have a vision for the future of the country” as it does not help industries but slashes funding for public healthcare and education.
Meanwhile, in Germany, campaign group “Gen Z regelt” (German for “Gen Z sorts it”) said it was organising protests in 73 cities and towns.
In Berlin, roughly 4,000 people attended a protest in the city’s Alexanderplatz square.
The Cologne protest drew fewer than the 5,000 people expected, though demonstrators still numbered in the thousands, police said.
Protesters gathered to call for greater education funding and to oppose a possible return to compulsory military service.
In Austria, several hundred people gathered outside the University of Vienna for a youth-led protest calling for more spending on education and less on weapons. Police dispersed the event after reported disturbances, saying officers used pepper spray and made several arrests.
In Croatia, students boycotted classes and staged protests in about a dozen cities, demanding greater investment in education, housing and public services rather than military spending.
Demonstrations across Europe were inspired by much larger protests in France that began in September and descended into violent confrontations with the police and looting.
On Tuesday, France’s Interior Ministry said a total of 146,000 people took part in protests across the country, with 28,000 in Paris alone. The CGT trade union put the nationwide total at just over 500,000 demonstrators.
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency.
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 percent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 percent in Spain, 11 percent in France and 20 percent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.

items.title: 'Standout candidate Murray should be Davis Cup captain one day'
items.summary:
Andy Murray: Great Britain's outgoing Davis Cup captain Leon Smith hopes Scot will one day take the role
Great Britain's outgoing Davis Cup captain Leon Smith hopes Andy Murray will one day take the role he is vacating; the Scot is not currently interested in taking over due to other commitments; Yo
items.text:
Andy Murray: Great Britain's outgoing Davis Cup captain Leon Smith hopes Scot will one day take the role
Great Britain's outgoing Davis Cup captain Leon Smith hopes Andy Murray will one day take the role he is vacating; the Scot is not currently interested in taking over due to other commitments; You can watch the ATP Finals in Turin this week on Sky Sports Tennis
Friday 20 November 2026 17:42, UK
Great Britain's outgoing Davis Cup captain Leon Smith hopes "standout candidate" Andy Murray will one day take the role he is vacating after more than 16 years.
Smith took over from John Lloyd in 2010 following a humiliating loss to Lithuania that left Britain facing relegation to the bottom level of the historic competition.
Harnessing the talents and commitment of Murray, who he coached as a junior, Smith led Britain back to the top tier and, only five years later, to a first title since 1936 when they defeated Belgium in 2015.
- Keep track of the full tennis schedule live on Sky Sports
- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract on NOW📱
Murray won all 11 singles and doubles rubbers he contested in 2015, as well as 33 out of 36 in singles in the competition overall.
The 39-year-old, who is currently head coach to Jack Draper, paid tribute to Smith, saying: "Winning the Davis Cup in 2015 with Leon as captain was one of the proudest moments of my career.
"He did a great job of bringing everyone together and making sure we all felt we had a part to play.
"I've obviously known Leon a long time, since he coached me as a kid. I think the most fun we had together was when I was playing Davis Cup and Leon was on the bench.
"I wish Leon all the best as he steps down, and good luck to the new captain."
Smith: Murray should be captain one day
Smith, whose final tournament will be next week's Finals in Bologna, where Great Britain face Germany in the quarter-finals, hopes Murray will one day take the role.
"I think it is timing for him, he's busy with his life," Smith said. "He obviously is the standout candidate, isn't he? For all the attributes and more.
"Hopefully it's something he's interested in the future.
"The Davis Cup, it's not just the ties itself. It's being at the events. It's supporting the players and their personal coaches on their journeys.
"And it's also the Olympics and his history in the Olympics is second to none.
"So I do hope it's something he does in the future, but I respect that it's not for him right now, and I can understand it.
"But I really hope at some point in the future that he does take it on."
'Greg Rusedski deserves to be in conversation'
Speaking on Sky Sports Tennis, Andy's older brother Jamie discussed the role with Gigi Salmon and Tim Henman.
The seven-time Grand Slam doubles champion said: "I think that's an interesting way to see how they're going to go about it. I think there's probably quite a few people that would quite fancy it.
"I think Greg [Rusedski] as well, with everything that he's done in his career, would definitely deserve to be in that conversation.
"I'm sure Andy will get asked about his interest levels. He certainly should be given everything that he's done for tennis in our country."
Henman reflected on Smith's tenure by saying: "A big part of that role was making sure that Andy turned up to play and then giving him the environment to go out and perform as well as he could.
"Andy at that time was loving playing Davis Cup, representing his country and the team went from strength to strength.
"When Leon started, they were at the bottom of professional tennis, but they worked their way up to lifting the trophy in Belgium."

Saturday
Football
8am (all times GMT)Matchday live
The international break is over as domestic football boogies back. Primed to feel the force is Dominic Booth at the helm of our essential gateway to the weekend’s action. Saturday offers a magnificent seven Premier League matches, bookended by Manchester City v Fulham and Newcastle v Arsenal. There is also a full programme of Championship, League One, and League Two fixtures, plus Celtic and Rangers taking to the Glasgow greensward in Scotland. In the WSL, Liverpool host Chelsea before rich kids London City prepare to receive Crystal Palace. For breaking news, reader input and good vibes aplenty – join the conversation at matchday.live@theguardian.com.
T20 cricket
8.15am Australia v England live
To the background buzz of Australian cricket ripping itself apart over sandpapergate, England kick off their T20 series at the same venue they became world champions four years ago. The Melbourne Cricket Ground has not always been a happy hunting ground for touring England sides but Harry Brook’s last two visits as captain have been triumphant. A two-day win at the 90,000-capacity venue in last year’s Boxing Day Test was not only the high point of a traumatic Ashes campaign; it was their first red-ball victory on Australian soil since 2011. MCG also hosted England’s T20 World Cup triumph in 2022, where Brook was part of the side that defeated Pakistan to lift the trophy behind enemy lines. Rob Smyth has over-by-over coverage with Ali Martin reporting from Melbourne.
Premier League
12.30pmManchester City v Fulham live
The lunchtime kick-off is a vital one for the hosts. City have wobbled of late, three straight Premier League defeats leave the beleaguered club in third with 21 points from the first 10 games of Enzo Maresca’s tenure. In stark contrast, the Cottagers are unbeaten in their last four games, after four defeats and two draws in their first six. Wins over Hull and Coventry came before draws with Aston Villa and Newcastle. Barry Glendenning helms the blog as Will Unwin reports from the Etihad Stadium.
Rugby union
2.10pmEngland v New Zealand
England are have been transformed since stumbling through the Six Nations and then falling to South Africa at Ellis Park, winning four consecutive Tests, amassing 36 tries and addressing their disciplinary lapses. Aided by thumping victories over Fiji and Japan, they have rebuilt impressively to secure a shot at reaching the Nations Championship final, but New Zealand provide the true measure of their progress. Only South Africa are higher in the rankings and a year out from the 2027 World Cup final, it is the opportunity for Steve Borthwick’s men to make a statement. Lee Calvert blogs the action and the trio of Robert Kitson, Andy Bull and Gerard Meagher making up our Twickenham reporting team.
Tennis
2.30pmATP Finals live
Katy Murrells is at the controls of our tennis liveblog as the semi-finals pan out in Turin. The first session starts at 2.30pm, with the evening match due to start at about 8.30pm.
Premier League
3pmClockwatch
Emillia Hawkins keeps the updates flowing on the five afternoon kick-offs: Aston Villa v Sunderland, Bournemouth v Nottingham Forest, Chelsea v Leeds, Coventry v Crystal Palace, and Tottenham v Ipswich – the pick of the bunch. Roberto De Zerbi seemed to be making an impact at Spurs before a defeat by Leeds tripped up his side. Their record is grim against the Tractor Boys: four defeats in their last five Premier league games.
Rugby union
4.40pmIreland v South Africa live
Lee Calvert is back on deck as Ireland risk a Springbok backlash from a side bruised by defeat by France and furious at their coach, Rassie Erasmus, for getting banned after his incendiary “match-fixing” comments. There is more at stake in this November’s meeting between the sides than last year’s chaotic Test. The Irish were down to 12 men at one stage and the Springboks won 24-13 for their first win in Dublin since 2012. Both countries are still in the running to top their respective pools and play in the final on Finals weekend at Twickenham. Brendan Fanning reports. 
Premier League
 5.30pmNewcastle v Arsenal live
City’s slump has allowed the defending champions, Arsenal, to seize early control and they will hope to continue their relentless start to the season. They head to Newcastle where a toxic reception awaits Bruno Guimarães as he returns to Tyneside in Arsenal colours for the first time since his summer move. The Gunners are five points clear of second-placed Brighton at the top after winning nine of their first 10 games. Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent hosts have managed just one win in their past five league matches, losing to Everton and Aston Villa along the way. Join Rob Smyth for MBM commentary, with Louis Taylor reporting.

Kimi Antonelli may have already won the drivers’ crown, but second place in the standings is still up for grabs and Max Verstappen can tighten his grip in Sin City. The Red Bull driver is 17 points clear of Mercedes’ George Russell, who moved back up to third place, one point ahead of Lewis Hamilton after his fourth place at Interlagos. Krishani Dhanji be live blogging the race in the small hours, with Giles Richards reporting from Las Vegas.

Mauricio Pochettino takes charge of Manchester United at Anfield just days after wrapping up his reign as USA men’s coach. Victory would give him instant momentum as he fights to lift the club up the table. Earlier, hard-charging Brighton will fancy their chances against Hull, who have not won a Premier League match since August. items.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary:
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:
- Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time bl
items.text:
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:
- Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions, which is formalized in Lean here.
- Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization. Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof.
- Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). (UPDATE: the moderators of the Lean thread are now focusing the discussion on the Lean-related aspects of the proof only.) I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task.
See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026
What you need to know
- Zelenskyy said the Russian attack included 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles
- At least 8 people were killed and several bridges and energy facilities were hit
- Poland called a violation of its airspace by the Russian attack an 'intentional provocation'
- France has called for a UN Security Council meeting in light of the attacks
Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:
German defense minister open to talks with Russia
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius "welcomed in every respect" a move by Russian President Vladimir Putin to consult Europeans on the future of Ukraine (see entries below for more details).
During a trip to the Polish capital Warsaw, Pistorius added that declining such an invitation to Moscow would send the "completely wrong signal."
"We need to talk. Only by talking can we ultimately achieve results," he said.
Pistorius said reaching an agreement was the goal — not simply sitting down in a room together.
"He [Putin] must now show that he truly means what he says and that he will then take the necessary steps to ensure that, at the very least, a ceasefire is established and that peace-sustaining stability can once again take hold in Europe," the German minister said.
The comments came the same day a pair of Russian missiles and a drone were reported to have violated Polish airspace (see entries below).
While Russian officials said Germany, France and the UK had been invited to send representatives to talks on Ukraine, no details about a time or place for such talks have been announced.
Denmark expels Russian attache after thwarted attempt to kill Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner
Denmark's PET intelligence service has said it suspected Russia was behind a plot to kill a US-Ukrainian rapper at a Copenhagen concert.
"In our assessment, this case shows that Russian intelligence services attempted to carry out a targeted killing in Denmark," PET head Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen told a news conference.
Kieffer-Kristensen added that Russia was suspected of enlisting the help of a local criminal gang for the killing.
The Danish Foreign Ministry subsequently summoned the Russian ambassador and expelled the Russian Embassy's defense attache, Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said.
The foreign minister also called on European countries to stop issuing visas to Russians and said the Danish government would have taken harsher steps if Russia had a larger diplomatic presence in Denmark.
Comparing before and after Ukraine's strikes on the Kerch bridge
This week, Ukraine launched a series of strikes on the Kerch bridge, which links occupied Crimea to mainland Russia.
The 19-kilometer (12-mile) bridge has both rail and roadways, part of which has been destroyed in the strikes.
The bridge is widely seen as a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, and damage to it is regarded as a significant psychological blow to Moscow.
Following the strikes, Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate and warned the response would be "far more painful" than the damage Ukraine had caused to the Kerch bridge, as seen in the sliding image below.
Ukraine child casualties at highest level in nearly 4 years — UN
At least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first 10 months of 2026, the United Nations said.
UNICEF, the UN's children's agency, said that between January and October, at least 114 children were killed and 1,030 injured.
The agency said it was the highest number of casualties seen in more than 3 years.
"That is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day" this year, said UNICEF spokeswoman Louise Wateridge.
Last month alone, at least 146 children were killed or injured across Ukraine, the UN agency said.
"Attacks involving missiles and armed drones continue to put children and families at risk in their homes, schools, and communities, including far from the frontline," UNICEF warned.
UK's Andy Burnham condemns Russian violation of Polish airspace
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has called Russia's violation of Polish airspace "utterly unacceptable."
"The incursion into Polish airspace is utterly unacceptable. I condemn it unreservedly," Burnham said at an EU-UK summit press conference in Brussels.
The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the "Coalition of the Willing" that groups allies of Ukraine, including the UK.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the move was a Russian provocation aimed at dividing Europe.
"Europe will not be deterred from our support for Ukraine," Streeting said. "We will not allow Putin to divide our continent, and we recognise that the frontline in Ukraine is the frontline for freedom and democracy everywhere."
Moscow invites Germany, France and UK for talks on Ukraine — Russian media
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov has reportedly invited representatives from Germany, France and the UK to Moscow for talks on the war in Ukraine, according to Russian news agency Interfax.
"We are waiting for a reply," the diplomat was reported to have said.
On Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said European officials would be invited to Moscow to discuss whether they should participate in US-led talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine.
Interfax reported that Ryabkov stressed that such a visit would not automatically mean that European nations would be involved in the negotiations on ending the war on Ukraine.
A statement from the French president's office said Europeans were ready to visit Moscow if given a full role in Ukraine talks.

items.text:
Gen Z in Germany: Better educated, bleaker future
November 20, 2026
It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing professional training or university. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city and finally starting to live independently is nearly impossible.
Nor do young people feel that politicians are finally taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It therefore shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe are taking to the streets this Friday to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 cities, coinciding with World Children's Day.
What particularly infuriates young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.
One example from the political realm was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.
It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran the headline: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."
"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests," he argues.
Gen Z is better educated but faces a bleaker future
However, eighteen-year-old Erik Sczygiol is an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW).This year's report is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z. The report is titled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future."
The United Nations surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries. Some of the findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them. Today, 78% of adolescents complete at least upper-secondary education. Yet finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise across the globe.
This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, financial independence is often not achieved until one's mid-to-late twenties, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities until one's early-to-mid thirties.
Young people are underrepresented in the German parliament
Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."
Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.
At least Brod is somewhat closer to the political decision-making process. He has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.
Political participation often remains purely symbolic
Nevertheless, both Florian Brod and Erik Sczygiol, who represents students, have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.
"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.
Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."
The promise that 'our children will have a better life' no longer holds true
Medical student Amélie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva this May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. items.text:
Top US Democrat warns Trump admin against destroying records
In a new letter, Congressman Jamie Raskin says officials in the US government are ignoring federal recordkeeping laws.
A top Democrat, who will wield significant investigative powers in the United States Congress starting in January, has warned US law enforcement agencies to preserve records, including encrypted communications on digital messaging apps.
In letters sent on Thursday to the US Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Congressman Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the next likely chairman of the US House Judiciary Committee, wrote to the cabinet-level agencies to remind their employees of a legal obligation to “safeguard” records against destruction.
Letters were also sent to the heads of three subagencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Prisons (BOP).
Raskin disclosed he has obtained evidence that government officials in the Trump administration have been using non-government apps, like Signal, to send disappearing messages.
The Maryland Democrat, who is currently the Judiciary Committee’s ranking member, appended a screenshot of a Signal exchange between FBI General Counsel Samuel Ramer and Drew Lynch, an associate of President Donald Trump’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, showing a conversation where messages were set to automatically delete after one week.
“The FBI’s top lawyer should be ensuring that all 35,000 FBI employees are preserving government and law enforcement records”, Raskin wrote to US Attorney General Todd Blanche.
“Instead, he has conducted official business on a platform specifically configured to erase communications.”
The incident, Raskin wrote, is “just one of many” that have been reported to the Judiciary Committee, raising concern among Democrats that the Trump administration could be ignoring federal recordkeeping laws by destroying documents before likely congressional investigations.
“There is significant evidence that Trump Administration officials have engaged in the widespread destruction, mutilation, and concealment of government records”, Raskin wrote. “This attempt to evade transparency extends to the highest levels of federal agencies, including top-ranking law enforcement officials”.
Raskin instructed the federal officials to take “immediate action to recover these records” from data backups or “associated metadata,” asking them to comply by December 3.
The Trump administration has signalled it intends to fight any probes by US Democrats, who won control of both chambers of the US Congress earlier this month in the country’s midterm elections.
According to a letter viewed by Al Jazeera, the White House’s top lawyer, Will Scharf, wrote to US House Democrats on Wednesday, pushing back against demands from the incoming Democratic majorities, such as Raskin’s, because the new Congress has not yet been sworn in.
“Your demands do not reflect a request of the House, Senate, or a committee to which that body’s oversight authority has been delegated,” Scharf wrote. “As a result, Ranking Member requests in the 119th Congress do not trigger any obligation to ‘accommodate[e] … the needs of the conflicting branches'”.
In response to Raskin’s letter, a White House official told Al Jazeera the administration complies “with all federal record retention laws and regulations”.
The DOJ echoed the White House’s response, saying it “follows all legal requirements for the management of federal records involving its official functions and decisions.”
“The men and women of the DOJ who work tirelessly to arrest and prosecute criminals will not be intimidated by a congressman who once called 2020 riots ‘magnificent’ and ‘nonviolent'”, the agency said about Raskin.
Al Jazeera also reached out to DHS, FBI, ICE and BOP for comment but has not yet heard back.

items.text:
UK far-right activist ‘Danny Tommo’ jailed for slashing migrant boat
Daniel Thomas livestreamed himself slashing a dinghy used to bring migrants from France to the UK.
A British far-right anti-immigration activist has been jailed for 15 months for criminal damage for slashing a small boat which had brought migrants from France to the United Kingdom.
Daniel Thomas, also known as “Danny Tommo”, is the founder of the British anti-migrant Patriot Platform group, which mobilised hundreds of protesters earlier this year. He pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month, after slashing the inflatable vessel while a French emergency responder was on board.
Sentencing Thomas on Friday, judge James Newton-Price said the offence “amounted to flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption” of French and British authorities’ important activities in the English Channel.
“They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover,” he added.
Thomas livestreamed himself on September 22 as he followed a small boat carrying migrants across the Channel, who were transferred onto another vessel and taken ashore.
The 37-year-old later approached the dinghy and slashed it with a knife, soon after a French rescue worker had stepped on board. British police arrested him shortly after the incident.
Prosecutor Joel Smith told Portsmouth Crown Court that Thomas had shouted “get off the boat, you’ve got time to get off the boat … take them back, no more of these”.
‘Thuggish’
Thomas appeared in court via videolink from prison, with his head bowed and rarely looked up as footage of the incident was played.
Judge Newton-Price accepted that “there was no immediate danger to the rescue worker”, but said Thomas’s actions were a deliberate attempt to disrupt rescue efforts.
The far-right activist had built a large online following and organised gatherings of protesters on the UK’s southern coast in response to the arrivals of small boats.
A government minister described the demonstrations as “thuggish”.
The court heard that Thomas had five previous convictions, including in 2016 for kidnapping.
Separately, he is set to stand trial in London next June accused of multiple offences, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing centre in Dover in March.
UK government data shows the number of people arriving in small boats to British shores has fallen, though the crossings remain a prominent political issue which has dogged successive governments. Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration activists have called for more action.

Cheavon Clarke catapulted himself into the top tier of the cruiserweight division with his stunning stoppage victory over Chris Billam-Smith.
Billam-Smith is a highly-experienced world champion, well known for hard-fought victories over the likes of Lawrence Okolie and Richard Riakporhe.
"I've always been world class. It's just waiting on the world to catch up and see it. That fight gave me the opportunity to do that. We're getting there," Clarke told Sky Sports.
When they fought at the Copper Box Arena earlier this month, Clarke did something no one had managed before - he dropped Billam-Smith (twice in fact) and stopped him.
"To Chris' detriment, he's a tough guy and in boxing it's not the place to be tough," Clarke said. "History is a great tell of the future. Every tough guy has a day where he's not tough no more. Unfortunately that was Chris' day."
Clarke has come back from defeat himself and doesn't rule out Billam-Smith doing the same.
"It doesn't mean that that's the end of it for Chris. Because he's been a world champion, he's got the experience, he can carry on," Clarke said.
"People need to stop writing him off. I've seen some comments online, just wild. It's not my business to be defending him, I'm not his lawyer… You just need to be factual."
Though he does expect Billam-Smith to take plenty of time to recover rather than pursue a rematch.
"There was talks of this after the fight, but who knows? What does it do for Chev's career right now, bearing in mind that I'm currently ranked above him," Clarke said.
"I'm looking to fight the guys above me and trying to make what makes sense for me."

items.title: Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
items.summary:
Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.
Less than half of Rep
items.text:
Trump initially accepted the midterm results, but most GOP voters doubt they were fair
President Trump may have initially accepted the results of his party's midterm losses, but data released Friday shows there is still broad distrust in the elections process among Republicans.
Less than half of Republican voters nationwide considered the midterm elections "free and fair," according to new polling by the University of California San Diego. Just 52% of Republicans said they trusted votes were counted accurately.
Loading...
In comparison, after the 2024 election that Trump won, more than 80% of Republicans said they had confidence in the vote-counting process.
While trust in elections often dips for voters of the losing party, the GOP has seen bigger swings in confidence in recent years, as Trump has falsely claimed that U.S. elections are corrupt.
"There are still a lot of people who remain unconvinced that they can trust elections," said Thad Kousser, a co-director of UC San Diego's Center for Transparent and Trusted Elections. "And they're predominantly located in one [political] party."
Overall, a wide majority — 66% — of Americans said they think the midterms were fair. That represents an improvement from before the election, when less than half of U.S. adults said they expected free and fair contests.
But that post-election increase in trust was buoyed by Democrats and independents — many of whom worried before Election Day about potential federal interference at the polls that didn't come to pass.
"It would be a mistake to [look at the 66%] and think, 'Oh, everyone has a pretty good view of the election,'" said Lauren Prather, also a co-director of UC San Diego's election center. "It really buries the lede a little bit about the partisan gap."
The widespread doubt among Republicans may be a reality check for those wondering whether Trump's brand of election denial has run its course in American politics.
On the one hand, there will be fewer politicians who deny or question election results in office next year. And the vast majority of election-denying candidates running for positions involved in overseeing statewide elections lost their races this year, according to tracking by the advocacy group States United Action.
Election experts have also celebrated as Trump and high-profile losing candidates on the ballot this year conceded their losses.
"Sure, I'll accept [the results]," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier on election night, as it became clear Democrats would retake the House and Senate. "Why wouldn't I?"
But just a few days later, he began conspiracy theorizing about those same results.
"Does anybody really believe that this 'Election' was honest," Trump posted online.
The new polling from UC San Diego shows that among Republicans, there still may be a receptive audience to such claims. When asked if politicians are discussing voter fraud too much, too little or about the right amount, just 15% of Republicans answered "too much."
"There is both demand among the Republican base for continued focus on this issue, and as we saw even after the election, politicians are continuing to supply it," Kousser said. "As long as those two dynamics are there, there's still going to be a market for these concerns."
To be clear, in most elections — domestically and internationally — supporters of the losing party usually see a dip in trust.
"It's sort of like asking people after an overtime basketball game, do you trust the referees?" Kousser said.
But in an ideal world, he said that oscillation would be more like 10 percentage points in either direction. Not the 30-point swing seen among Republicans between 2024 and 2026.
The numbers do still represent an improvement from 2020, however. At that time, leading up to the Jan. 6 riot at the U.S. Capitol in 2021, just 22% of Republicans said they had confidence in the nationwide vote count, according to similar polling done by MIT's Election Data and Science Lab.

items.text:
James Anderson: England legend loses Italia T10 league debut for Napoli Knights in first match since Lancashire exit
James Anderson was released by Lancashire at the end of the County Championship season and has joined Surrey in 2027; Anderson is among the players in action for Napoli Knights, a T10 franchise league in Italy
Friday 20 November 2026 18:02, UK
James Anderson’s franchise cricket return ended in defeat as Napoli Knights lost to Rome Gladiators by six wickets in their Italia T10 league opener.
Anderson is co-owner of Napoli Knights, with the 44-year-old's appearance his first since being released by boyhood club Lancashire at the end of the season.
Napoli Knights are one of six teams in the nine-day tournament at Roma Cricket Ground, running until November 28, with Anderson's side restricted to 73-9 after losing the toss and batting first.
- James Anderson 'sad' and 'shocked' by Lancashire release
- Stuart Broad blasts Lancashire's 'disrespectful' treatment
- Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract
Anderson finished nought not out from one delivery faced, scampering a bye from the final ball of the innings, before taking 0-14 from two overs during Rome Gladiators' successful chase.
England's history-making Test bowler conceded just three from a tight opening over of Rome's chase, before being hit down the ground by Singh for a maximum - during an 11-run over - when returning for a second stint later in the innings.
Anthony Mosca fired an unbeaten 45 from 27 deliveries and Jaspreet Singh ended 15 not out from nine, as Rome Gladiators claimed a five-wicket win with two balls remaining.
Wayne Madsen, captaining the Napoli Knights: "It's fantastic to have Jimmy [Anderson] here. He's inspirational to so many of us.
"To be playing with him, and for him to share his knowledge with this group, is amazing. I think, as we've seen, he has still got the skill to go out there and perform at the top level."
Napoli Knights have further matches against Brescia Lions (Saturday), Venice Livewire (Sunday), Milan Icons (Monday) and Bologna Hurricanes (TBC).
Anderson has joined Surrey ahead of the 2027 season in the Rothesay County Championship, having been left "sad" and "quite shocked" by his contract not being extended by Lancashire.
Upon the announcement of his move to the Kia Oval, Anderson said: "It's an honour to join a club like Surrey and I can't wait to start a new chapter in my career. I still feel like I have a lot to offer, taking wickets, trying to help the team win games of cricket.
"I also think that I can bring a lot to the team off the field and help those young players who are looking to develop their skillset and go on and represent their country."
Anderson, who turns 45 in July of next year, will get the opportunity to add to his haul of 1,193 first-class wickets and perhaps more silverware to a glittering CV.

items.title: Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada
items.summary:
Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada
- Published
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".
In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charg
items.text:
Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada
- Published
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".
In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".
However, he feels some of it has gone too far.
"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.
"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."
United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.
In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.
Man Utd happy with summer transfers; Pochettino wants say in future deals
Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".
Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.
Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.
Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.
However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.
"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.
"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.
"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.
"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."
When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.
"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.
"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."
We have to put Man Utd into a different place - Pochettino
Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".
Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.
He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".
The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.
"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.
"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."
Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.
Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.
United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.
Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.
"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.
"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."

items.summary:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exer
items.text:
Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
- Published
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

items.text:
‘A more expensive EU is not a better EU’: Austria's Minister for Europe, Claudia Bauer
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
This week's programme hosted Claudia Bauer, Austria’s Federal Minister for Europe, Integration and Family while she was in Paris for the recent G7 meeting. She offered her thoughts on the diplomatic moves surrounding Ukraine, transatlantic relations, EU enlargement and a headscarf ban in Austrian schools that has caused disquiet. We also talked about the thorny negotiations involved in the EU’s next long-term budget: the Multiannual Financial Framework.
Bauer shared her perspective as one of the EU’s "frugal" member states when it comes to financial matters. "I think there needs to be a more balanced proposal on the EU budget. And that's what we are aiming for," she said. "It is clear that a more expensive European Union is not a better European Union. The so-called ‘frugals’ – I call them the net contributors, because we have nine countries out of 27 that are net contributors to the European Union, and this third of the member countries finances two-thirds of the EU budget."
Asked about the proposal championed by France to raise extra revenue through ‘own resources’ – taxing digital services and cryptocurrencies, for example – Bauer replied:
"We are open for this discussion and we are also very constructive in this discussion. But we do not see ‘own resources’ as a silver bullet." She added that Austria is also opposing CORE – originally an EU Commission idea that could create a new form of corporate tax for the EU budget. "Another tax for companies in Europe; this works totally against our common goal of strengthening our competitiveness and of strengthening our workforce here in Europe, our production and industry here in Europe," Bauer emphasised.
Austria is a big supporter of EU enlargement to the Western Balkans and Bauer said that enlargement is the EU’s "most important strategic instrument, our most important geostrategic instrument." But she also stressed that membership of the bloc has to stay merit based. "There cannot be a fast track for Ukraine. The same rules must apply to all the candidate countries, and there are necessary reforms that have to be made also by Ukraine. We are not supporting the idea of two classes of candidate countries."
Bauer added that "our main goal must be that there will be, hopefully sooner than later, a lasting peace, a fair peace in Ukraine. That's what we are working for."
Asked about how the defeat of US President Donald Trump’s Republican party in the US midterms might affect transatlantic ties, Bauer said: "A little bit more predictability would be good for all of us. We need a strong and stable transatlantic partnership. But we must be clear: for far too long we in Europe relied just on the United States. And now we learned that we have to do our homework as well, when it comes to our resilience, when it comes to security policy, and also on trade policy."

items.text:
10 years after divisive Brexit referendum, UK weighs a ‘Breturn’ to the EU
Prime Minister Andy Burnham returns from the UK-EU summit with a potential new deal and a new start.
A decade after the narrow vote to leave the EU, the United Kingdom is showing every sign of buyer’s remorse.
For many, the bitterly fought contest over the referendum on whether to leave the EU was unpleasant and divisive.
Couples and families reportedly split over where they stood on the referendum. Each side of the debate – Leave and Remain – became a cipher for how people saw themselves and their country in a changing world.
As the campaign unfolded amid accusations of foreign influence and dirty tricks, the murder of a politician, a debate over economics and political sovereignty, a visceral fight intensified over identity, belonging and competing visions of what it meant to be British.
Critics and pro-Brexit slammed various exit deals that successive governments negotiated with Brussels as somehow a betrayal of what had originally been a binary choice.
The EU, the trading bloc the UK sat uneasily within for nearly half a century, remains the country’s biggest trading partner.
On Friday, in a joint news conference with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, following the latest UK-EU summit in Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed the first in a series of expected deals with the EU as rebuilding “the bridges that were broken all those years ago”.
The agreements, which cover three main areas – easing trade restrictions, expanding opportunities for young people to live and work across borders, and addressing carbon levies – were characterised by Burnham as “a good deal for Britain” and regarded as first steps towards bringing the UK back into the EU’s orbit.
Does the UK want to rejoin?
Some in the UK believe that leaving the single market and customs union brought little tangible benefit while creating additional paperwork, border checks and barriers to trade with the UK’s largest export market. Others have no regrets about leaving the bloc.
According to polling expert Sir John Curtice, surveys show an average of 62 percent favour rejoining, against 38 percent for staying out, once undecided respondents are excluded.
“Whatever the nuances, the UK public are certainly in a different place on the EU than [they were] in 2016,” he told Al Jazeera.
Could the UK Breturn?
According to some analysts, the government – which is not bound by a single written constitution – could, with the EU’s agreement, begin the process of rejoining without holding another referendum, or even including the commitment in an election manifesto.
However, doing so would inevitably be politically difficult and, according to Professor Curtice, almost certain to be highly unpopular.
“The Brexit referendum in 2016 was not legally binding,” Sionaidh Douglas-Scott, the chair in Law at Queen Mary University of London, wrote by email. “Legally, it could have been ignored altogether. But it was thought to be politically unacceptable to ignore the public’s vote in the referendum. And political parties can ignore their election manifesto pledges at their peril,” she said, referring to parties’ reliance on public trust to support any agenda.
“I suspect Burnham might be tempted to have a referendum on the issue of rejoining the EU, feeling that public opinion had changed sufficiently to render a rejoin vote likely, although that’s by no means certain,” she said. “Some senior members of the [governing Labour] party … clearly feel that rejoining should be a manifesto pledge. So, politically, steps might be taken to make it more acceptable.”
Meanwhile, questions remained over the terms on which the UK might rejoin the bloc, whether it would be required to adopt the euro – a prospect it had previously resisted – and what form the EU itself might take following elections in some of its most influential member states, including France, Germany and Spain.
Polling suggests a distinction between support for closer relations with the EU as opposed to support for full membership.
While some surveys put support for rejoining at about 35 percent when closer ties were offered as an alternative, Curtice said support for closer relations was often less firmly held.
“Much of that support is soft – people say they somewhat support rather than strongly support” closer ties, he explained. By contrast, around half of those supporting rejoining the EU say they “strongly support” it, suggesting a deeper commitment to that option.
Similarly, at home, many of the more prominent figures of the original campaign to leave Europe have resurfaced and appear to be marshalling their forces against any return or realignment.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, one of Brexit’s most prominent campaigners, returned to Brussels on Thursday to oppose the prime minister’s efforts.
Other figures associated with the Leave campaign have also re-emerged, including former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and his former cabinet ally, Michael Gove, now a magazine editor. They have revived loosely sourced claims about the financial cost of rejoining the EU – or even of having remained a member. The campaign group Stay Out, for instance, puts the annual cost at 39.3 billion pounds (approximately $51.4bn), equivalent to 750 million pounds (about $982m) a week.
“I think we should think about two things when we think about Brexit and the potential to rejoin: trauma and salience,” Anand Menon, professor at King’s College London and director of UK in a Changing Europe, said. “Some people felt traumatised by the first debate and don’t want to revisit it. At the same time, the issue has lost its salience. The public don’t consider it one of the main issues facing the country,” he said.
“If you cast your mind back to 2016, those supporting Leave, like Nigel Farage, took the EU, which the public never really thought about, and linked it in the public’s mind to something they absolutely did

items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
items.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has solved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic a
items.text:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has solved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’ most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics, and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

items.text:
WHERE WERE WE?
Just like taking the Manchester United job or listening in on a conversation with Stephen Warnock, the men’s international break can be a long, hard slog, a domestic hiatus so long that we can forget both basic hygiene and how the clubs are faring in the Best League in the World™: the Championship the Premier League. So after desperately trying to break into either tears or just a smile at Harry Kane’s appearance record – no dice, unfortunately – here is a rundown on the state of play for each club, as we prepare for a weekend of football that might actually make us feel something.
1 Arsenal There are some genuinely likable things about the Gunners – Bukayo Saka, Paul Merson being a bit giddy, Ben White’s apathy to it all – but Arsenal fans were a lot easier to manage when they weren’t this good. It’s theirs to lose, etc.
2 Brighton Turns out all you need to turn your club into genuine title contenders is a world-class recruitment programme and Pascal Gross to accidentally realise that he’s the second coming aged 35.
3 Manchester City Enjoy it while it lasts, lads.
4 Liverpool These lot haven’t been title contenders since Mohamed Salah started playing like Robert Snodgrass and haven’t looked like vastly improving since replacing the right-winger with various different, expensive left-wingers.
5 Chelsea Anything could and probably will happen with the Blues, and that’s not a compliment.
6 Everton The Toffees should be worse than last season – Iliman Ndiaye has left, Jack Grealish issued a grovelling apology after going awol, their only striker is Thierno Barry – but instead they are much, much better. David Moyes, the genius grandpa of the league at 63, will set a new Everton record for games managed this weekend (593).
7 Bournemouth The Dorset Hydra from Greek mythology. Every time you cut off its head, or sell a defender to PSG or Real Madrid, they come back stronger. Since Alex Scott was injured on 3 October, Bournemouth lost at Chelsea and then won eight on the bounce. Make it make sense.
8 Brentford This underdog narrative is wearing a little thin now. Brentford are just a well-oiled football machine but they have no mates and worse, no enemies. What a sad little life. Enjoy Tin Pot qualification. We hope it makes you very happy.
9 Leeds The Yorkshire club might be 78% Dominic Calvert-Lewin at this point, so only Lucas Radebe knows where they will be when the striker gets knacked, but Daniel Farke is doing a fine job with Leeds in the top half. For now.
10 Aston Villa It would be hard for any club to lose Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Ollie Watkins, Youri Tieleman and Emi Martínez in one transfer window and improve. Not much more to say. Why do we like Zion Suzuki so much? Genuinely not sure.
11 Tottenham Whisper it, but are Spurs back (to being a mid-table team again)?
12 Newcastle One win in six and a kit that looks like a barcode means it’s been a poor campaign thus far, which Matthias Jaissle and co will hope to resurrect this weekend against – checks notes – the champions. Ah.
13 Hull City A remarkable achievement that the promoted side are not anywhere near the bottom three considering there is absolutely nobody, including Sergej Jakirovic, who can name 11 current Hull players off the top of their heads.
14 Ipswich Town Shining bright like Gary O’Neil’s teeth. Keep this up and they might even survive.
15 Fulham Quick tip for Álvaro Arbeloa: when you said on Friday that “Fulham is not a jail – everyone that is here is because they want to be here”, it really makes it sound like Fulham is actually a jail, which nobody wants to be in. Roll on Manchester City (A)!
16 Nottingham Forest It’s entirely believable that Forest will follow up their 3-1 win over Manchester City with victory at Bournemouth this weekend. It’s also entirely believable that Oliver Glasner will be sacked by Christmas and Forest will be playing in the Championship next season. It’s all part of the Evangelos Marinakis Experience, baby.
17 Coventry City Genuinely quite nice to see that sky blue kit back in the top flight. All Cov fans would snap your hand off for 17th come the end of the campaign.
18 Manchester United Mauricio Pochettino has the chance to do something very, very funny over the next few months.
19 Sunderland Turns out qualifying for Europe isn’t all it’s made up to be.
20 Crystal Palace The Eagles are surely too good to go down? Their trip to Coventry this weekend absolutely stinks of a six-pointer. Hard not to believe that Thomas Frank’s lovely locks will sort out the mess in south London. Imagine if Adam Wharton had Thomas Frank’s hair? OK, that’s enough Football Daily for today.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time. I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United, Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match” – a drone operator who filmed United’s first training session under their new head coach at Carrington has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgment”. Welcome to Manchester, Mauricio.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 I’m a bit late to the party in terms of commenting on the ‘perfume in Poundland’ litigation (Football Daily letters passim). However, I can’t help thinking that David Beckham could have avoided all of this palaver if he’d arranged for Dior to manage his line of fragrances – it seems to have worked out swimmingly for Robbie Sauvage” – Paul Taverner.

items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
items.summary:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (v1), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another
items.text:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 (v1), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title:Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.
