items.title: 'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus
items.summary:
'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus
- Published
Already circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent da
items.text:
'No-one is going to break us' - defiant Boks face Ireland without Erasmus
- Published
Already circled as one of the must-see fixtures in a packed November schedule, interest in the meeting between Ireland and South Africa has intensified following their contrasting disciplinary fortunes in recent days.
Not for the first time, Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus landed himself in hot water with the powers-that-be for criticising match officials.
After receiving a six-match ban for questioning the integrity of referee Andrea Piardi and television match official Matteo Liperini in South Africa's defeat by France last week, Erasmus has been defended and condemned.
There is no doubt, however, over where the Springbok camp stand, with assistant coach Mzwandile Stick throwing his support behind Erasmus.
"He's been hands-on with our team [in the build-up], and we're in a good space," Stick said on Friday.
"Irrespective of what has happened, we love him, we appreciate him, and no-one is going to break us. I can tell you that for sure."
Erasmus also said South Africa let their country down against France, with captain Siya Kolisi bristling at a suggestion that it was a "dramatic" assessment.
"It might sound dramatic to you, but to us it means so much more," Kolisi said during his pre-match news conference.
"Rugby has done a lot for our country, and it's done a lot for many of us who come from South Africa.
"We know how happy people are and what the mood is like when we win, and when we lose, it gets tough. People care a lot about it.
"When we play, we think about the people back home. We don't take representing the country lightly because we represent every single person in South Africa when we put on that jersey."
Ireland v South Africa
Nations Championship
Saturday 21 November, 16:40 GMT
Aviva Stadium, Dublin
Live on 5 Sports Extra, BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app, with accompanying live text commentary
While Erasmus has dominated headlines this week, he will not be in attendance at Aviva Stadium on Saturday.
Instead, in a bizarre twist, the two-time World Cup winner will host a watchalong of the game from the team's Dublin hotel, with the conditions of his suspension prohibiting him from matchday contact with players and management.
Erasmus was not the only South African to receive a suspension this week with back row Jasper Wiese banned for four games for a dangerous ruck clearout against France.
While Wiese's fate did not attract the same level of scrutiny, South Africa's sense of injustice will perhaps be fuelled by the sight of Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast on Saturday.
As predicted by Erasmus, Prendergast was cleared to face the world champions after being cited for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Fiji back row Peceli Yato.
"I will tell you now for free, if that was a Fijian player tackling an Irish player with that hip-drop, that player would be in Fiji now," said Stick.
"If that was a Fijian player, he would be sitting in Fiji now doing some extra lessons of how to tackle."
Ireland focused on erasing scrum pain
Focused on erasing the pain of last year's 24-13 loss to the Springboks in Dublin, Ireland have sidestepped questions about Erasmus this week, with head coach Andy Farrell opting not to comment on his opposite number's suspension.
Irish captain Dan Sheehan said the commotion has not "affected the squad at all".
"Obviously it's a big media story for fans to get behind, but in terms of us playing the match it has zero impact," he said.
While there may be added scrutiny on referee Christophe Ridley, Sheehan said he plans to leave the official alone unless compelled to bring something "major" to his attention.
The Irish skipper has enough on his plate anyway. In addition to leading his side against the back-to-back world champions, Sheehan has been thrust into the number eight role.
The 28-year-old has won all 42 of his previous caps at hooker but moves to the back row with Caelan Doris, Jack Conan, Sean Jansen and James McNabney all ruled out.
Ireland hope Sheehan's inclusion in the back row will facilitate his powerful ball-carrying capabilities, but he insists he is not going to "overthink" it.
"I just get on with stuff. Like, eight on my back, just pick the ball up and go," said Sheehan, whose only previous start in the position was in Leinster's win over Munster last month.
"It can't be that complicated. That's my approach to it, to be honest."
Had it not been for the furore surrounding Erasmus, chances are the pre-match talk would have been dominated by scrums.
Last year, Ireland were shown five cards and conceded six penalties and a penalty try during a chastening night against the Springbok scrum.
That set-piece shellacking may have given the Irish pack nightmares over the past 12 months, and while South Africa won nine scrum penalties against France, Kolisi expects a closer contest in Dublin this time.
"Their scrum is much better than it was a year ago," he said.
"You can see they're getting penalties. But our focus is not on what they're going to do. It's about making sure we stick to our plans and do what we need to do in the scrum."
The Springboks have been boosted by the return of record cap holder Eben Etzebeth, but his second-row partner Ruan Nortje was ruled out through injury on Friday. He has been replaced by Franco Mostert, who was not originally in the matchday squad.
Ireland - who have lost their past six contests against New Zealand, France and South Africa, the three teams above them in the world rankings, by double-digit margins - have also been forced into a late change, with Thomas Clarkson replacing Sam Illo as the replacement tight-head prop.
The myriad permutations mean Ireland and South Africa could meet again in the finals weekend at Twickenham.
Either way, Saturday's sold-out contest in Dublin promises to deliver enough drama to tide fans over until next year's World Cup in Australia, where they could contest the final.

items.summary:
France investigates actor Depardieu, writer Houellebecq over alleged gang rape
French police are investigating allegations actor and convicted sex offender Gérard Depardieu raped and assaulted a woman with the complicity of bestselling author Michel Houellebecq during a 2018 film shoot, two sources
items.text:
France investigates actor Depardieu, writer Houellebecq over alleged gang rape
French police are investigating allegations actor and convicted sex offender Gérard Depardieu raped and assaulted a woman with the complicity of bestselling author Michel Houellebecq during a 2018 film shoot, two sources following the case said Friday. The plaintiff has accused the film's director Guillaume Nicloux of being complicit in the abuse.
French police are investigating allegations disgraced film icon Gérard Depardieu and Goncourt Prize-winning author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot, two sources following the case said Friday, confirming a report by investigative website Mediapart.
Houellebecq, who also starred in the film, is being investigated for complicity in the sexual abuse, the sources said.
The accusation is the latest in a flurry against the 77-year-old actor, who on Monday dropped his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women during the filming of another movie.
Read moreFrench cinema icon Depardieu withdraws appeal for 2025 sexual assault conviction
Depardieu is to learn next week if he will stand trial for raping another actress, Charlotte Arnould. A judge has ordered a trial, but Depardieu has rejected the allegations and appealed.
In the new case, the alleged abuse occurred in December 2018, during the shooting of "Thalasso", a film starring the two men as versions of themselves directed by Guillaume Nicloux, who has been accused of complicity in the sexual abuse, one of the sources said.
The woman, an actor and dancer who was 32 at the time, told Mediapart that Depardieu digitally penetrated her while Houellebecq pinned her down during one scene.
The author also imposed an oral sexual act on her without her consent while the cameras were rolling, she told the publication.
The woman's lawyer did not wish to respond to an AFP request for comment.
Depardieu's attorneys did not immediately respond.
Watch moreGérard Depardieu: The rise and fall of a French film icon
AFP contacted Houellebecq via his publisher, but he did not comment.
The 70-year-old, who is among France's most translated authors, is also under investigation for alleged incitement to discrimination in France over comments he made in 2022 about Muslims.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Anthropic shares fall a day after blockbuster opening
- Published
Anthropic's share price has dropped back towards its initial public offering (IPO) price a day after its soaring market debut, as the broader tech sell off continues.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
However, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 10% to about $87.30, close to its IPO price of $83, and the broader stock market declines seen on Thursday continued.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.8% in morning trade, the S&P 500 was down 1.2% while the Dow Jones Industrial Average remained largely flat.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.
Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.text:
NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 20 – The Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity has launched a mobile eye care programme targeting rural communities in Africa, with Morocco and Mozambique selected for the first phase.
The initiative, unveiled on Friday, November 20, 2026, will provide vision screening, diagnosis and treatment of eye conditions, as well as support for cataract surgery, targeting approximately 15,000 beneficiaries across the two countries within the first six months.
The programme is being implemented in partnership with the Ministries of Health in Morocco and Mozambique, with plans to expand to other African countries where geographical distance and limited access to healthcare continue to prevent communities from receiving essential eye care services.
The mobile clinics will be integrated into existing national health systems, with patients requiring specialised treatment referred to public health facilities.
UAE Minister of State Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan Al Nahyan said the initiative reflects his country’s commitment to extending healthcare services to underserved populations.
“Working hand in hand with the governments of the Kingdom of Morocco and the Republic of Mozambique, these mobile clinics will bring eye care directly to rural communities, ensuring that distance is no longer a barrier to treatment,” he said.
He added that the initiative would address practical barriers to healthcare access while empowering thousands of people to lead healthier and more productive lives.
Globally, at least 2.2 billion people live with vision impairment, with the majority in low- and middle-income countries. Of these, at least one billion cases could have been prevented or treated through access to appropriate eye care services.
Foundation Director-General Dr Shamma Khalifa Al Mazrui said many cases of vision loss could be addressed through relatively simple interventions, including prescription glasses and cataract surgery.
“Almost all cases of vision loss can be prevented or treated through appropriate care, including simple interventions such as prescription glasses and cataract surgery. Yet, this care remains out of reach for many people,” she said.
Al Mazrui noted that restoring sight goes beyond improving individual health, creating opportunities for education, employment and economic independence.
“Restoring sight does more than improve a person’s health; it can transform their life, giving them new opportunities to learn, work and earn a living, with positive effects on their family, community and national economy,” she added.
Morocco’s Minister of Health and Social Protection Youns Bjijou said the partnership would complement ongoing government reforms aimed at extending quality healthcare beyond urban centres.
“We welcome our partnership with the Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity, which supports these efforts by bringing eye care services closer to rural communities and enabling more people to access timely diagnosis, treatment and care,” he said.
Mozambique Health Minister Ussene Hilário Isse said the programme would help eliminate delays and long-distance travel that could expose patients to the risk of preventable blindness.
“The success of any health initiative is measured by its impact on patients’ lives,” he said.
He added that his government was committed to ensuring more people receive timely eye examinations and treatment without having to travel long distances.
“This aligns with the vision and guidance of His Excellency Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique. We welcome our partnership with the Mohamed bin Zayed Foundation for Humanity to translate these efforts into tangible outcomes that create a lasting impact on the lives of our communities,” Isse said.
In Morocco, the programme will also deploy a mobile surgical unit to support cataract operations in collaboration with local healthcare facilities.
Local healthcare professionals will work alongside the mobile medical teams to diagnose and treat common eye conditions, distribute prescription glasses and identify patients requiring surgical intervention.
The initiative is also expected to generate expertise and lessons that will inform future phases, with the foundation prioritising sustainable, country-led efforts to expand access to eye care across Africa.

items.summary: - 1. Grealish missed Everton’s past four games mainly as a consequence of missing training before last month’s Caraba
items.text:
- 1. Grealish returns after four games missed David Moyes has confirmed Jack Grealish is fit and available for Everton’s visit to Brentford on Monday after his recent disciplinary breach. Grealish missed Everton’s past four games mainly as a consequence of missing training before last month’s Carabao Cup win over Newcastle. His last appearance for the team was in the 2-0 loss to Chelsea on 17 October, but Moyes is now prepared to welcome the playmaker back into the fold. “He’s back in training and back in around the team,” the Everton manager said. The 31-year-old played in a behind-closed-doors fixture against Derby last week and apologised on social media for being unable to help the team, who have performed well in his absence. Moyes said of the apology: “I don’t do social media but I’ve heard about it.” Asked whether he had received a similar apology from Grealish in person, the Everton manager added: “We’ve just been getting on with our work. We’ve got a lot of other players here who we need to focus on as well, I can’t just concentrate on one player, and I’ve been trying to make sure everybody gets the right preparation for our next game against Brentford.” The Scot backed Jordan Pickford to respond strongly to the threat from James Trafford to his England place after the Leeds goalkeeper’s inclusion and impressive display in the Nations League win over Spain. “I don’t think it will have a great effect on him,” claimed Moyes. “If you’re playing for England you will always have other players chasing you. I still think Jordan Pickford is out there on his own at the moment. If anything, he’s getting better. It will be good for us now that he’s getting competition [with England].” Andy Hunter
- 2. Maresca backs Fernández but hints at tweaks Enzo Maresca has said he may need to tweak the balance of Manchester City’s midfield amid their faltering Premier League form. City went into the November international break on the back of three consecutive defeats in the league, having begun the campaign with seven wins on the bounce. Maresca’s side are third in the table, six points off leaders Arsenal, and face Fulham at the Etihad Stadium on Saturday. Maresca defended Enzo Fernández, whose performances have prompted debate over his best position and whether he leaves City’s team unbalanced. Maresca has mostly opted to play the £125m signing from Chelsea deeper in midfield alongside fellow summer recruit Elliot Anderson, with the more defensive-minded Ayyoub Bouaddi, who also arrived in the summer, largely a substitute. “For sure there are things we need to do better in terms of balance,” Maresca said. “But the same midfield that won seven games in a row is the same midfield that lost three games in a row. “We won games with Enzo, we lost games with Enzo. I know that when there is a defeat, we are all looking for the reason why. Sometimes we probably need more balance, we need different kinds of players. [It] depends a little bit on the game. The idea is to continue in attack in the same way, creating chances, but finding a balance when we defend.” Maresca also dismissed the notion that any uncertainty surrounding City’s financial case with the Premier League has negatively affected recent performances. It has been nearly two months since City were found guilty of more than 100 charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules, and they are waiting for the outcome of their appeal. All three of City’s league defeats have come since the ruling. “I don’t think the players are thinking too much about the noise,” Maresca said. “I don’t think they are worried about it.” Dominic Booth
- 3. Iraola: drone filming ‘shouldn’t be legal’ Andoni Iraola believes Manchester United have an advantage on Sunday with Mauricio Pochettino set to take charge of his first game but criticised unauthorised drone footage of the Argentinian’s first training session. Pochettino faces a daunting maiden outing when United travel to face Liverpool at Anfield. A drone operator apologised after posting a 12-minute video from Carrington on YouTube – since removed – which Liverpool head coach Iraola said he has seen. “Yesterday they were sending me the footage but I think the important part of this is it shouldn’t be legal,” said the Spaniard. “It happened to United but it could happen today to me. Yesterday you had access to our training, the cameras recorded also 15, 20 minutes of our training, you know who trained with us, you know who didn’t train. We know the same but it’s not a matter of the advantage, I think it’s the fact someone can do this. I think there is a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things you have to respect and I don’t think it’s nice for any club.” With Pochettino having left his role as US boss to take charge at Old Trafford, there will be a considerable element of the unknown for Liverpool. He added of former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino: “We’ve faced each other and obviously he has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at, we can look at games from the US. But it’s true they have this small advantage that we don’t have references to prepare because they can go different ways that we don’t know right now.” Liverpool have been boosted by the news Virgil van Dijk, Ryan Gravenberch and Jeremie Frimpong are all set to be available, while the international break has seen long-term absentees Conor Bradley and Giovanni Leoni take a step forward. Press Association

Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence a
items.text:
Qatar and Germany deepen strategic ties during emir’s Berlin visit
German chancellor says Qatar pledged $16.5bn in new investments as the two countries deepen defence and technology ties.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence and diplomatic cooperation, broadening a relationship long focused on trade and investment.
At a joint news conference with the emir on Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Qatar had pledged an additional 15 billion euros ($16.5bn) in investment, while the two governments planned closer cooperation on security and technology.
Merz said the investment would strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), computer chips and aviation. He also expressed Germany’s interest in developing defence industry partnerships with Qatar, while the two countries agreed to work together to improve protection against cyberattacks.
The discussions come as Qatar continues pushing for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas supplies.
Sheikh Tamim also held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who proposed a regional security conference for the Middle East.
Their meeting on Friday covered efforts to end the Iran war and restore maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a joint statement by both countries.
Steinmeier suggested bringing regional governments together to build trust and address security disputes.
The emir invited him to the Doha Forum, an international policy conference in Qatar on December 5–6, to discuss the proposal further with other countries.
At the emir’s news conference with Merz, the German leader acknowledged Qatar’s role in mediating between the US and Iran and called for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen permanently. He also urged Tehran to halt its military nuclear programme.
Sheikh Tamim stressed that “peace and sustainable peace and security can only be reached through a political agreement”, adding that dialogue is the only way forward. He also described Germany as an important partner.
Sheikha Alanoud bint Hamad Al Thani, a fellow at the Middle East Council for Global Affairs, a regional research institute, told Al Jazeera in Berlin that the relationship had previously been driven mainly by commerce.
“But now we’re seeing a strategic dialogue,” she said, pointing to increasingly similar security concerns, including drone attacks on Qatar and hybrid warfare threats facing European countries.
That shift builds on a 2023 agreement to establish formal strategic talks between the two countries. Sheikh Tamim told Steinmeier on Friday that Qatar wanted the first round to take place, according to Qatar’s state news agency, QNA.

items.summary:

items.text:
How Orchestra Noir turned classical music into a cultural movement
Ashley Branch, Orchestra Noir's operations manager, hurriedly completes her final tasks before curtain call at the Warner Theater in Washington, D.C. It is two hours before the ensemble's Saturday night concert and her main goal is simple: plan to deal with whatever she didn't plan for.
The D.C. show comes partway through the ensemble's 20-city The Culture 2000s tour, which has taken the group to cities like Jacksonville and Philadelphia.
Founded in 2016 by music director Jason Ikeem Rodgers, the all-Black Atlanta-based orchestra performs classic hits spanning the genres of jazz, blues and R&B. Branch has been with Orchestra Noir for about two years, hired to bring relief to Keisha Rodgers, the orchestra's original operations manager, who now serves as president of operations. On show nights, it's Branch who is directing the final details on show prep.
In its early days, the Orchestra Noir team was small — just Keisha and Jason handling everything. While Jason was responsible for all music-related details, Keisha handled other tasks, such as creating the logo and website.
"I wore every single hat there was to wear," Keisha told NPR. "It was just very day-to-day. I mean, every little thing you could think of operationally was me."
But over the last decade, Orchestra Noir has expanded to 23 musicians and a leadership staff of four people. The orchestra averages about 20 shows per tour.
Saxophonist Taj Davis and violinist Nicole Wright have been with the ensemble for three tours. They say the size of the production has grown considerably since they joined.
"Every go round is a new element," Davis said.
The latest season added several new details to their performances — including a full display screen cycling through visuals from previous performances, fog machines and lighting and choreography threaded throughout the show.
"Every time I come back, I'm excited," Wright said, "because not only am I experiencing something different, but the audience is too." The theme for each tour, Rodgers explained, comes from whatever is igniting his creativity at the moment. For their most recent The Culture 2000s tour, Rodgers said they really wanted the "Bad Gal Rihanna energy."
"I chose the theme based on basically what inspired me at the time. And that's kind of where I want to go. I want to go deep into the 2000's," he said.
When it comes to picking which songs to perform and how they will be arranged, Rodgers compares it to developing a secret sauce he's been trying perfect "for a long time."
"We developed the formula where we can orchestrate and we can arrange," Rogers said. "We can orchestrate for those songs and arrange those songs in a way that is still so authentic, like how we're playing the melody, which instruments should have the bass line or the the harmony." "So it's really about seeing the orchestration in each song," Rogers continued. "Now when I hear a hip-hop song or a R&B song — I don't even hear the words anymore. I just hear instruments."
The journey to the stage
Preparation for an Orchestra Noir show starts long before the curtain rises. Wright logs two hours of individual practice daily. She writes out compositions by hand and thinks through fingerings and lyrics before bed. She says the show's music is often top of her mind as she moves through the day, even when her violin isn't in her hands. Wright says that her intense focus on the details of the show's music ahead of the show allows her to "just let loose and become one with the audience" once showtime arrives.
Davis takes a similar full-body approach. He listens to the repertoire while driving, catching details such as notes he may have missed in previous runs. He also exercises four to five times a week — including weightlifting workouts and walking.
Focusing on his endurance on stage is vital — since each Orchestra Noir performance demands a high level of stamina due to the ensemble's musicians performing choreography while also playing their instruments.
"Taking care of myself physically helps me when it's time to perform. It also gives me a chance to clear my mind and stay disciplined," Davis said.
On performance days, pre-show rituals also keep the musicians grounded. Davis plays long tones on his saxophone — sustaining single notes to center his breath and tone. Wright practices specific musical cues, calls her mother and will try on dresses until she finds the perfect one to wear on stage. And both of them remember to pray.
"Me and God are walking the entire time together," Wright said with a laugh.
A night to remember
By the time the lights go down, the audience inside Warner Theatre is already buzzing with excitement.
Orchestra Noir takes the stage in custom black-and-red letterman jackets that feature red-and-black sleeves with the letters "ATL" stitched on the right.
They open with Usher's 2004 hit "Yeah!" — with musicians rushing in from both ends of the stage and smoke sprouting up from the stage floor.
When an electric guitar joins the orchestra for Jagged Edge's "Where the Party at," the room shifts even higher. Then comes Ciara's "Like a Boy" — which features a violin solo from Wright that she plays so intensely that her bow snaps mid-solo.
Orchestra Noir closes the night with Lil Boosie's "Wipe Me Down." By this point, nearly the whole crowd is standing, with several audience members already making their way towards the stage.
As a part of their post-show ritual, the musicians come to the end of the stage to meet the people who came out to hear them perform. It is a cherished tradition that makes them feel even closer to the multigenerational audience supporting them from city to city.
"[During the 2025 season] out in California, someone in the audience came and cried," Davis recalled. "They just moved to Cali and haven't had anything for them — and then seeing us made that huge difference for them. So, it's a great thing. It's a blessing."
"

The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other en
items.text:
US Senate passes bill to speed up energy project approvals
The legislation aims to lower energy bills by making energy project approvals faster and limiting court challenges.
The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects as lawmakers face pressure to bring down electricity bills and meet growing demand fuelled by the growth of artificial intelligence.
The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday as 15 Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backed the bill and two Republicans voted against it.
President Donald Trump had urged senators to pass the measure and said he would sign the bill if it passes the House of Representatives.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten timelines for federal reviews for energy projects and limit how approvals may be challenged in court.
It would change several environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh a project’s environmental effects and gives the public a chance to weigh in before a project is approved.
The four senators who coauthored the bill, two from each party, argued that Americans are tired of paying high utility bills while projects that could lower them are stuck in the planning phase.
“We are going to make it easier to build in America again and make life more affordable for American families,” Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah said.
Lee negotiated the deal with fellow Republican Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.
The bill would also require large AI data centres to pay for more of the cost of upgrading power grids to serve their needs.
The vote came after rising electricity bills and opposition to data centres became major issues in the midterm elections this month. Democrats campaigned on promises to rein in the industry and swept to victory. They won control of both chambers of the new US Congress, which will convene on January 3. Until then, Republicans hold slim majorities in both chambers.
Industry groups representing both renewable energy developers and oil and gas companies backed the bill, saying current delays can stretch timelines by a decade or more.
Why did critics oppose it?
Environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and the National Wildlife Federation, warned that the bill would weaken protections for water and wildlife and make it harder for communities to challenge project approvals.
Other groups said it would lead to more fossil fuel development.
“Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centres, oil and gas pipelines and [liquefied natural gas] terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the US,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project.
She called it a “gift to some of the biggest polluters in America”, arguing that any gains in renewable energy would be outweighed by emissions and pollution from the fossil fuel industry.
Critics also took issue with how quickly the bill was moving, arguing that it was being rushed through Congress.
Democratic Senator Maria Cantwell from Washington state said after meeting with tribal leaders that it would undermine tribal nations’ sovereignty and weaken protections for their water, land and wildlife.
She called for more time to consider those concerns and amend the bill.
Some Democrats who opposed the bill also argued the party should wait until January to push through stronger legislation that limits fossil fuel development while doing more to expand wind and solar power.
The Senate passed the measure without adopting amendments pushed by Oregon’s two senators, including one that would ban data centres on public land and another that would prevent the Trump administration from cancelling energy grants and other Democratic initiatives for “purely political purposes”.

items.text:
TL;DR:
We bought a 3000 EUR Framework Laptop 16 for one of our developers. It was broken out of the box. Three months, around thirty support emails, two replacement parts and a trip to their repair center later, Framework concluded “No Fault Found” and blamed the keyboard layout of an OS that wasn’t even installed when the problem first showed up. I’m done with them.
Some context first#
I have been a Framework fan for a while. At my company, developers pick the machine of their choice and several work on Framework laptops or desktops, we have about quite a few of them around, and I have been recommending them to pretty much anyone who asked me what laptop to buy so far. Repairable hardware, Linux-friendly, a company that seemed to care about the people using its products: it was an easy recommendation to make.
So when Q joined the team and needed a workstation, we ordered a Framework Laptop 16, around 3000 EUR once configured.
Three months later, I’m pissed off at Framework and have banned future purchases from them at my company. Not because the machine arrived broken, this happens and I’ve been around hardware long enough to know it, but because of how unprofessional and useless the support has been from the first email to the last.
OH and feel free to share, friends don’t let friends enter hell.
Day one: broken out of the box#
The laptop arrives early August. Q assembles it, powers it on and is greeted by a “missing input module” screen, before reaching the BIOS, before any operating system is even installed. Keep this detail in mind, we’ll get back to it.
The keyboard isn’t detected when centered, and when moved to the left it shows up as… a numpad. In that state, nothing works: not the keyboard, not the touchpad, not the numpad. There’s a BIOS option, “Force Power for Input Modules”, that bypasses module detection. With it enabled, everything works. Without it, the machine has no keyboard and no touchpad. It is recommended NOT to turn it on permanently as it might be harmful to the hardware, as stated on their own website.
I open a ticket on August 13th.
August: the script loop hell#
What follows is two weeks of support reading from a script, one step per email, one email per day or two:
- is it out of the box? any damage on the packaging? which OS, which kernel, which BIOS version?
- do a mainboard reset by pressing the chassis switch ten times
- reseat the midplate
- try Force Power On (we had already told them it was the only thing that worked)
- send photos of the keyboard, the midplate, the connector, the whole laptop from six angles, and a video
- reset the BIOS to defaults
- reinstall the BIOS and the drivers bundle (a Windows drivers bundle, for a problem that happens before any OS boots, on a machine that doesn’t run Windows…)
- try different input module combinations
We did all of it. We sent the photos and the video in a shared drive. Each reply came from a different agent who clearly hadn’t read the thread, and asked for something we had already provided.
On August 24th I lost patience and wrote that this was a 3000 EUR laptop that didn’t work, that my co-worker had been without a usable machine of his own for over a week, and asked them to either send replacement parts or take it back and refund us. I even went all Karen and asked to involve a manager.
Their answer: please send a clear photo of the midplate and the underside of the keyboard. The same photos, again. No manager involved to break the script because no flying fucks were given.
We did their diagnosis for them#
Q then replied from his own address, which apparently is a problem, because support spent the next ten days asking him to “verify the shipping address” of the order, which he did, several times.
Meanwhile, tired of being asked to repeat steps,
he updated the keyboard firmware himself (only possible with Force Power On, since the keyboard is otherwise not detected),
installed Framework’s own framework_tool,
and ran a proper isolation:
$ sudo framework_tool --inputdeck
The result was unambiguous:
the keyboard module reports the ID of a numpad, KeyboardB.
The firmware therefore sees two numpads and no keyboard,
considers the input deck incomplete,
and never enables the power rail for the input modules,
which is why everything is dead and not just the keyboard.
He moved the keyboard alone across slots: it misidentifies itself in every position. He moved the numpad alone into the same slot: it identifies correctly. He removed everything: the baseline is clean. The wrong ID follows the keyboard. The keyboard is faulty.
He sent all of this to support on August 28th with a full report and a one-line reproduction command.
September: they replace the wrong part#
On September 7th, support concludes… that the midplate needs to be replaced. Not the keyboard, the only part that a reproducible diagnostic, run with their own tool, had just pointed at.
The midplate arrives a week later. The problem is, of course, still there because… GOTO previous paragraph. Q asks them whether they’re sure it’s not the keyboard, given that he proved it with the diagnosis.
Their answer ?
Back to the queue. Back to photos: the packaging box from different angles including the interior, the midplate front and back, the keyboard top and bottom, close-ups of the sockets. Photos they already had.
At this point, Q is no longer a developer but has become a profesionnal photographer.
October: a new keyboard, a new bug#
On October 8th, two months after the laptop arrived, Framework finally agrees to replace the keyboard. What they should have done on the first week…
The new keyboard is detected, the original bug is gone,
but there is a new one:
pressing C sends a c followed by a Delete escape sequence.
$ showkey -a
c       99 0143 0x63
^[[3~   27 0033 0x1b
        91 0133 0x5b
        51 0063 0x33
       126 0176 0x7e
An external keyboard on the same machine produces a single c, as it should.
FU-CKIN’ HELL it never ends…
You can’t use a keyboar

items.text:
‘Expel invaders’: The dangerous promises of Spain’s far-right Vox party
Spain heads to a snap election on November 29 with Vox campaigning on mass deportations, ‘remigration’ and ‘national priority’.
Santiago Abascal, wearing a blue suit and tie, looks straight into the camera. His campaign poster makes three promises: giving Spanish nationals priority in access to benefits, cutting regulation and “remigration”.
“It’s common sense,” the poster of his far-right Vox party reads.
With little more than a week to go until Spain’s November 29 snap election, opinion polls put Vox in third place behind the conservative Popular Party (PP), which is leading the race, and the governing Socialist Party.
But with the Socialists’ potential allies fragmented and the PP projected to fall short of an outright majority, Vox could emerge as a kingmaker.
The party, which once struggled to win a single seat in parliament, could join a PP-led coalition or back a minority PP government from outside the cabinet.
What is Vox, and who founded it?
Abascal was a regional lawmaker for the PP in the Basque Country. He left the party in 2013, accusing then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy of being too soft on the issue of Catalan separatism. He went on to cofound Vox.
The new party positioned itself to the PP’s right, making Spanish unity its central cause. It called for an end to the country’s system of regional autonomy and championed the idea of the “true Spaniard”, who was Catholic, Castilian-speaking and loyal to the monarchy.
Over time, the party started to adopt themes and tactics from other European far-right parties.
“At the beginning, they were the ultra-conservatives of the right, but then they started to study the handbook of the populist radical right across Europe, and they became the Spanish version of it,” said Carles Ferreira, lecturer in politics at the University of Girona.
In January 2017, Abascal made his international debut at a gathering of Europe’s far right in the German city of Koblenz alongside France’s Marine Le Pen and Frauke Petry, then-leader of the Alternative for Germany. But Vox was still a minor force at home, having won 0.2 percent of the vote and no seats in the previous year’s general election.
How did Vox break through?
That October nine years ago, Catalonia held an independence referendum in defiance of Spain’s Constitutional Court. A few weeks later, the Parliament of Catalonia unilaterally declared independence, plunging the country into a constitutional crisis.
Vox, which had filed a legal complaint over the preparation for the vote, used the crisis to raise its national profile over its opposition to Catalan independence.
It worked. Just over a year later, the party made its electoral breakthrough, winning 12 seats in the regional parliament of Andalusia in southern Spain. Four months later, it entered the national parliament for the first time by winning 24 seats.
Vox had transformed from a fringe party with zero representation into a relevant political force.
What does Vox want?
The first bullet point in its manifesto calls for the “immediate expulsion of all invaders”.
Abascal has accused the Socialist government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people”.
“It may well be that the upcoming elections will be the last ones to be decided by the Spanish people,” Abascal said on Thursday on X.
He wants to ban the mass regularisation of undocumented immigrants and deport them.
His manifesto calls for “remigration”, a plan to facilitate the expulsion of people who the party says do not contribute or who rely on public benefits.
Throughout the eight-year tenure of the current government, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, according to the National Statistics Institute.
Vox is also campaigning for “national priority”, a system that would create a two-tier society in which Spanish nationals would have better access to social benefits.
Its exclusionary discourse often focuses on Muslim migrants.
“With Catalan independence no longer dominating the political debate, Vox has shifted its focus to what it calls the ‘Islamisation of Spain’ and the threat of a ‘Spanish caliphate’,” said Steven Forti, professor of contemporary history at the Autonomous University of Barcelona. “By hammering away at the issue, the party has turned it into a rallying point for voters.”
Vox draws on the idea of Hispanidad, a shared Hispanic identity, to portray Latin American migrants as culturally closer to Spaniards.
Spain has long welcomed Spanish-speaking people from Latin America. They represent the largest group of undocumented and documented foreigners in Spain, according to the Spanish think tank Funcas.
Vox’s idea of an “Iberosphere”, Forti added, invokes traditional Catholic values and a shared language and culture rooted in Spain’s colonial past. In that telling, Latin American migrants are welcome because they are “the children of our colonisation”.
On social issues, the party is staunchly conservative. It opposes abortion. Its politicians have derided LGBTQ advocacy as the work of a “lobby”, and Vox rejects treating gender-based violence as a distinct legal category, arguing that domestic violence laws should apply regardless of the victim’s sex.
It was the only party to oppose renewing Spain’s cross-party pact against gender-based violence in 2025 and has called for suspending an agreement that specifically protects women from violence by current and former partners.
Yet this year’s party manifesto is less specific about what it wants to do, calling more broadly for replacing “gender ideology” laws and strengthening police and judicial protection for women facing violence.
Who votes for Vox and why?
Traditionally, its core electoral base has been young, white and male.

items.text:
10 games, 0 points & 30 goals conceded - why Charlton are struggling
- Published
Charlton Athletic achieved the unthinkable last season when they earned promotion to the Women's Super League - but it has been a harsh introduction.
After 10 games in the top flight, Karen Hills' side are yet to pick up a point and have scored just five goals, conceding 30.
They have already lost to the other promoted sides - Birmingham City and Crystal Palace - and are six points adrift at the bottom of the table.
The club expected a tough challenge as they made the jump up to the WSL for the first time but the results have still hit them hard.
"I'm trying everything I can," manager Hills said following their 2-0 defeat by West Ham last weekend.
That result came a week after Charlton's 3-2 loss at Crystal Palace where they had been leading with 16 minutes to go.
So is it time to consider relegation, even in November, or is there still hope for Charlton to turn things around?
Why have Charlton struggled?
Charlton pipped better resourced teams in the WSL 2 last season, eventually beating top-flight side Leicester City in a play-off to secure promotion.
An incredible 27-game unbeaten run ended in March but was founded on an effective defensive structure and often heroics by goalkeeper Sophie Whitehouse.
However, the step up has proved difficult with inexperience and tight finances standing in the way.
Statistically, Charlton rank bottom in the WSL for average possession (30%), shots on target (17), passing accuracy (66%) and successful passes (1,689).
They have conceded nine times from set-pieces - the most in the WSL - and 14 of their total goals against have come in either the first or final 15 minutes in games.
The only other sides to lose their first 10 games in a WSL season are Doncaster Rovers Belles in 2016 and Yeovil Town in 2017-18. The Belles went on to win just one game as they were relegated, while Yeovil failed to win any, drawing two and finishing bottom, only avoiding relegation because of a league restructure.
Experienced defender Ashleigh Neville, who joined Charlton from Leicester City in the summer, told BBC Sport: "We knew it was going to be a tough start to the season.
"I was really excited to embrace that challenge. It's been difficult with results but when you look at the first game compared to now, I'd like to hope that people can see we're trying to build something.
"We're trying the hardest we can off the pitch to get to terms with how quick the game is compared to the WSL 2 and the quality of players we're up against.
"But it's still a joy to come into work and people are wanting to be better, asking how they can improve and move forward."
This month, manager Hills insisted Charlton "will never throw the towel in" but admitted results are "hurting" the club.
Neville added: "It is not at the forefront of things but we've been really unlucky with the injuries that we've had in our attacking line.
"We're lacking in confidence going forward, and creativity for what we can actually provide.
"It's a vicious circle. If you haven't got confidence because you're losing games, how do you still get that confidence in games where we need it the most?"
- Whitehouse's penalty masterclass sends Charlton into WSL 
  - Published23 May
- How WSL 2 title contenders Charlton are defying the odds 
  - Published2 May
Is there still a financial gulf?
Charlton are one of only three clubs without Premier League male counterparts to offer financial backing in the WSL and that restricts their freedom in recruitment.
It has not helped that summer signing Linda Lif Boama suffered a serious knee injury in September, defender Grace Johnston was ruled out in October and Paula Partido had to return to parent club London City Lionesses for knee surgery.
Charlotte Newsham, who played a key role in their WSL 2 promotion run, was also sidelined by an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury before the play-off victory.
While Charlton sought out shrewd signings in the summer, rivals Birmingham City were able to spend six-figure sums on Manchester United duo Lisa Naalsund and Millie Turner.
The Blues also broke their club record in January - a reported £316,000 fee for Wilma Leidhammar - while Oceane Hurtre was signed last summer to boost their second-tier title hopes and has now scored seven goals in 10 WSL games.
Fellow promoted club Palace picked up four-time WSL winner Bethany England and one of the WSL 2's standout players Lexi Lloyd-Smith in the summer.
"WSL 2 teams have to be even more ready for the WSL while they're still in the WSL 2 so that when they do make that jump, it's not a huge gap," said Hills.
"The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see some of the players the top teams have brought in and the finances they have.
"It's a big challenge for us. We're finding that out on a weekly basis."
Charlton benefited from the WSL's expansion this summer to 14 teams from 12 as organisers try to bridge the gap between the leagues and to increase the number of matches.
It was well-received by fans and those within the game, but Hills says it will still take time for WSL 2 clubs to catch up.
"If you look at the bottom three teams [in the table], it's all the newly-promoted teams. The level that we're coming into is already very well established."
Neville added: "I think the financial side plays a massive part. We do our bit where we can. But it's hard to bring in the experienced players you need."

Carys Douglas
items.text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
- Published
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.
Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.
Zeta-Jones who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.
But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and that she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".
During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.
"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.
"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.
Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".
"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.
Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".
"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.
She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."
Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.
She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.
The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.
Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".
"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.
Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.
Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.
"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.
"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.
"The Gower Peninsula is breathtaking."
She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".
"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

items.title: Children Take Their Place In Kenya’s 2027 Election As National Campaign Launches
items.summary:
As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, millions of children will have no say at the ballot box, though the outcome will shape their lives.
On World Children’s Day, D&R Impact, Shining Hope for Communities (SHOFCO), Nation Media Foundation and the Centre for Behaviour Change and Communicati
items.text:
As Kenya prepares for the 2027 General Election, millions of children will have no say at the ballot box, though the outcome will shape their lives.
On World Children’s Day, D&R Impact, Shining Hope for Communities (SHOFCO), Nation Media Foundation and the Centre for Behaviour Change and Communication (CBCC) are launching If You Ask Me, a non-partisan campaign that brings children into the conversations and decisions that affect them.
The date marks the anniversary of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, adopted in 1989, which recognises every child’s right to express their views and have them considered in matters affecting their lives.
“Storytelling and media have the power to shape how societies think, what they prioritise and ultimately how they act. Through this campaign, we want to harness that power so that millions of Kenyans hear directly from children, and so that their stories influence public policy and the choices we make about our country’s future,” said Eugene Mbugua, Founder of D&R Studios and D&R Impact.
Over the next year, children aged five to fifteen from every region of Kenya will share their experiences, concerns and hopes for the country. Kenyans will hear from them through television, radio, print, digital platforms and community engagement. Six short films premiered at today’s launch event, giving audiences their first direct window into children’s perspectives.
Speaking at the launch, Kennedy Odede, Founder and CEO of SHOFCO and Guest of Honour, said: “I grew up in Kibera, and I know what it means for a child to have something important to say with nobody asking. Through SHOFCO’s community networks across Kenya, children from informal settlements will be heard by the people who make decisions about their lives.”
The campaign aims to influence public policy, legislative priorities, government planning and resource allocation in education, healthcare, safety and protection.
It will culminate in a Children’s Manifesto, shaped by children and backed by actionable policy recommendations. The Manifesto will be presented to all key
political parties ahead of the party primaries, and to the Presidency, the Chief Justice, the Chair of the Council of Governors and county leadership, with the aim of securing commitments that hold beyond the election cycle.
If You Ask Me is independent of all political parties and candidates. Through the election period it will champion peace, national unity and inclusion, with child safeguarding and meaningful participation at the centre of its work.

items.title: Kansas hosts become guests as Algeria repays World Cup welcome
items.summary:
Kansas hosts become guests as Algeria repays World Cup welcome
A bond between the people of Kansas and Algerians has deepened since the city hosted the North Africans during the World Cup.
Algiers, Algeria – Tommee Sherwood never expected that Algeria would come to play such a big role in his life.
items.text:
Kansas hosts become guests as Algeria repays World Cup welcome
A bond between the people of Kansas and Algerians has deepened since the city hosted the North Africans during the World Cup.
Algiers, Algeria – Tommee Sherwood never expected that Algeria would come to play such a big role in his life.
Until recently, the 70-year-old from Lawrence, Kansas – a retired university custodian, musician, and volunteer English teacher for refugees – had never been to North Africa before and knew Algeria mostly from the film The Battle of Algiers.
He was aware, though, that Algeria had given refuge to members of the Black Panther Party in the 1970s, including Pete O’Neal, chairman of the Kansas City chapter.
“That connection between Algerians and Kansas City goes way further than most people realise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sherwood was among 38 residents of Lawrence who visited Algeria from November 9-15 at the government’s expense as a gesture of gratitude from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune for the way their small university city had welcomed the Algerian national team, which used Lawrence as their official base camp during the World Cup.
Five months on, the football was long over, but the genuine bond it had forged between two communities separated by 8,000km (5,000 miles) had only grown stronger.
On a boat in the Bay of Algiers on their first day in the country, a DJ was playing.
“He started playing some old jazz music,” Sherwood recalls in audio messages sent to Al Jazeera. “And he was playing some old timers – some old Kansas City guys that I used to know. It really touched me.”
He gave the DJ a small gift and took photographs. The next day, the same DJ was playing at a different event. He came over to Sherwood and handed him three vintage 45s – old recordings of Algerian singers.
“He told me one of them sang a song to the French. It’s called ‘We Stay, You Go’. I really loved that,” Sherwood said. “These records, if they were made of gold, they wouldn’t be any more valuable to me.”
Sherwood describes the encounters with the DJ as “an example” of the hospitality they were shown by everyone during their time in Algeria.
“I never imagined that the World Cup would open such possibilities for cultural exchange and communication and I’m kind of astounded by it,” Sherwood said.
Five months earlier, Lawrence had hosted Algeria’s national team and its fans with a warmth that touched Algerians. Storefronts on Massachusetts Street flew Algerian flags. The city screened every Algeria and United States match on large outdoor screens. The Kansas University (KU) band played the Algerian national anthem for the team before training.
Algeria was among the 50 countries whose visa applicants faced a $10,000 bond requirement for the tournament, which meant few people from Algeria could make the journey. But the Algerian community in the US, estimated at no more than 50,000 across the country, also came to Lawrence in large numbers.
Saajida Andalsi, an Algerian whose mother has lived in Kansas for more than 36 years, served as an informal bridge between the different communities during the World Cup.
Originally from Algeria, the 24-year-old had not been back for 15 years, but was part of the November delegation. Remembering how Lawrence transformed during the tournament, the 24-year-old said: “My mum kept saying: ‘I didn’t go to Algeria. Algeria came to me’. Lawrence was like a city in Algeria.”
In July, Tebboune ordered the establishment of a twinning agreement between the Algerian town of Tipaza and Kansas City and extended invitations to 100 visitors at the state’s expense.
For Ruth DuWitt, director of community engagement at Explore Lawrence, the city’s tourism bureau, the trip to Algeria deepened her knowledge about the country’s struggle for independence.
Standing in the Casbah of Algiers, she watched the KU band and an Algerian group take the stage together. The Algerian conductor raised his baton over the KU ensemble and directed them through The Star-Spangled Banner, before the KU director conducted Algeria’s national anthem.
“We are standing in that very place – the Casbah – about freedom and revolution and all that spirit,” DuWitt says. “I’m getting choked up just thinking about it.”
Andalsi watched the same scene.
“It showed that there wasn’t just connection behind soccer. It was also music. It was the similarities in us just as humans,” she said.
When both bands played together, the crowd was invited into the middle to dance. “It felt like a movie. Nobody could have imagined that happening.”
‘Everyone benefits’
Madjid Khettar, an Algerian who has lived in Kansas with his family for 13 years, did not make the November trip but has watched the after-effects of the World Cup reshape his daily life.
“Today, when I meet an American and tell him I’m Algerian, he immediately talks to me about the World Cup,” he says. “Even at the football pitch, if one of us is wearing the national team shirt, Americans come up and say they know we’re Algerian and they’re happy to meet us. That didn’t exist before.”
He describes how, when fires broke out in Algeria in August, Americans in Kansas asked how to send aid, and donated when collection links were shared. “That didn’t exist before either.”
Elizabeth Moore Aubin, who was US ambassador to Algeria from December 2021 until January 2026, was part of the Lawrence contingent during the tournament and joined the November delegation to Algiers. She visited more than 50 of Algeria’s 58 provinces or “wilayas” during her posting and built a significant online following.
“As two people groups, Americans and Algerians have more in common than they both realise,” she told Al Jazeera.
She added that it was “great to see subnational diplomacy at work”, but said bonds built through sport need institutional support to last.
“Academic, cultural and sports engagements can all help deepen our ties,” she said. “Those ties then mean more economic and cultural exchange. Everyone benefits.”

items.summary:
Mika Baur: Celtic midfielder ruled out for 'considerable' period with ankle ligament damage
The 22-year-old is expected to be out for at least 10 weeks; he injured his ankle in Celtic's win against Kilmarnock before the international break; Martin O'Neill's side return to Scottish Premiership action
items.text:
Mika Baur: Celtic midfielder ruled out for 'considerable' period with ankle ligament damage
The 22-year-old is expected to be out for at least 10 weeks; he injured his ankle in Celtic's win against Kilmarnock before the international break; Martin O'Neill's side return to Scottish Premiership action on Saturday at home to St Mirren
Friday 20 November 2026 15:50, UK
Celtic midfielder Mika Baur faces a lengthy period on the sidelines with an ankle injury.
The German midfielder, who signed from Paderborn in the summer, is facing around ten weeks on the sidelines with the injury.
He left Celtic Park on crutches after he was forced off during their 1-0 win against Kilmarnock before the international break.
Manager Martin O'Neill said: "He'll be out for some considerable time. It's a real shame, he was playing great for us."
"There's talk about ten weeks, but I spoke to Mika yesterday and he's a quick healer. There are things he can't do for a while; his foot's in a boot.
"He was on fire, he was doing great for us. It is a blow and it seemed so innocuous as well.
"I thought he'd been kicked, but it was the other foot he landed on and he's just gone over on it."
Celtic could also be without Benjamin Nygren for Saturday's Scottish Premiership return against St Mirren.
The midfielder missed the second of Sweden's recent double-header, with O'Neill confirming his absence from club training.
He said: "Nygren didn't train today, but we'll see how he is in the morning - he's got a sore heel. He's been feeling it for a couple of weeks."
Celtic face a gruelling five-match stretch of games over the next two weeks, with a visit to Portugal to face Torreense in the Europa League after St Mirren.
They then travel to Hearts, live on Sky Sports, before taking on Dundee at Dens Park, then a home game against St Johnstone.
The defending champions are four points ahead of Old Firm rivals Rangers at the top of the Premiership, having played a game more.

items.title: Why injured Joao Pedro may be Chelsea's most important player
items.summary:
Why injured Joao Pedro may be Chelsea's most important player
- Published
Who is Chelsea's most important player?
Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.
The debate star
items.text:
Why injured Joao Pedro may be Chelsea's most important player
- Published
Who is Chelsea's most important player?
Cole Palmer and Moises Caicedo are names that would probably feature in any debate, but Joao Pedro's recent absence has certainly strengthened the argument in his favour.
The debate started again among Blues fans over the past couple of weeks following their 1-0 defeat by Sunderland, the latest in a run of poor results without the Brazil striker.
The 25-year-old will miss Leeds United's visit on Saturday with a thigh injury after Chelsea lost three of their previous four matches without him, although one defeat came in a penalty shootout against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.
Having suffered a 2-0 home defeat by Tottenham in that run, manager Xabi Alonso has faced criticism over his side's lack of identity and some of his personnel decisions, particularly when attempting to replace Joao Pedro.
Danny Welbeck, who was expected to provide cover after his summer arrival from Brighton, has started only one Premier League match during Joao Pedro's injury absence.
Instead, Pedro Neto has twice been deployed through the middle, in the home win over Manchester United and the defeat by Sunderland, while Morgan Rogers started as the central striker against Spurs.
Striker Emmanuel Emegha, signed from Strasbourg over the summer, hasn't started a league game but has struggled with fitness issues of his own.
The continued absence of Joao Pedro is certainly proving costly before the busy winter schedule, with fifth-placed Chelsea already 11 points behind Premier League leaders Arsenal.
Having been handed both a new contract until 2034 and the number nine shirt vacated by Liam Delap in August, Chelsea regard their £55m signing from Brighton in 2025 as a key figure in Alonso's plans.
Asked about scoring more goals without the striker on Friday, Alonso said: "Yes, we need the whole team for that. It's not just the strikers who can score, we can score in set-pieces from defenders, midfielders, so it's teamwork for sure.
"Joao is an important player but we need to be this time without him. So far we have tried different options and we need to keep trying. I think that there are more explanations for one defeat than missing just one player.
"The other players, they need to step up and they need to show that they are ready to compete and ready to play for Chelsea."
Does the data back up Joao Pedro's importance?
There is little doubt Alonso has suffered when Joao Pedro has been unavailable, as did his predecessors. The numbers are undeniable.
- Since the start of the 2025-26 Premier League season, Chelsea have averaged 1.8 goals per game with Joao Pedro, compared to 0.6 without.
- Their expected goals (xG) drop from 1.8 per game with him to 1.1 without, highlighting a decline in Chelsea's attacking output rather than simply their finishing.
- Chelsea average 4.8 shots on target per game when the Brazilian plays, compared with 3.9 when he does not.
- Chelsea have failed to score in only 12.2% of Premier League matches involving him, compared with 71.4% when he has been absent.
Those numbers are also reflected in the results.
- Chelsea have lost without scoring in just 7.3% of league games featuring Joao Pedro, compared with 71.4% without him. Three of their Premier League defeats this season were without him, while they have scored in every game that he has featured.
- Chelsea's points-per-game average falls from 1.5 to 0.9 when he is unavailable.
Joao Pedro, who has also operated as a number 10 and on the wing for Chelsea, appears to improve the output of those around him.
During the past season and a half, Palmer has played 2,317 Premier League minutes alongside him and 528 without him.
Palmer has scored 12 goals and registered four assists with the Brazil forward in the side, equating to 0.6 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Without him, Palmer has managed one goal and no assists, equivalent to 0.2 goal involvements per 90.
Palmer's chance creation actually increases when Joao Pedro is absent, rising from 1.4 chances created per 90 minutes to 1.9. However, his goals return falls from 0.5 per 90 to 0.2, suggesting the striker's presence is more closely linked to Palmer's goalscoring output than his creativity.
The pair have developed a productive partnership. Joao Pedro has assisted four Palmer goals, while Palmer has provided three assists to the ex-Brighton forward..
There is less data available for Rogers given his more recent arrival, but the trend is similar.
Rogers has played 523 Premier League minutes alongside Joao Pedro and 360 without him. With Joao Pedro available, Rogers averages 0.7 goals per 90 minutes and 0.9 goal involvements per 90. Without him, those figures fall to 0.3 goal involvements per 90.
While the sample size remains relatively small, the figures suggest Chelsea's attacking players generally produce more when Joao Pedro plays.
All three of his assists this season have been for either Rogers or Palmer, sparking early season excitement about Chelsea's new trio, with nicknames like 'JP Morgan' and 'CPR' having been given to them.
With 20 goals and eight assists, Joao Pedro has been directly involved in 36.4% of Chelsea's 77 Premier League goals since joining the club.
Whether he is the Blues' most important player remains open to debate.
The statistics do show, however, that their points return with him in the side is consistent with Champions League qualification, whereas their return without him is not.
Alonso's team have yet to demonstrate they can perform at the same level when the Brazilian is unavailable.

items.title: Alcaraz shrugs off fitness issues as he beats Cobolli in 65 minutes
items.summary:
ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz shrugs off fitness issues to ease past Flavio Cobolli and complete flawless group-stage record
Carlos Alcaraz will now take on Ben Shelton in the semi-finals of the ATP Finals; he topped the Ivan Lendl Group with a flawless 3-0 record after beating Flavio Cobolli on Friday
items.text:
ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz shrugs off fitness issues to ease past Flavio Cobolli and complete flawless group-stage record
Carlos Alcaraz will now take on Ben Shelton in the semi-finals of the ATP Finals; he topped the Ivan Lendl Group with a flawless 3-0 record after beating Flavio Cobolli on Friday; watch the ATP Finals on Sky Sports
Friday 20 November 2026 15:46, UK
Carlos Alcaraz didn't appear bothered by his various fitness issues as he extended his winning streak to 12 matches after beating debutant Flavio Cobolli 6-4 6-1 at the ATP Finals on Friday in just 65 minutes.
Alcaraz had already booked his spot in the semi-finals of the tournament following his victory against Daniil Medvedev, with the Spaniard now set to face Ben Shelton at the elite eight-man end-of-season event.
The seven-time Grand Slam champion broke the Italian's serve in the opening game of both sets and ended points quickly on his way to posting a flawless 3-0 record in the round-robin stage.

- Download Sky Sports app for analysis, news and video 📺

Alcaraz needed just 65 minutes to win his latest match and clocked up 29 winners in the process.
"I tried to play as aggressive as I can; hitting the ball as hard as I could, trying not to move that much," Alcaraz said.
Alcaraz had an elastic black band on his injured left thigh and a strip of tape on his right knee.
He appeared to sustain the injury during his match against Medvedev. It heightened concerns about his fitness, with Alcaraz having already missed four and a half months of the season due to a right wrist injury.
"The challenge now is not on the court, it's off the court," Alcaraz said. "To do whatever it takes to be in a good shape, to feel physically ready for tomorrow.
"It's going to be a really important half a day that I have ahead of me with my team, with my physio, with the doctor," Alcaraz added.
The semi-final will be a rematch of the US Open quarter-final between Shelton and Alcaraz. While Shelton won that five-set clash in New York, Alcaraz recently got revenge at the Paris Masters final.
In the other semi-final, top-ranked Alexander Zverev will face the winner of tonight's clash between Medvedev and Frances Tiafoe, which is live on Sky Sports Tennis,
Alcaraz is attempting to win the trophy at the ATP Finals for the first time. He lost to Jannik Sinner, who is currently out with a right knee injury, in the final a year ago.
"The way that I felt on the court today was incredible," Alcaraz said. "I'm getting more confident after every match."
'It was a shot-making extravaganza from Alcaraz'
Sky Sports Tennis' Tim Henman said:
"It was an incredible shot-making extravaganza from Alcaraz.
"He's got that in his locker; we knew he was into the semi-finals, but if he was to write the script for a match that he came into with a bit of an injury, I mean, that was absolutely perfect.
"It was an hour and five minutes; he didn't really have any extended rallies. I think there were only one or two that were over nine shots. His timing was exquisite, so job done today, that's for sure."
Speaking on Cobolli, Henman added:
"Cobolli has had a tough few days here. Obviously, playing at home and the matches haven't gone his way.
"He just didn't have enough in his locker to have an impact on Alcaraz."

Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola
